News.title: Hero Oregon teacher breaks silence and recalls terrifying moment she wrestled school shooter for gun after he killed 4
News.content:
Next

A HERO teacher has recounted the terrifying moment she tackled a teenage gunman who opened fire at an elementary school, killing four.

Three children, aged five, eight and 11, were shot dead alongside a teacher in the horrifying rampage at an Oregon elementary school on October 15.



Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were left fighting for their lives after the school shooter force his way inside Silver Rail Elementary School.

Elementary teacher Cassidy Schutz, 28, recalled how she tackled mass shooter Griffin J. John to the ground and wrestled him for his gun.





In an emotional statement released by Bend-La Pine School District on Friday, she said: “There are no words to describe the depth of sadness I am feeling following the events of October 15th.

“This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives.”

Describing the deadly rampage, she said: “It all happened so fast, and I wish with everything in me that we had more time.

“The pain of this loss I will carry with me forever.”



Police Chief Mike Krantz hailed Cassidy as one of the heroes who helped stop the gunman, a former student at the school, from committing more harm.

Speaking at a press conference after the mass shooting he said: “She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed.”

Police sources claimed the teen was using a large pump-action shotgun purchased by his mum.



The horrifying kill spree was ended after hero dad Kaylub Giamanco burst into a classroom and saw Cassidy battling with the teenage killer – before shooting him dead.

Police were first alerted to the attack at 12.59pm.

Three minutes later desperate cops had swooped in on the school – but it was already too late for the victims.

Three pupils, one of who has been named as Rhoam Summer, 5, were found dead as well as teacher and volleyball coach Megan Lambert, 25.

Wheel-chair bound Saylor Graham-Poarch, 7, has recently been moved out of intensive car after being shot in the face.



Teacher Becky Drury, 54, had her hand almost completely severed by the gunfire and has previously said she survived by playing dead.

In shocking recollections, the teacher said she raced to lock her classroom door – but the shooter “was already there”.

Becky added: “Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.

“Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else” she said in a statement to KPTV.



The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a national database.

News.title: Hospitals ‘broken into’ sparking fears ‘vulnerable’ patients’ information could be leaked online – as cops launch probe
News.content:
SECURITY 'BREACH' Hospitals ‘broken into’ sparking fears ‘vulnerable’ patients’ information could be leaked online – as cops launch probe







Next

NHS bosses have hit out at urban explorers who allegedly broke into two hospitals and filmed inside areas containing sensitive patient records.

The individuals reportedly entered secure areas at St Cadoc’s Hospital in Caerleon and St Woolos Hospital in Newport.



Cops have now launched a probe into the alleged incidents after those thought to be responsible videoed inside the sites and shared the footage on social media.

Some of the areas accessed are understood to contain sensitive information, including historic patient records, WalesOnline reports.



Health board bosses have been left “concerned” and condemned the incidents.

They warned the sites are not abandoned buildings, but working hospitals with vulnerable patients and staff inside.

Gwent Police is understood to be investigating the break-ins.

Aneurin Bevan University Health Board (ABUHB) said it had been forced to increase security at both sites following the “distressing” incidents.

It also confirmed it was working with police to support their investigation and had contacted the Information Commissioner’s Office.

Jenny Winslade, the health board’s executive director of nursing and deputy chief executive, said: “Like many of our staff and patients, I was deeply concerned and upset to learn that individuals unlawfully entered areas of St Cadoc’s Hospital and St Woolos Hospital again over the weekend and then shared the footage online.



“To be clear, these are hospitals with vulnerable patients and staff, and not abandoned buildings as is being claimed.

“These hospitals care for some of the most vulnerable people in our communities.

“Patients and their families rightly expect to feel safe, secure, and treated with dignity when they are in our care.

“Seeing individuals accessing clinical environments illegally is understandably distressing for patients, families, and staff alike.”

She added that the incidents had also left hospital workers feeling anxious about their own safety.



Ms Winslade said: “Our staff come to work every day to care for others, and incidents like this can leave people feeling anxious and concerned about their own safety and security.

“Nobody should feel like this.

“We want to be clear that individuals gained entry unlawfully, and there is now a criminal investigation by the police.

“We have already increased security measures across both sites to provide additional reassurance and protection.”

The health board said the extra security measures came at a significant cost to the NHS.



It warned the money would otherwise have been available to support patient services, particularly as the health board remains in a critical incident due to operational pressures.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ms Winslade added: “While these measures are necessary, they come at a significant cost and require resources that would always be better directed towards patient care and supporting our communities.

“Our focus remains on keeping our patients, families, and staff safe, and we will continue to work closely with the police and other partners as their investigation progresses.”

News.title: E-bike rider, 15, dies after being struck by Audi in horror crash – as devastated mum pays tribute to ‘light of my life’
News.content:
'MY NUMBER ONE' E-bike rider, 15, dies after being struck by Audi in horror crash – as devastated mum pays tribute to ‘light of my life’







Next

A HEARTBROKEN mum has paid moving tribute to her 15-year-old son after he died in a horror collision.

The boy – who was named today as Harley Hartley – was riding his off-road e-bike on October 1 in Bradford, West Yorkshire, when he was involved in a collision with a black Audi S3.

Harley was taken to hospital with serious injuries after the collision at about 5.30pm.

But despite the best efforts of doctors, he sadly died from his injuries on October 28.





Paying tribute to her son Harley, his mother said she had been “left numb, broken-hearted, every emotion you could ever feel”.

She said: “I always longed for a boy and after three girls I finally got him, my life felt complete.

“Chunky 9lb 2oz blue-eyed boy. He would do anything for anyone, all you had to do was ask.

“My son, the light of my life, you knew exactly how to play me to get anything and everything you wanted.



“You will forever be my number one, I got you son always, love Mum.”

The Major Collision Enquiry Team is investigating and continuing to appeal for witnesses.

Officers are urging anyone who witnessed the collision, or who saw the movements of either vehicle prior to it, to contact them.

Anyone with footage which may assist this investigation is also asked to make contact.



Information can be given on 101, or via the Live Chat facility on our website, quoting reference 13260559556.

News.title: Teacher, 36, who had BABY with her student, 13, pleads guilty as she faces five years in jail
News.content:
TWISTED MISS Teacher, 36, who had BABY with her student, 13, pleads guilty as she faces five years in jail







Next

A NEW Jersey primary school teacher who gave birth to her 13-year-old student’s baby has pleaded guilty in the sexual abuse case.

Laura Caron, 36, is facing five years in prison on charges she raped the boy, who insists he is not a victim and demands that her charges are dropped.



“They need to drop all charges. I wasn’t groomed or raped or manipulated by her,” he told the Daily Mail. “She never initiated anything.

“I started everything. If it was up to me she wouldn’t have been in jail. It’s been six or seven years. I’m 19 about to be 20.”



Part of the defendant’s bail conditions include having no contact with the baby’s alleged father.

“I can’t talk to them. I wish I could but I can’t and it sucks,” he said.

What has also been troubling him is seeing Caron being called a “predator” in the media.

The two first met when she taught him and his brother fifth grade at the Middle Township Elementary School in Cape May Court House.

The family remained close with the teacher – even allowing their two sons and daughter to have sleepovers at her home, according to the Daily Mail.

Prosecutors say their relationship began when he was aged 11 in 2016 and continued until he was 15.



He moved in with Caron when he was just 11, and she got pregnant two years later.

The boy’s sister said she remembered going to sleep with her brother in the same room – but woke up to find him in Caron’s bed, the criminal complaint alleges.

She added that the teacher started sleeping with her brother when he was 11 years old.



Keeping the abusive relationship a secret, Caron supposedly told friends at a baby shower that the father was “out of the picture”.

When the boy’s father saw a photo of Caron’s daughter on Facebook, he was alarmed by the likeness with his son.

He contacted the authorities and the police opened an investigation.

The boy now blames his father for the fallout and for the teacher being jailed.

He says they are now estranged, adding: “‘All of this started with a Facebook post from my father. I didn’t want her violated like that.”



Caron, a former basketball player at Pennsylvania’s Cabrini University, was charged in January, 2025, with aggravated sexual assault, sexual assault and endangering the welfare of a child.

Cape May County Prosecutor Jeffrey H. Sutherland confirmed she has now pleaded guilty to the charge of second degree Endangering the Welfare of a Child with Sexual Conduct.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Teachers hold a position of great trust, and the allegations in this case represent a deeply troubling breach of that trust,” Sutherland said in his announcement.

Her sentencing will take place at the start of next year.

News.title: PM ‘tinkered around edges’ & failed to deal with welfare and defence, blast voters in damning Budget poll
News.content:
NOT ENOUGH PM ‘tinkered around edges’ & failed to deal with welfare and defence, blast voters in damning Budget poll







Next

MOST BRITS think the Budget just “tinkered around the edges” and failed to solve our economic problems.

It was also seen to benefit people on welfare handouts more than the working class.

While the vast majority of Brits think we are still woefully underprepared for a military attack.



The shocking findings are contained in a new snap Budget poll carried out by More In Common and UCL Policy Lab and shared with The Sun on Sunday.



The survey suggests Andy Burnham’s “breathing space” Budget has failed to live up to the new PM’s promises of sweeping change.

Although he has managed to avoid the massive backlash Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves encountered after their big tax-hiking fiscal statements.

Luke Tryl, More in Common’s executive director, said: “People certainly think Burnham ‘gets it’ a lot more than his predecessor.



“But they also want to see that there’s a serious, long-term plan to fix Britain.

“And people think the Budget has left big questions – particularly on welfare and defence – unanswered.”

Mr Burnham was installed as PM on a promise to tear up the political status quo and “end 40 years of neo-liberalism”.



Chancellor John Healey unveiled his Budget on Wednesday, which avoided the big tax rises of Rachel Reeves – although taxes on banks and gambling went up.

Its most eye-catching giveaway was a £100 energy bailout to 20 million Brits.

But the poll revealed that 60 per cent of Brits think the Budget just “tinkered with small things”.

Some 46 per cent said it was “not radical enough” to deal with the country’s economic problems while 43 per cent said it was “too short-term”.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget – delivered on Wednesday – would benefit the “working people of Britain”.



But in a blow to No11, the poll of 1,749 adults suggests the country thinks it favours people on welfare.

Benefit claimants are the group most often named as the Budget’s main beneficiaries, at 23 per cent.

Just 17 per cent said the main beneficiaries are the working class.

And just 9 per cent said the middle class – suggesting the ‘Squeezed Middle’ are feeling particularly hammered by Labour’s tax and spend policies.

On defence, Mr Healey said he would increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030 – but refused to say how he would pay for it until next year’s Spending Review.



Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has accused No10 of failing to invest the cash needed to make the UK resilient to foreign threats, and the poll suggests Brits agree with her.

A staggering 61 per cent say Britain is not resilient to military threats from another country, like Russia.

Some 68 per cent say we are vulnerable to a large-scale cyber attack on the NHS, banks or the government.

While 67 per cent say we are not resilient to a global economic shock, 66 per cent say we are not resilient to a widespread power cut and 62 per cent say we are vulnerable to extreme weather like flooding or droughts.



The government has launched a national campaign urging Brits to prepare for disasters by having an emergency stash of cash, food and water at home.

But the poll’s findings suggest the public still feel massively under prepared for these threats.

In a finding that will raise alarm bells in Downing Street, the poll also found that Brits think the Budget falls short of the PM’s radical promises.

Researchers asked about 11 policy promises Mr Burnham had made – from bringing down the cost of living, to getting growth in every postcode and ending 40 years of neoliberalism.

On every single one of these issues, more Brits said the Budget fell short of the PM’s promise than lived up to it.



On bringing down the cost of living, 51 per cent of Brits said the Budget failed and 27 per cent said it lived up to the PM’s pledge.

On reducing the benefits bill, 49 per cent said it failed while just 19 per cent said it succeeded.

And on improving Britain’s defence and security, 42 per cent said it failed while 24 per cent said it lived up to promises.

James Cartlidge, Tory shadow defence secretary, slammed Mr Healey’s failure to properly fund defence in the Budget.

He said it is outrageous that Mr Healey – who quit as Defence Secretary over Keir Starmer’s refusal to find more cash for defence – has not found a penny more.



He said: “Andy Burnham and John Healey bottled it. They have failed to properly fund defence right when the world is at the most dangerous it has been in years. While they are letting the welfare bill spiral out of control.

“They have failed Britain.”

But the survey was not all bad news for the new Prime Minister.

LUKE TRYL: Budget poll reveals £100 off bill smight not cut it Andy Burnham and John Healey might breathe a sigh of relief after their first Budget this week. They have avoided the backlash of last year’s Budget, and their big policy is aimed squarely on the thing most Briton’s care about – sky high energy bills and the cost of living, where they now have a big lead over the other parties. But many Britons, don’t think £100 off their bills isn’t enough to cut it. As one woman in a focus group on the night of the budget told us, the policy was a “lovely gesture”, but one that won’t even touch the sides with bills set to rise again this winter. She’s not alone: three in five Britons say the Budget is tinkering around the edges, while less than one in five say that it is dealing with the big problems the country is facing. Perhaps most risky for Burnham, most don’t think the Budget is living up to the promises he’s made: only a quarter say it delivers on his pledge to bring down the cost of living, and few think it will make a difference to the economy. That’s not too say that Brits don’t appreciate small, everyday improvements, and they certainly think Burnham ‘gets it’ a lot more than his predecessor. But they also want to see that there’s a serious, long-term plan to fix Britain. And people think Budget has left big questions – particularly on welfare on defence unanswered Only a quarter of Britons think that the government has a clear plan get the benefits bill down – something voters of all stripes are worried about. And people on benefits are one of the only groups that people tend to think will benefit from this Budget. Meanwhile Kemi Badenoch’s may have struck a chord when she took aim at Healey – arguing that Britain lacked resilience to deal with a crisis. Asked about a range of scenarios, from international economic shocks to a cyberattack or extreme weather, most Brits say the UK does not feel resilient and there is worry about the future. Burnham has convince people he cares, that’s no mean feat in politics and this Budge that avoided some of the public opinion clangers of recent years. The challenge now is proving that he’s got a real plan to keep Britain safe and deliver the change he promised.

Andy Burnham and John Healey’s approval ratings remain about the same as they were before the Budget, with 43 per cent saying the PM is doing a good job while 30 per cent say he is doing a bad job.



And around half of those surveyed – 48 per cent – say the Budget was neither better or worse than they expected.

Mr Healey to avoid announcing big tax hikes which did so much to wreck the reputation of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

Instead he decided to raid the country’s piggy bank by cutting the UK’s fiscal ‘headroom’ instead.

The poll suggests that this has saved him from the post Budget backlash the Starmer-Reeves regime suffered.

Just 32 per cent expect the Budget to have a negative impact on them personally – compared to 50 per cent last year.



And 30 per cent said Mr Healey had done well in delivering the Budget compared to 26 per cent who think he did badly.

Last year, just 23 per cent said Ms Reeves had done well and 44 per cent said she had done badly.

Mr Tryl added: “Andy Burnham has convinced people he cares, that’s no mean feat in politics.

“And this Budget avoided some of the public opinion clangers of recent years.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The challenge now is proving that he’s got a real plan to keep Britain safe and deliver the change he promised.”

News.title: M6 closed after van fire erupts and ‘significant’ amount of fuel spills on road – as drivers warned of hour-long delays
News.content:
TRAVEL CHAOS M6 closed after van fire erupts and ‘significant’ amount of fuel spills on road – as drivers warned of hour-long delays







Next

THE M6 has been closed after a van fire erupted and a “significant” amount of diesel spilled across the carriageway.

Emergency services and contractors are at the scene dealing with the blaze and treating the road surface following the spillage.

The motorway is slammed shut southbound between junction six at Gravelly Hill Interchange and junction five near Castle Bromwich in the West Midlands.

The closures were put in place at 4pm to allow the vehicle to be recovered and the carriageway made safe.





Drivers have been warned to expect delays of up to an hour on the approach.

A National Highways spokesperson said: “The M6 in the West Midlands is closed southbound between J6 (Gravelly Hill Interchange) and J5 (near Castle Bromwich) following a van fire and a significant diesel spillage, with closures implemented at 4pm to allow emergency services and contractors to treat the road surface and recover the vehicle.”

News.title: How Xmas market hotspot is world’s newest Narco State – kids as young as SIX recruited into AK-47-wielding TikTok gangs
News.content:
Next

A TODDLER pedals through the streets on a tricycle, clutching a mobile phone as he keeps watch for police.

Nearby, teenage gunmen armed with Kalashnikovs are fighting bloody turf wars over drug-dealing hotspots, while children barely old enough for secondary school wield military-grade guns and launch grenades.



But this is not some cartel-ravaged corner of South America.

It is the sinister underbelly of Belgium, where criminal kingpins are turning a favourite British winter getaway into a battleground for Europe’s booming drugs trade.

And fuelling the gangland gold rush is a tidal wave of potent “Cali weed” smuggled across the Atlantic from Canada, with Belgian customs seizing a staggering 32 tonnes of cannabis in 2025 – a 500 per cent surge from the previous year.



Once dubbed Europe’s cocaine capital, Antwerp has seen cannabis seizures overtake cocaine for the first time, fuelling fresh fears that Belgium is sliding towards becoming a “narco state,” a judge has warned.

The term refers to a nation whose economy relies on the drug trade and government corruption to survive.

Belgian criminologist Professor Jelle Janssens told The Sun: “I think we are somewhere at the beginning and the middle of criminal organisations gaining a foothold in Belgium, and they are here to stay, and work towards this criminal governance.”

Meanwhile, European port security and transnational trafficking expert Eski Yarin warned of the growing violence linked to the booming drug trade.

He told The Sun: “The main risk of drug trafficking is that there’s more and more, often violent, crime involved – like the use of arms.”



Professor Anna Sergei, an expert in sociology of law and deviance, added: “In Antwerp it has mostly taken the form of explosives and shots aimed at houses as warnings.”

But the bloody turf wars have spread far beyond Antwerp’s docks, with rival gangs battling for control of lucrative drug-dealing hotspots across Brussels.

Among the areas caught in the crossfire is Saint-Gilles, a neighbourhood near the Eurostar station connecting the Belgian capital directly to London St Pancras.

Behind its picturesque cobbled squares, bustling restaurants and cafés, residents have been left terrified by the escalating violence.



Restaurant owner Salvatore recalled the horrifying moment bullets ripped through the neighbourhood as families with children dined on his terrace.

He told the BBC: “We dropped to the floor. I had clients eating on the terrace with children”.

It was the third shooting to rock the area in just three days, prompting him to ask: “Are we in an American gangster movie? This needs to stop.”

Drug gangs are openly flogging narcotics in broad daylight beside children’s playgrounds in Brussels, with dealers raking in up to £43,000 a day just 400 metres from a police station.



Janssens revealed that children as young as six who are playing around the area are being offered £175 (€200) to spy on police, while officers have even reported toddlers pedalling around on tricycles with mobile phones as gang lookouts.

He told The Sun: “Police officers told me that toddlers were being used. Toddlers on the tricycles pedalling away with cell phones.”

And the youngsters are not simply watching from the sidelines, with children aged just 14 and 15 arrested amid a wave of shootings involving AK-47s and other military weapons.

Janssens, an organised crime expert at Ghent University, warned that Brussels was facing an “increasing number of shootings and casualties” as rival gangs battled for control of the city’s streets.



The violence has spread into residential neighbourhoods, where dealers operate makeshift drug markets known as “fours” – French for “an oven” – while lookouts watch for approaching cops.

The French drug slang refers to a highly active, fixed drug-dealing location, typically operating in housing estates, public parks, or urban street corners.

Experts say the idea is inspired by notorious drug hotspots in Marseille and Naples, with gangs throwing grenades and shooting relentlessly.

One blast targeting a shisha bar involved in the dirty drug rift in St Gilles instead shattered 15 windows at a nearby pre-school, while another explosion damaged around ten cars.



Brussels recorded 102 shootings in 2025, with another 62 reported by the time of the investigation, alongside 22 explosions.

And prosecutors fear the violence is far from over.

Brussels chief prosecutor Julien Moinil warned: “So is it going to stop? I don’t think so. Do you think it’s going to calm down? No. Are there risks of new shootings? Yes. And are there risks for citizens? Yes.”

Police also intercepted two suspects armed with Kalashnikovs and handguns in a Saint-Gilles park following a string of shootings in August, while gunmen opened fire on a police station in neighbouring Anderlecht.

More than 200 drug-dealing hotspots have been identified across Brussels, where gangs openly sell crack and cocaine as rival gunmen battle for control of lucrative patches.



One local resident, Murielle, described how the trade had exploded in recent months, with customers even queuing to buy drugs.

She told the BBC: “Things have changed in the past six months. The business has intensified. Sometimes you even see consumers queuing to buy drugs. And now gangs are fighting over this spot.”

And the bloodshed has reached the police themselves, with two gunmen on a scooter spraying a station with bullets from what appeared to be an AK-47 before speeding away.



Expert Janssens said some hotspots were “very, very lucrative”, as drug dealers rake in up to £43,000 a day.

Janssens revealed that dealers approach homeless migrants and asylum seekers sleeping rough in Brussels, offering them free drugs before trapping them in a cycle of addiction.

He said gangsters initially offer a sympathetic ear, allegedly telling desperate people: “Hi brother, we know you’re in pain, have some. It’s on the house.”

But after several days of free handouts, the dealers start demanding they “work for it” and start selling to their new customers when they come back for another dose.

The ruthless recruitment drive extends to children, with cops uncovering a TikTok video offering youngsters aged six to 12 €200 for a Wednesday afternoon watching for police, Janssens said.



Jurgen de Landsheer, another local resident told the BBC: “We see a lot of young people getting paid a few hundred euros. They get a weapon, AK-47 or other heavy weapon, and then they get a mission. To shoot a person in the leg, for example, or to try to kill somebody. And they get very little money for this.

“The biggest danger is a stray bullet.”

Others are recruited through Snapchat and Telegram to retrieve hidden narcotics from shipping containers, move drugs through the streets or carry out attacks on rival gangs.



Professor Sergei said around a quarter of those arrested in the cases she described were minors, many of whom were abandoned by their bosses when caught.

And the young recruits are becoming “younger and cheaper”, according to port security expert Eski, with jobs that once earned around £1,000 now reportedly being carried out for a few hundred euros.

He told The Sun: “The people behind it safeguard themselves by having these armies of kids doing their dirty work. Whether it’s taking the drugs out or having a turf fight.”

But the criminal kingpins are not just putting drugs into children’s hands.

Some are being armed with deadly Cobra fireworks and grenades to unleash devastating attacks on the homes and businesses of rival gangsters.



Eski said youngsters were being tasked with “placing firework Cobras, like semi-bombs, or grenades in front of shops of rival gangs.”

Professor Sergei warned: “In Antwerp it has mostly taken the form of explosives and shots aimed at houses as warnings.”

The weapons have turned quiet residential streets into battlegrounds, with research finding heavy fireworks banned for consumer use involved in around 80 per cent of explosive attacks examined.

And innocent families are being caught in the crossfire.

In January 2023, an 11-year-old girl was killed in Merksem, Antwerp, after gunmen opened fire on a garage door at a property reportedly linked to a relative of a wanted drug trafficker.



The previous year, an Albanian smuggler with fake British papers was assassinated in broad daylight.

On Christmas Eve of 2023, a teenage firebomber unleashed a devastating attack on De Nachtegaal restaurant in Antwerp, forcing owner Nathan Steveniers and his girlfriend to leap from their first-floor balcony as flames engulfed the building.

The 17-year-old attacker later admitted carrying out the bombing for cash but refused to reveal his payment, while getaway driver Sumeet P., 31, was jailed for six years.



Cops had initially stopped the pair in a BMW shortly after the explosion but let them go despite smelling petrol, only to catch them later in the Netherlands.

The restaurant was gutted and never reopened, with Sumeet also ordered to pay £159,605 in damages.

But behind the bloodshed lies a sprawling international drugs empire exploiting Belgium’s position as one of Europe’s busiest shipping gateways.

The latest gold rush centres on Canadian cannabis, with Chinese-linked gangs accused of exploiting the country’s legal marijuana industry to disguise vast illegal growing operations as legitimate medical farms, The Telegraph reported.

Since recreational cannabis was legalised under former prime minister Justin Trudeau in 2018, smugglers have allegedly used medical production permits to conceal industrial-scale cultivation before shipping the potent drug to Europe.



With Canada’s saturated market driving down prices, marijuana worth around £800 per kilogram can fetch £4,500 once it reaches Europe, according to Belgium’s customs chief Kristian Vanderwaeren.

The lucrative cargo travels through Canadian ports including Vancouver, Montreal, Halifax and St John’s before crossing the Atlantic to Antwerp.

Janssens confirmed Belgian police had detected a growing influx of cannabis from Canada, describing “some sort of new route that has opened”.

And it seems “Cali-weed”, a stronger version of the illegal narcotic, has been a popular demand.

Eski said: “California weed is known for its high quality, because of the vegetation over there and because of the weather.”



But the criminal trade is not limited to cannabis and cocaine, with Belgian and Dutch gangs also churning out ecstasy and amphetamines for export to Britain and Latin America.

Janssens revealed that a single ecstasy laboratory could rake in £870,000 (€1million) in a year, while traffickers are developing increasingly sophisticated ways to disguise shipments.

Some drugs are concealed inside clothing using substances that can later be extracted and reconstructed in specialist laboratories, allowing smugglers to move narcotics disguised as ordinary goods.

And while Antwerp acts as a gateway into Europe, Janssens estimated that around 80 per cent of drugs entering the port were destined for other countries, leaving roughly a fifth in Belgium.

Behind the shipments is a tangled web of international crime clans, with Albanian-speaking syndicates, Italy’s notorious ’Ndrangheta and Dutch-based Moroccan networks all involved in the trade.



Janssens said around 40 per cent of communications intercepted during the Sky ECC encrypted-phone investigation were in Albanian or regional dialects, exposing the influence of criminal groups linked to Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia.

The so-called Mocro Maffia, meanwhile, built its fortunes smuggling cannabis and hashish from Morocco’s Rif region before expanding into cocaine around a decade ago.

And Russian-linked criminal networks have increasingly offered “crime as a service”, supplying forged documents and weapons to other gangs, Janssens warned.

He also pointed to reports from France alleging criminal groups had carried out killings on behalf of Russian military intelligence, highlighting the growing overlap between organised crime and wider geopolitical threats.

But Belgium’s biggest weakness may lie inside the very ports responsible for keeping its economy moving.



Bart Willocx, the president of the Antwerp court of appeal told The Guardian: “The amount of money that is involved – to influence people, to corrupt people and to bribe – it is so big that it is really a danger for the stability of our society”.

Criminal syndicates are bribing dock workers, exploiting security passes and manipulating container movements to sneak lucrative shipments past customs officers.

Corrupt employees can pocket around £40,000 for rerouting a single container, while others are blackmailed through threats against their families.

Eski said: “These port employees, these dockers, are corrupt to the bone.”

The expert warned that gangsters use “social engineering” to identify vulnerable workers, sometimes recruiting former employees to target old colleagues or threatening them with photographs of their children.



Janssens said the criminal infiltration goes even deeper, with gangs planting insiders in legitimate companies and encouraging students to enrol in maritime logistics courses to gain access to the shipping industry.

He warned of “infiltration in government services” and private businesses, with criminal recruits operating as secret “Trojan horses”.

And even Belgium’s prisons are struggling to keep the gangsters at bay.

Janssens claimed prison guards are being offered €8,000 to smuggle smartphones into jails, allowing criminal bosses to maintain contact with their networks from behind bars.

Those who refuse can face threats against their families, echoing Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar’s notorious “silver or lead” ultimatum – you either take the bribe or face execution.



At Haren prison, one of Belgium’s newest jails, Janssens claimed just 200 guards were working despite a requirement for 400, leaving overstretched staff vulnerable to intimidation.

He warned: “They’re all afraid. They’re all being pressured, they’re all being intimidated.”

And the criminologist fears Belgium could eventually produce its own version of notorious Dutch-Moroccan cartel kingpin Ridouan Taghi, whose criminal network became known as the “oiled killing machine”.

Janssens said the country had not yet reached that level of organised violence but warned: “We could be, if we’re not careful.”

He recalled the horrifying discovery in the Netherlands of a shipping container converted into a torture chamber, complete with a dentist’s chair allegedly intended for pulling out victims’ teeth and nails.



And as the criminal empire grows, Belgium’s justice system is struggling to keep up.

Janssens revealed Brussels prosecutors had warned parliament that the country’s overstretched authorities were losing ground to the gangs.

He quoted their bleak assessment: “Criminals are laughing with us.”

Despite working at full capacity, prosecutors were unable to tackle the growing threat, he said, warning: “Basically we’re losing this fight.”

News.title: Farmer strangled 82-year-old dad and buried him on family land after row over being ‘cut out of will’
News.content:
‘I SAW RED’ Farmer strangled 82-year-old dad and buried him on family land after row over being ‘cut out of will’







Next

A FARMER strangled his dad to death and buried him in a shallow grave on family land after fearing he would be “cut out of the will”.

Charles Wright, 52, had a “blazing row” with his 82-year-old dad, Brian, over the future of Hall Farm in Nottinghamshire before he throttled him on November 20, 2025.



Two days later, Wright took his own life and his body was found in an outbuilding area on Hall Farm in a “tragic” sequence of events.

In a voice note, Wright had said Brian was “thinking of replacing him” and giving the “lion’s share” to another relative.



It continued: “I just had a flash of red and after 25 years and everything I have given him, he was just cutting me out like that.

“I just saw red, dragged him out of the car and throttled him.”

Wright then said he intended to take his own life.

The haunting recording was sent to cops on November 22, two days after his dad was reported missing after failing to show up for his wife’s hospital appointment.



At an inquest at Nottingham Coroner’s Court, Senior Coroner Mairin Casey said: “The horror of this, I’m clear in my mind, will have affected all of those who have survived in a very deep and painful way.”

The court heard that Brian – a churchwarden at St Bartholomew’s Church – had called his son “useless”, “not capable of farming” and that it was a “mistake to let him farm that land”.

Locals previously described the 82-year-old as a “lovely man” who fundraised for the local church.

Describing the recording, Detective Chief Inspector Ruby Burrow said: “Charles stated that he had killed his father and intended to kill himself.

“He described that his father Brian had criticised him and there had been a disagreement about finances.



“He stated he had buried his father Brian on the family farm.”

The churchwarden had been reported missing shortly before midnight on November 20.

The next day, Wright, his brother James and a mechanic at the farm spoke to DCI Burrow about Brian.

Wright told the cop about “difficult family dynamics” and strained relations, including issues around finances, the inquest heard.

“He described an argument he had had with his father. He described his father had been critical towards him and he, himself, had taken some time to calm down,” said DCI Burrow.



Brian was said to have “left in the opposite direction” after a small row between him and Wright.

Later that day, the churchwarden’s vehicle was found in an unusual place, sparking panic about his whereabouts.

DCI Burrow added that a collision had occurred on November 22 involving a “vehicle and two gentlemen”, where the driver colliding with them “apparently deliberately”.

She said that Wright had aimed at his brother, who was running with a friend, and “caused injury”.

Wright ended his life the next day while Brian’s body was found in a shallow grave three days later, with the cause of death given as pressure applied to the neck .



For help and support, call the Samaritans for free from a UK phone, completely anonymously, on 116 123 or go to samaritans.org.

The court also heard how there had been previous friction at the farm, with a firearms licence withdrawn from a relative.

DCI Burrow said: “The evidence shows that Charles Wright murdered his father, and that there was no third-party involvement in the death.

“The evidence showed [Charles] took his own life, and that there was no third-party involvement in that either.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Coroner Ms Casey described it as a “truly tragic case”.



She said: “Whatever tensions there may have been leading to this tragedy, we have here the loss of two men, who were fathers to surviving children, and a grandfather.”

News.title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied frontline city
News.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content.

Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the frontline city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".

Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."

The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.

Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.

Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.

As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.

Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.

"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.

That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.

Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.

Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on busses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.

On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers. Others experienced emotional reunions.

News.title: Emotional reunions with loved ones for Oleshky evacuees
News.content:
People evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky were reunited with their loved ones after crossing from Belarus into Ukraine on Saturday.

This comes as a ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump took effect across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday.

Families were reunited at a site in the region of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine after arriving in buses and ambulances.

They had previously travelled via Crimea and Russia after their evacuation from the Ukrainian town on Friday.

Ceasefire measures will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.

The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from the site in the Chernihiv region, near the northern Ukrainian border with Belarus.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
News.content:
The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.

In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.

Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to Â£11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of Â£13.21 an hour.

In a BBC interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?

"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.

It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.

Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.

"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.

"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."

"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

News.title: 'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final

The winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.

Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the Â£83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities.

"I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.

The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.

Reuniting with Ranganathan on the comedian's BBC Radio 2 show on Saturday morning, Croft said they had been worried about being seen together in public before the final.

"We were having dinner and we're not exactly a likely duo and the whole restaurant was like, 'we like you on Traitors and hope you win'," he said.

Croft added that he had woken up on Saturday "with a light sense that I don't have to keep the secret anymore. It's been killing me".

Ranganathan, 48, started his show by saying: "Last night, I don't know if you're aware, was the finale of The Celebrity Traitors and I won."

He said he was "delighted to win" but admitted he probably wouldn't have done so without Croft convincing him to banish the last remaining traitor, King Kenny.

"It's taken the gloss off it slightly that everybody's saying, 'you better thank [Croft] every day for the rest of your life'," he added, with his typical deadpan-humour.

But 24-year-old Croft said he thought Ranganathan had played the game in a "lovely" way.

"People are seeing how smart you are and how you're actually so on it, and you're such a good judge of character," he praised.

News.title: Europe can no longer rely on US to 'bankroll' its defence, Starmer says
News.content:
Sir Keir Starmer has said Europe should build a common security framework, warning the change in its defence relationship with the US is permanent rather than "an aberration of the Trump presidency".

The former prime minister was speaking at a British Irish Chamber of Commerce (BICC) dinner in Dublin, external on Friday evening.

Sir Keir said a "common security framework" for Europe was needed as much as a common market, with the UK at its centre.

He warned that "things will not go back to the way they were," adding that the US had made clear it will no longer "bankroll" its European allies.

Press Association reported that he told the crowd in Dublin City Hall his comments did not mean "the US relationship is no longer important".

Rather he said the UK-USA military, security and intelligence alliance was "far too strong for that".

But he said Europe must be enabled to "take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security".

"Europe has twice been caught asleep â failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events," he said.

"First when Russia's attack on Ukraine exposed long-standing European weaknesses on defence and security; and second when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up," he added.

He added: "I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

Sir Keir was at the dinner to be awarded an honorary life membership from the BICC.

News.title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
News.content:
As Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.

In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal.

"Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.

From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.

News.title: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
News.content:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.

The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.

One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.

This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.

On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lÃ¨se majestÃ© law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.

This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.

"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

News.title: Responsible or panicked? Meet the people around the world already preparing for crisis
News.content:
Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (Â£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement.

"It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.

A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.

Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.

His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.

Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.

In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.

Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".

News.title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but not reparations
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.

He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".

The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.

It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. As King Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.

During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities.

On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.

"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in a piece for the Guardian, external.

He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation".

He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference".

The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour.

Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.

He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."

In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said: "I do think we have a duty there and saying sorry is always quite a good thing."

Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing".

"Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footingâ¦ it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."

Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point.

"My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.

Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.

Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.

News.title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.

She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care.

The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.

Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.

Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.

In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.

But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.

But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.

The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.

The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.

In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

News.title: Everton striker's relief family not home during burglary
News.content:
Everton striker Thierno Barry has said he was relieved that his family were not at home when it was burgled while he played in a cup match.

His home in Greater Manchester was targeted while he was playing for Everton against Newcastle United in a Carabao Cup tie at the Hill Dickinson stadium on Thursday.

The Frenchman, 24, posted on Instagram "things could have been much worse" had his partner and toddler not been in the stands.

A spokesman for Greater Manchester Police said an investigation was ongoing.

Barry posted that he would not put his family "at risk" in the future by posting about his life on social media.

He said: "Maybe I've been too open about my family's life and mine, potentially putting them at risk, all just to show my lifestyle and inspire others through my journey and success, hoping to motivate them to do the same.

"My childhood was never easy, but I've always believed that when you give yourself the best possible chances, there is always hope.

"Unfortunately, in life, there are people and things beyond our control."

News.title: UK has 'no authority' over case of woman killed by father in US
News.content:
The mother of a British woman who was shot and killed by her father in Texas has been told that police in the UK have "no lawful authority to intervene" as the family tries to find answers.

Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington was shot in the chest on 10 January 2025 in Prosper, Dallas - found by a UK coroner to be an unlawful killing.

However, no criminal case was brought against her father Kris Harrison, after a grand jury in Collin County declined to indict him.

Lucy's mother Jane Coates wrote to Cheshire Police urging them to "gather evidence" here locally, and then "liaise" with US authorities - but the force has responded and said it was "constrained" by law and jurisdiction.

In a letter to Coates, Deputy Chief Constable Mike Evans said: "Whilst we may share the family's concerns and understand their desire for further scrutiny, we have no lawful authority to intervene in decisions taken by those agencies."

Last month, Coates flew to Texas in a bid to meet the district attorney in Collin County and to call on him to reinstate the investigation but was told he would not speak to her.

News.title: Motorcyclist dies after falling into sea in cliffside beauty spot crash
News.content:
A man has died after falling into the sea following a crash involving his motorbike, police have said.

Officers from North Wales Police were called to reports of a crash involving a black motorcycle on Marine Drive on the Great Orme in Llandudno, Conwy county, at about 22:31 GMT on Thursday.

A multi-agency response including police, the RNLI and HM Coastguard was launched and the man was recovered from the water and airlifted to Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor, where he was pronounced dead.

Police are looking to speak to the driver of a black vehicle - possibly a Ford Fiesta - that they believe was in the area at the time.

The incident happened about one mile (1.6km) from the Toll House towards the direction of the Great Orme summit.

The Great Orme is a headland which rises up to 207m (679 feet) above sea level and has sheer cliffs.

The man's kin have been informed and the coroner has been notified, police said.

Sgt Alun Jones said the force's thoughts were "with the man's family and friends at this very difficult time".

News.title: Man guilty of rape after woman's phone recording
News.content:
Al-Shammari, a Kuwaiti national living in Taunton, was remanded in custody to be sentenced on 27 November.

Al-Shammari denied rape but was found guilty by a majority verdict.

The jury heard Al-Shammari had known the woman for a few weeks, having met her on a night out, and they had slept together once.

On the night of the incident, he tried to persuade her to come out for the evening and when she said no, he convinced her to let him come to her home.

After a few drinks he asked to stay the night and she agreed to let him sleep on the sofa, telling him they were just friends.

The court was told Al-Shammari went to the woman's room and they did start to have consensual sex, but the woman later told police she was feeling "more and more uncomfortable". She said she asked him to stop but he did not.

The jury heard the recording in which the woman said "no" and "I don't like it".

In his police interview, Al-Shammari denied rape and told officers the woman had wanted sex but the positions they tried hurt her so he stopped.

A spokesperson for Avon and Somerset Police said: "Rape is a crime which often happens behind closed doors, leaving a jury to decide which of the two people is telling the truth.

"This is an unusual case as the survivor provided key evidence by recording the attack.

"Avon and Somerset Police remain committed to thoroughly investigating reports of sexual offences, supporting victims and pursuing offenders through the criminal justice system.

"The circumstances of this case highlight the importance of consent in sexual relationships.

"No means no, whether you've had consensual sex before or not. If you have any doubt about their consent, stop."

News.title: 'Greedy' solicitor used fake will-writing invoices to defraud cancer charity out of thousands
News.content:
A solicitor defrauded a cancer charity out of thousands of pounds after submitting fake invoices for work he had not carried out, a court heard.

Michael Fogg, 47, of Cyncoed, Cardiff, offered his services to Cancer Research UK's free will writing scheme, but when the charity contacted people he claimed to represent, they said they had not used the solicitor.

The hearing was told the money it lost as a result of Fogg's actions could have paid for 48 biopsies.

He was sentenced to 10 months' imprisonment, suspended for two years in a hearing at Newport Crown Court on Friday.

An investigation was launched by Cancer Research UK after emails and addresses for Fogg's clients were found to be non-existent.

Judge Carl Harrison said: "You had a position in the legal profession which allowed you to fund your greed."

News.title: Call for lottery gambling controls after dad's death
News.content:
A coroner has called for the National Lottery to be included in a self-exclusion gambling scheme after a man with a gambling addiction took his own life.

Stephen Goff, 54, died at his flat in Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire, on 18 August 2025, an inquest heard.

Emma Whitting, senior coroner for Bedfordshire and Luton, said there was a risk of further deaths unless the National Lottery draw was covered by GAMSTOP.

The system prevents people who register with it from accessing gambling websites and apps licensed in Great Britain.

The coroner has sent the Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report, external to the Gambling Commission and GAMSTOP.

A spokesperson for the commission said that following the inquest, they had "been working with Gamstop and Allwyn, the National Lottery operator, to consider whether further protections are needed in this area".

News.title: Binance says it covered 90% of losses from $6.3 billion hack so far
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Binance has replaced 90% of the cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.3 billion hack of its platform, the exchange said on Saturday.

The repurchases were funded with company money, it said in a statement posted on X. The remaining 10% is made up of tokens that are less liquid, which means they may take longer to buy, according to the statement.

"We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X on Saturday.

Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, lost more than $6 billion worth of crypto in the hack, which analysts blamed on North Korea.

Crypto prices fell on Friday as the exchange sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe.

( Ellen M. Banner/The Seattle Time )

Teng said on Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.

The exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds after the hack but it said on Saturday that it was still on track to re-open withdrawals on Sunday.

Around $6.34 billion of company funds has been set aside internally to cover the losses, Binance said.

The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures insurance fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X.

The exchange has also taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT on October 31, as part of its proof-of-reserves process.

Users holding the 10 listed tokens – BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC – would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum 1:1 ratio once the full proof was available, it said.

News.title: Harry Kane parades Ballon d’Or – before missing penalty in Bayern Munich draw
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Harry Kane paraded the Ballon d’Or, but then missed a second-half penalty and hit the post, as Bayern Munich drew 2-2 with rivals Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga in his first match since Monday’s award ceremony.

The England captain scored 73 goals in 64 appearances for club and country last season and became Bayern’s first Ballon d’Or winner since 1981 when he was crowned the world’s best player in London.

open image in gallery Harry Kane acknowledges the fans while holding his Ballon d'Or trophy ( Getty )

Kane was applauded onto the pitch by both teams as Bayern hosted Germany’s Der Klassiker, while the anthem Land of Hope and Glory was played to the fans in Munich’s Allianz Arena.

Kane was joined on the pitch pre-match by his wife, Katie Goodland, as well as their four children. He was the final player to emerge onto the pitch and carried the trophy with him before speaking to the crowd.

“Hi everyone, I just wanted to say I’m extremely proud to be a FC Bayern Munich player,” Kane told the crowd. “The support you have shown me since I arrived has been incredible.”

open image in gallery ( Getty )

open image in gallery ( Getty )

Kane was an unused substitute in the 6-1 German Cup second-round ⁠demolition of Magdeburg on Wednesday before ​missing ⁠from the spot with Bayern 1-0 up. He also hit the post, one of four times Bayern ⁠hit the woodwork.

Fabio Silva snatched the equaliser in the 89th minute to leave both teams on 18 points, with Bayern top on goal difference. In a rollercoaster first half Bayern hit the woodwork through Michael Olise ‌and missed a golden chance for Ismael ‌Saibari, who was injured in the process, before the visitors had a goal overruled by VAR.

Bayern, also hit by injuries to Serge Gnabry and Olise, struck in the 38th thanks through Konrad Laimer's goal on the rebound, after his first effort was blocked by Dortmund's Gregor Kobel. With Bayern coach Vincent Kompany recovering after his collapse last week, Bayern's full back Laimer was more threatening than Kane, who sent his 56th minute spot-kick against ‌the crossbar.

open image in gallery Kane sent his penalty crashing against the crossbar ( Reuters )

Dortmund scored through Serhou Guirassy on the hour mark but their joy only lasted six minutes as Dayot Upamecano tapped in `a Kane assist from close range. Kane's low shot ⁠bounced off the post before Silva bagged the equaliser. Bayern's Lennart Karl still ‌had time to ​see his shot in stoppage ‌time bounce off the crossbar ​and cap a frustrating day for the champions.

Kane not only become the first English player to win the Ballon d’Or since 2001 when he beaten Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal to the award, but also the first Bundesliga player since 1996 to win the prize. Last season Kane scored 36 Bundesliga goals, despite starting only 25 games, and scored in every round of the German Cup, including a hat-trick in the final, as Bayern won the double.

Includes reporting from Reuters

News.title: Tottenham punish Jean-Philippe Mateta’s moment of madness to earn third straight win
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Resurgent Tottenham made it three Premier League wins in a row for the first time in 20 months with a comfortable 2-0 victory over 10-man Crystal Palace.

Buoyed by only a second triumph at Chelsea in 36 years last weekend, Spurs’ task was made more routine by a 13th-minute red card for Palace forward Jean-Philippe Mateta for a studs-up tackle on Micky van de Ven.

open image in gallery Mateta was sent off following a VAR review ( PA )

VAR intervened to assist referee Michael Oliver and it was largely one-way traffic after with Archie Gray able to open the scoring with a header after 25 minutes.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team started the second half impressively and eventually doubled their lead with 17 minutes left through former Brighton centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke.

It allowed De Zerbi to hand a league debut to Spurs’ teenager Luca Williams-Barnett on an enjoyable night for the north London club, but this latest defeat will increase the scrutiny on under-fire Palace boss Pierre Sage.

James Maddison was available for Spurs but De Zerbi decided to put the playmaker on the bench after his injury scare at Chelsea, with Dominic Solanke recalled in attack.

Palace boss Sage had eased speculation over his future with a midweek Carabao Cup win at Fulham, but the visitors’ task in north London was made more difficult in the 11th minute.

Tottenham captain Van de Ven showed his pace to nip in ahead of Mateta, who caught the Dutch defender with a studs-up tackle on the Achilles, and while referee Oliver initially gave out a yellow card, it was soon upgraded to a red after a VAR review.

open image in gallery Pierre Sage is under more pressure after falling to a sixth Premier League defeat of the season ( Getty )

After a bright start for Palace, where Daichi Kamada had tested Antonin Kinsky early on, it was now an uphill battle for Sage’s men.

Two excellent crosses by Mathys Tel failed to find a Tottenham player soon after, but the deadlock was broken in the 25th minute.

Mohammed Kudus sent in a dangerous corner kick to the back post where Gray headed in his third goal for Spurs and second against Palace.

open image in gallery Gray scored Tottenham’s opening goal at the back post ( Reuters )

Home fans chanted about Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane with 28 minutes on the clock, but without his predatory instincts it stayed 1-0 until half-time, with a powerful Omar Marmoush shot blocked by Axel Disasi.

Pedro Porro was introduced for Gray at the break to continue his comeback from a hamstring injury and Tottenham started the second half with improved intent.

Fernandes had a volley blocked by Dwight McNeil before a smart shot on the turn by Solanke was saved by Henderson.

Solanke was replaced by Conor Gallagher minutes later and after Tel sent another effort off target, Andy Robertson was denied by Henderson from close range.

It felt a matter of time until Spurs grabbed a second and it eventually arrived when Fernandes produced a sensational cross for Van Hecke, who had his initial header tipped on to the crossbar by Henderson and managed to bundle in whilst laying on the floor in the 73rd minute.

open image in gallery Van Hecke nodded in from the goal-line ( PA )

Gallagher and Tel almost scored before Williams-Barnett got the nod with two minutes left and should have claimed an assist when he raced past Anan Khalaili, but Kudus failed to score at the back post.

Dejan Kulusevski, in his third appearance since a 526-day absence, nearly added the cherry on top, only for Henderson to tip over to ensure it finished 2-0.

News.title: Manhunt begins after pregnant woman shot dead and others injured at Spirit Halloween
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Read our Privacy notice

A pregnant woman was killed and six others injured Friday in a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in California, with three victims left fighting for their lives as police hunt for the gunman.

Constance Hages, 31, passed away from gunshot wounds in the shooting that happened Friday around 8:30 p.m. inside the Spirit Halloween at the Solano Town Center shopping mall in Fairfield, about 45 miles northeast of San Francisco, police said.

Hages' family told detectives she was pregnant at the time of the shooting. The Solano County Coroner's Office will confirm the information following an examination.

“Our thoughts and prayers remain with the victim’s family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” police said in a Facebook update Saturday.

Three other victims, a 16-year-old boy, a 19-year-old man and a 32-year-old man, remain in critical condition. A 23-year-old man is also hospitalized in critical but stable condition, police said.

Three victims, aged 16, 19 and 32, remain in critical condition, while a 23-year-old man is critical but stable, police said ( Getty )

Two additional victims, aged 19 and 43, were treated for gunshot wounds and have since been released from the hospital.

Investigators believe the shooting was a targeted attack involving a suspect inside the store. Detectives are reviewing surveillance footage and other evidence as they work to identify the person responsible.

“Our department extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the victim who died from their injuries. We also extend our thoughts to the other victims who were injured during this shooting. We are not releasing the identities of any victims at this time,” police said in an update Saturday afternoon.

No arrests have been announced in connection with the shooting.

“We recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created throughout our community, particularly with the many Halloween events and celebrations planned for today,” police said. “We understand that an incident of this nature is frightening and deeply unsettling.”

“We encourage everyone to remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity. The safety of our community remains our priority, and our department remains committed to working alongside our community to ensure everyone can enjoy a safe Halloween,” the department added.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information that could help investigators is asked to contact the Fairfield Police Department at 707-428-7600 or email 1030mall@fairfield.ca.gov.

Meanwhile, across the country in Madison Heights, Michigan, a 21-year-old Detroit man is dead after being shot multiple times during an argument inside a Spirit Halloween store.

The suspected shooter’s wife, Alanna, claims her husband fired in self-defense after being confronted by a man he knew and had a history with as they left the store with their three children, she told ClickOnDetroit.

She said the man reached into his pockets, prompting her husband, a concealed pistol license holder, to open fire.

Police, however, plan to pursue criminal charges.

Spirit Halloween told The Independent in a statement: “We are deeply saddened by the tragic incidents that occurred at our Spirit Halloween stores. Our thoughts and prayers are with the families of the victims of these heartbreaking events.”

The seasonal retailer, which typically operates from late summer into early November, added that it is fully cooperating with local law enforcement agencies in both cases.

“Out of respect for those impacted and to support the ongoing investigations, the affected stores will remain closed until further notice,” the statement concluded.

News.title: Canelo vs Mbilli LIVE: Start time, undercard, updates and results from controversial Riyadh fight tonight
