World.title: Why I’m grateful my son is getting the Halloween-Día de Muertos experience I never had
World.content:
The funny thing about growing up in California with Mexican immigrant parents is that you are perpetually intimate with, and distant from, your Mexican roots. Every holiday season, therefore, becomes a delightfully unique interpretation of both cultures mashed together.

Tamales wrapped in banana leaves and filled with turkey for Thanksgiving? Opening gifts at midnight for Noche Buena, and then again on Christmas morning? Getting your face smashed into a birthday cake?

These are all welcome in my life as a Mexican-American who must constantly toggle between my two identities on both soils.

Sometimes, though, one cultural norm or ideology can overtake the other, leaving one half egregiously overlooked, if not completely erased. For me, that has always been the case with Día de Muertos.

Halloween was the festive U.S. tradition my household embraced in its most suburbanized form: dressing up as Ninja Turtles, trick-or-treating with pumpkin-shaped buckets, and devouring pounds of Jolly Ranchers, fun-sized Snickers and M&Ms for weeks after.

I’ve never been the king of spooky season, but I’ve also never avoided it. As I grew older and met my wife, our family Halloween tradition became dressing up in custom-made outfits that reflected our personalities or the region we lived: two high school teachers dressed as our favorite punctuation marks; two Boston post-grads dressed as the local subway trains. (Spoiler: this year we are dressing up as Chedraui employees.)

And yet, despite traveling to Mexico regularly throughout my life, and having immigrant parents who spoke Spanish and were connected to their roots in Veracruz in different ways, I don’t have any real Día de Muertos memories from my childhood.

Finding the tradition

It wasn’t until the 2010s that I recall the concept entering mainstream culture in California and elsewhere beyond Mexico. For my wife and me — both as a couple, but also in our respective Mexican-American upbringings throughout the 1990s and 2000s — we never experienced our parents or family members building altars in our California homes. Not until maybe around Pixar’s “Coco” (2017), that is.

That tradition has quickly spread. Within the past decade, it has become more commonplace to see altares, ofrendas and Día de Muertos-themed households worldwide. Of course, it existed long before “Coco,” but it wasn’t as ubiquitous as it is today.

When my son was born in 2023, my wife and I had already spent significant time in Mexico, including traveling to Oaxaca for a month during Día de Muertos season and fully immersing ourselves in its wondrous spirit of parades, parties and gravesite visits.

We had learned, while exploring Mexico’s vast regional scenes and lodging with family members in various states across the span of multiple summers, about the importance of Día de Muertos as a form of intimate ancestral remembrance. In contrast to the candy-collecting rampage we’d always known the end of October to be, we’ve been able to incorporate those important elements of Día de Muertos into our lives — and in our son’s understanding of this time of the year.

Now, having fully transplanted our lives to Veracruz, we get to experience the best of both worlds as a young family: the playful, goofy costumery and decorations of Halloween, combined with the artisanal charms and spiritual connectivity of Día de Muertos.

I wouldn’t have it any other way.

Building core memories

Undoubtedly, our son’s autumnal memories will be completely different than ours: Instead of knocking on doors in a cul-de-sac with a group of neighborhood kids, he’s going to a field of cempasúchiles in a mountainous pueblo to get his photo taken on a horse that is whimsically painted like a calavera. Instead of visiting the pumpkin patch and riding a train through cornstalks and bales of hay, his abuela and bisabuelo are coming over to our house to eat pan de muerto and build a collective family altar with photos of family members that he, or even I, will never meet.

Each has their own joys and core-memory-building functions, and I enjoy them both. I hope he does, too.

It’s true that our current community doesn’t offer much traditional Halloween vibes, in the Americanized sense. You may see a decorative witch or black cat dangling from a window, here and there. Earlier this week, I walked past a large inflatable ghost on someone’s balcony, but it was awkwardly angled to avoid the mess of wires that complicate our narrow, colonial streets.

It’s just a different atmosphere in these smaller Mexican cities and towns, and the sidewalks don’t really allow for large groups of children to roam around without parents losing their minds over incessant traffic safety.

Trick-or-treating vs. Día de Muertos parades

In 2024, we flew to Mexico City for Halloween and Día de Muertos. It was noticeably different from our experience in Veracruz. A local group of parents organized families online for a neighborhood walk, with designated homes that had registered in advance, so we knew who would be giving out candy.

Similarly, we went to a mercado in Mexico City that weekend for a “calaverita” — a Mexican version of trick-or-treating, where kids dress up and go stall to stall asking for treats.

In those instances, my son, wife and I got to experience some of that old-school Americana by walking around Mexico City with strangers — some, but not all of them, international — and knocking on doors (or wandering shop aisles) together. That version of Halloween offers a communal, neighborly bonding that isn’t always seen during other holidays, which more often than not take place inside homes with close family members, rather than out in public and in the streets. We certainly could use more of it.

Then, there’s the other side of it all: attending a Día de Muertos parade and being part of a collective throng of spectators, while ceremoniously dressed performers and various forms of alebrijes dance, flutter and chant around you. (It’s worth noting that Día de Muertos parades, like the one in Mexico’s capital, are relatively new traditions in many areas; they weren’t commonplace when I was growing up, but are a part of Día de Muertos’ increasing popularity.)

I’m glad my son will get to be immersed in those cultural experiences in ways my wife and I weren’t for Halloween.

Fusing traditions in an ever-connected world

Having access to those dual experiences is a life hack, really. That’s not to say that Halloween has never existed in Mexico, or that Día de Muertos is nonexistent in California. In each case, the cultural traditions are becoming more fused than ever before, largely thanks to social media, travel access and other global factors.

You no longer have to be in Oaxaca’s Centro to experience Día de Muertos, nor do you have to reside in a U.S. suburb to appreciate Halloween. Depending on where you are, you may not be able to fully replicate the magic of the other — but you learn to salvage whatever aspects you can.

By being in Mexico, we are reminded that we will always have generous access to, and understanding of, both celebratory worlds. That’s ultimately the beauty of being a Mexican-American binational family, no matter the seasonal holiday or time of year.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Do Mexicans celebrate Halloween? It’s not what you’d expect
World.content:
I have to be honest here. Growing up, I did get excited about Halloween parties at school.

Although some colleagues might be flabbergasted by this, as a kid, my friends in elementary school did organize trick-or-treat evenings — which were mostly about the treats, honestly — and children invited each other to their houses to play dress-up and paint their faces as pumpkins and skeletons.

However, for the November festivities, my family always made a point to put a special emphasis on building our Día de Muertos altar at home. It kind of felt more important, in a way, than just getting your pumpkin or vampire disguise. Still, as the air grows colder and the moons appear larger at night, the question arises: Do Mexicans celebrate Halloween? Well, it’s a bit more complicated than you might expect.

When the barrier between the two worlds grows thin

As the November festivities draw closer, you might come across the debate on social media. More nationalist and opinionated Mexicans will defend our millennia-old traditions over the hyper-Americanization of our fall festivals. Incidentally, there is a similar debate among our fellow countrymen regarding why pan de muerto should only be eaten during this time of year, and we have discussed it at length on MND before.

And the people who share this point of view do have a point. Setting up the altar for the dead, waiting for our deceased relatives to return and share a meal at home once more, is something we inherited from our parents, who in turn inherited it from their grandparents, and so on.

The pre-Hispanic roots of this ritual are enough to warrant an article in their own right — covering the spiritual light of the cempasúchil flower and the way the barrier between the two worlds seems to grow thin at this time of year. But that is not all. Although it is a custom with distinctly Mexica origins, it manifests in widely diverse cultural ways across the country: The massive ofrenda created annually at UNAM is vastly different from the long nights people spend in Pátzcuaro, Michoacán, awaiting the return of their departed loved ones.

We even have a word for them: nuestros muertitos, our beloved deceased. The suffix -ito or -ita in Mexican Spanish implies not only a diminutive form, but also a relationship of affection and respect inherited from Nahuatl -tzin, the honorific suffix used for high-ranking officials as well as for our mothers and fathers.

In preparation for their return, we prepare the favorite foods of our dearly departed — like mole de olla for a dear auntie, or the Diet Coke my grandma used to enjoy so much. Some people leave cigarettes for a brother who has passed away, or even traditional candies like Pulparindo or Pelón Pelo Rico.

So, yeah, you can see how these festivities might weigh a lot more on us than simply going trick-or-treating. Why then, why do we see children running around dressed as skeletons, ghosts and pumpkins as Oct. 31 approaches?

Día de Muertos vs. Halloween: Is there a disagreement about this in Mexico?

First of all, it is worth emphasizing that Mexico is an incredibly culturally diverse country. Even taking into account the legacy of the Mexica Empire — which spread many Day of the Dead practices across the nation — and the overwhelming influence of contemporary globalization, one cannot truly generalize about how the tradition is observed throughout the country. To do so would almost be disrespectful to the 68 official Indigenous languages (with their 364 linguistic variants) and the unique ways in which each culture shows respect and affection for its departed loved ones.

What I mean by this is that there is no single way to celebrate Day of the Dead in Mexico — or Halloween, for that matter.

That said, how right Porfirio Díaz was when he said that Mexico was very far from God, but very close to the United States. Given the geographic, commercial and political proximity we share with our northern neighbors — who are increasingly coming to share our country with us — it is only natural that Mexicans also join in the Halloween festivities.

We love dressing up, eating candy until we’re stuffed and having an excuse to run through the streets dressed as pumpkins. Who doesn’t, right?

Why the answer is complex

We could easily say, however, that both celebrations coexist today — and even engage in a dialogue. On more than one occasion, I have seen jack-o’-lanterns on Día de los Muertos altars. You can even hear children on Oct. 31 asking, “¿Me da mi calaverita?” — the hyper-Mexican version of “Trick or treat!”

Now, while all this is true, it would be somewhat simplistic to say, “Yes, in Mexico we celebrate everything.” Although it is true that we never lack reasons to throw a party here, the reality is that Halloween celebrations are more of a recreational activity than a cultural one. Day of the Dead is something we collectively look forward to and honor with greater solemnity — ranging from our intimate family traditions at home to the grand public displays we see in the streets year after year.

So yeah, if you ask a Mexican if they celebrate Halloween, they’ll probably say they do — but that they observe Día de Muertos.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to set out a Coke for my grandma; she’s on her way back from the other side.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the Mexico News Daily Features desk. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams anthropology. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Yet another Mexican national dies in the custody of ICE: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Last week, 56-year-old Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a Dallas resident of decades and lawful green card holder, died at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas. His daughter says staff at the center would not give him his heart, diabetes and blood pressure medications, and that he told her they ignored him when he reported trouble breathing and tightness in his chest. The Webb County Medical Examiner is performing his autopsy, and no cause of death has been released. He is the 18th Mexican national to die in U.S. immigration custody or during enforcement operations since January 20, 2025.

For those of you keeping track, that is 15 deaths of Mexican nationals in custody and 3 during enforcement operations — 18 in total since Trump took office for a second time. Human Rights Watch counted 52 deaths of people of all nationalities in ICE custody in the 500 days between January 20, 2025, and June 4, 2026, roughly three a month. AFP reports that at least 30 people died in U.S. migrant detention centers last year, the most since ICE was created.

It’s easy to write off the 18 deaths as statistics or soundbites in the daily news cycle. It’s easy to say they were “criminals that shouldn’t have been here in the first place.” So let’s look at the facts, drawing on a recent profile conducted by CNN.

All 18 were men. The youngest was 19, the oldest was 68.

Some had spent decades in the U.S. ICE says one entered in 1976, and another had lived here about 35 years, worked in construction and had three U.S. citizen children. Andrade-Covarrubias lived in Dallas for decades. Others arrived recently: ICE says one entered in 2022 and another in December 2023.

ICE’s own descriptions of their records vary widely. One was sentenced in 2005 to 20 years for attempted sexual contact with a minor. Others were detained for driving without a valid license, littering or public intoxication. For several, CNN’s profiles cite no criminal charges or record.

The 17 deaths CNN profiled occurred in at least 8 states. This suggests a pattern rather than a single “bad cop” or rogue department. The Department of Homeland Security denies that deaths in its facilities have increased and says detainees receive proper medical treatment.

There are an estimated 38 million people of Mexican origin living in the U.S. today. Given the current environment in the country, many in this community have a relative, friend or neighbor who is living in fear or has been mistreated.

Latino voters also helped elect the current administration. Trump won 46% of the Latino vote in 2024, according to exit polls, up from 32% in 2020. Pew research finds that approval among Latino voters who backed him has since fallen 27 points, to 66%. These figures cover Latino voters broadly, not Mexican-Americans specifically.

The key issue I am raising here is about how people should be treated.

This is not about whether one belongs to the left or right political party, or about opposing border control. I am not suggesting that a country shouldn’t enforce its borders. Of course it should. The border has not always been secure, and immigration policy has often been applied inconsistently or unfairly, if at all. Those convicted of crimes should be punished. Overstaying a visa is a violation of federal immigration law and should have consequences.

The issue is how people are treated once the government has them in its custody. Many Americans who agreed that “something needed to be done” have been repulsed by ICE tactics in their communities. U.S. politicians have not agreed on updated, sensible immigration policy in decades. But whatever the policy, a person in federal custody is the government’s responsibility. We have all read about ICE signing bonuses, hiring sprees, pressure to meet arrest quotas, the lack of collaboration with local authorities and expedited, insufficient training.

Consider the reverse. If one American were dying in a foreign government’s custody nearly every month, we would expect State Department warnings, a drop in tourism and a damaged reputation for that country. The comparison is not about crime or illegal migration. It is about deaths in the custody of a state. That is why Mexico’s government has demanded investigations and filed criminal complaints with U.S. prosecutors.

Many readers will hear “Americans killed in Mexico” and think of drug violence. That is a different matter. These deaths happened in government custody, under government responsibility. That is the standard we would demand for our own citizens abroad.

Neighbors, not enemies

Many Americans have Mexican neighbors and workers they value and live alongside. Many of those same Americans now feel anger over rising costs and failing institutions and leadership, on both the left and the right. In recent polling, nearly eight in 10 Latino voters said they were “very concerned” about the cost of food and consumer goods, above the roughly two-thirds of Americans overall.

Directing that anger at each other is a mistake. Americans can be forgiven for being overwhelmed by inflation, gas prices, interest rates, midterms, job-loss fears and AI risks. But whatever our views on immigration, we should not lose sight of how people are treated while they are in the government’s care.

What you can do

If you are an American living in Mexico, try to understand the anger that locals might have towards the United States. Mexicans are watching their citizens die in U.S. custody, and their government has condemned the deaths and begun filing complaints with U.S. prosecutors. That anger is aimed at a policy and likely at government officials, not at you. It’s important to listen and acknowledge their frustrations. Write to your senators and congresspeople. Tell them the “how” of enforcement matters: medical care, transparency and accountability for deaths in custody are minimum expectations. Our immigration policy needed to change. Most people accept that now, but roughly three people dying in federal custody each month should make us all ask what is going on. Write to MND. We invite you to write us about how you see this issue where you live, or experiences you have had talking to locals in Mexico about this issue.

I sincerely hope that this will be seen not as a Republican or Democrat issue but one of basic human rights and decency, and as a result, be acted on quickly before there are more tragic incidents.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: New episode: The real story behind Mexico’s record exports
World.content:
Mexico’s exports are booming. In fact, in July they increased by 44% compared to last year, and are up almost 28% year to date. Mexico is now firmly the largest exporter to the United States, ahead of Canada and China.

One would think that kind of growth would be exceptional for Mexico and its economy. But is it really as good as it sounds?

A few reasons for caution:

The growth is concentrated. Electrical and electronic equipment, including AI servers, jumped 134% in July and overtook autos for the first time. Auto exports are roughly flat this year, and oil exports are down.

Imports are booming too. They are up about 26% year to date and grew 45.7% in July, producing a rare monthly trade deficit. Imports from Taiwan have more than tripled. If imports are up as much as exports, what is Mexico adding?

Value added is thin. An estimated 3 cents of every dollar of electronics exports is Mexican added value, roughly a tenth of what Mexico adds in the vehicle segment.

The economy isn’t keeping pace. Mexican GDP is generally expected to grow only 1.2%-1.5% this year, well below the U.S. growth rate.

So what is really going on, and what does it mean for Mexico?

Check out this week’s “Confidently Wrong” podcast as we dig a bit deeper into the numbers for a better understanding of the real implications.

World.title: How CFE plans to raise a billion dollars to expand Mexico’s electrical grid
World.content:
The Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) plans to raise approximately US $1 billion through a share offering in CFE Capital, its financial subsidiary.

The objective is to attract capital from domestic and foreign investors to finance new transmission lines. The private investment will supplement the government funds budgeted to CFE.

CFE Capital operates through a structure similar to a real estate investment fund known as Fibra E, which allows investors to share in the revenue generated by infrastructure assets.

CFE Chief Financial Officer Eugenio Amador Quijano told Bloomberg Línea that officials will meet investors in New York early in November, with the intention to finalize the offering before the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

According to Quijano, the state-owned company aims to expand its electricity transmission network by nearly 7% during the current administration, compared to growth of less than 1% over the previous eight years. It also seeks to facilitate the integration of new power generation projects, including the 32 gigawatts planned by 2030.

The CFE considers the new lines necessary to connect power generation plants with consumption centers and to meet growing electricity demand.

In August, CFE Capital requested authorization from the National Banking and Securities Commission (CNBV) to conduct a follow-on public offering in Mexico, accompanied by an international private placement. This offering would be a new issuance, following the initial public offering (IPO) in February 2018, which raised 16.4 billion pesos (US $880 million).

However, the vehicle remained virtually inactive following its market launch, as the CFE did not subsequently expand its portfolio of transmission assets or carry out any new offerings. Over time, liquidity declined, and ownership ended up primarily in the hands of Mexican pension funds.

For this new transaction, the CFE aims to place approximately one-third of the securities with foreign participants.

If the new operation goes through, the transaction would be the largest public offering of shares in Mexico since 2020, Bloomberg reported.

The projected capital raising is part of a broader strategy. According to the Energy Ministry, the CFE’s strengthening and expansion plan includes investments totaling nearly US $37.5 billion.

Within that program, the transmission segment accounts for approximately US $6.9 billion through 2030, of which nearly US $2.5 billion would be channeled through CFE Fibra E.

The $1 billion currently envisioned would, therefore, represent a portion of the required financing.

With reports from PropModo and El Tiempo

World.title: Canadian ambassador’s message to Mexican business: Invest in us
World.content:
Canadian Ambassador to Mexico Cameron MacKay urged the Mexican private sector to increase capital investment in Canada, emphasizing the necessity of “rebalancing the asymmetrical bilateral investment flow” between the two North American partners.

Speaking during an investors symposium panel entitled “Unlocking the Next Trillion: Mobilizing Long-Term Capital for Regional Development,” the diplomat noted that although Mexico has considerably improved its investment conditions, risks and uncertainty persist.

MacKay pointed out that approximately US $66 billion has been deployed by Canadian manufacturers, corporations and institutional investors into Mexico, while Mexican companies have invested only about US $3-4 billion in Canada.

Insisting that Canada offers favorable conditions for attracting new investments, MacKay outlined several key competitive advantages, including Canada’s 6.4% marginal tax rate tailored specifically for new projects, which the ambassador described as “very competitive.”

“That’s half of what it is in the United States and the lowest in the OECD,” he said, referring to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, of which both nations are members.

Mackay also spoke about the importance of solidifying corporate supply chains ahead of the scheduled U.S.–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) trade review, while highlighting the critical importance of a coordinated front between Canada and Mexico.

Regarding the future of the USMCA, MacKay pointed out that the United States has made it clear that free trade in North America will not return to what it once was, increasing the importance of the Canada-Mexico Action Plan 2025-2028.

“Around 80-85% of trade between the three nations is duty-free and we have to see what we do with the remaining 15%,” he said.

MacKay also voiced concern regarding the operating environment for Canadian companies in Mexico. Earlier this year, he noted that Canadian operators face “concrete, non-abstract headwinds that slow down investment cycles.”

The symposium, sponsored by the Milken Institute, sought to address the question: How can Mexico align institutional capital, government priorities and private investment to finance key sectors, while leveraging the USMCA to strengthen investor confidence and supply chain integration?

The expressed goal was “to examine how trade-policy certainty, innovative financing structures and effective partnership frameworks can turn development priorities into bankable projects.”

Speaking before MacKay, Mexico’s Finance Minister Edgar Amador did not address the asymmetrical imbalance during his keynote address.

Amador told the assembled national and international investors that Mexico’s economy is gaining momentum and preserving an upward trend.

He highlighted factors such as a strong labor market, steady foreign direct investment and decreasing inflation as key elements supporting Mexico’s economic outlook.

With reports from Reforma, El Economista and El Financiero

World.content:
A firefighter at a burnt-out car in Paris during the riots of 17 October 2026. (Photo: Jorge Jaramillo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Saturday, 31 October, 1:35 p.m. ET (6:35 p.m. Paris) · Source: French Interior Ministry, Paris Police Prefecture, regional prefectures

France marched for a third Saturday in a row, and the crowds were smaller. The Interior Ministry counted 320,000 people nationwide, down from 410,000 a week earlier.

The coalition of student and high-school unions behind the day says 500,000 came out. Our guide to why is France protesting explains the anger over prices and school conditions, and the France protests hub tracks every step.

Order: 70,000 police and gendarmes deployed; tension flared late in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Rennes and Grenoble.

What next: Unions have called a national strike and marches for Thursday, 5 November.

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: France Deploys 70,000 Police for Protest Day

In plain English Three Saturdays in a row, French people have marched over high living costs and poor conditions in schools and universities. The marches were called by a coalition of student unions, the Yellow Vests (the hi-vis-jacket protest movement born in 2018) and labour unions. The government and the organisers each publish their own crowd count, and the two are never close.

A Calm Afternoon, a Tense Evening

At 2 p.m. Paris time (9 a.m. ET), the situation was “broadly calm”, with no notable incident, according to the authorities and Radio France reporters. The first tension came late in the afternoon, in Rennes, Marseille and Lyon.

In Paris, police headquarters (the prefecture) counted 70,000 marchers, and the youth coalition 200,000. The procession moved largely calmly towards Porte de Charenton, a gate on the city’s southeastern edge, where tension broke out at the end. Officials had feared 300 to 600 far-left militants.

File photo: the Hôtel de Matignon, the prime minister’s office in Paris.

Four Cities, Two Sets of Numbers

In Rennes, the regional prefecture counted 13,500 marchers and the FSU, a teachers’ union, 25,000. At the end, a group of 50 to 100 people dressed in black clashed with police.

In Marseille, the prefecture said 10,000 people joined a rally that had not been declared in advance. Projectiles were thrown at police around 4 p.m. Paris time (10 a.m. ET).

In Bordeaux, the prefecture counted about 11,000 marchers and unions 70,000. In Grenoble, roughly 10,000 gathered, and police used tear gas.

Why Both Sides See a Smaller Movement

The organisers’ own figures also fell: they counted 800,000 on both 17 and 24 October, and 500,000 now. Whoever is counting, Saturday’s crowd was the smallest of the three Saturdays since 17 October.

That matters because a shrinking crowd weakens the case that the movement is still growing. The next test is Thursday, 5 November, when unions have called a national strike and marches.

What It Means for US Readers

Travellers should expect more disruption on 5 November and check is it safe to travel to France before booking. Smaller crowds help the government in Paris, while the strike call keeps pressure on it.

Investors in French assets can read lower turnout as a small easing of risk, which we follow in the France 2027 poll tracker. A violent strike day would reverse that.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto betting exchange, prices a French state of emergency by 31 December at 7.5%, with about US$2.7 million traded. Kalshi, regulated in the US by the CFTC, prices the same event before 1 January 2027 at 10%, and a declaration before 1 November at 3% (1:32 p.m. ET).

What Is Not Known

No national tally of arrests or injuries for Saturday has been published. Counts from the ministry and the organisers cannot be reconciled.

It is also unclear how many people will return on 5 November, or whether Halloween night will bring more clashes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people protested in France on 31 October?

The Interior Ministry counted 320,000 nationwide, including 70,000 in Paris. The youth unions claimed 500,000, with 200,000 in Paris.

What happens next in France?

Unions have called a national strike and marches for Thursday, 5 November. It is the next test of whether the movement can regain size.

World.title: Court Bars Paris Union March From Bastille
World.content:
File photo: students march in Paris on 6 October 2026. Photo: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Published Saturday, 31 October, 12:22 p.m. ET (5:22 p.m. Paris) · Source: Council of State, Paris Police Prefecture, French Interior Ministry, unions

Paris police wanted Saturday’s marchers out on the outer boulevards. For one night a judge sided with the unions, and on Saturday morning France’s highest administrative court sided with the police.

The Council of State, which hears appeals against government decisions, banned the march of unions and student groups from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation, two landmark squares in eastern Paris. It is the latest turn in the France protests.

Key Facts What happened: France’s highest administrative court banned the central Bastille-to-Nation march.

Who decided: The Council of State overturned a Paris court and backed the police ban on Saturday morning.

What next: Marchers must use the outer-boulevard route; unions meet to decide their response.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a crypto-based betting exchange, prices a French state of emergency by 31 December at 7.5% (12:17 p.m. ET, 31 October).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: France Cost-of-Living Protests Draw 320,000

In plain English The Council of State is France’s top court for disputes with the government, and it can rule fast in urgent cases. The CGT, the General Confederation of Labour, is one of the country’s biggest trade unions.

A Night in Court, a Morning Reversal

The Paris police prefect, Patrice Faure, had banned the Bastille-to-Nation route and offered another one. The unions and student groups went to the Paris administrative court, and on Friday, 30 October, it allowed the central march.

The government appealed. On Saturday morning the Council of State cancelled that decision, banned the central route and approved the police alternative from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton, two city gates in eastern Paris, along the outer boulevards.

Why the Judges Sided With the Police

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who oversees the police, cited serious risks to public order. He pointed to the damage done on 17 October, two weeks before this march.

How Unions and Students Reacted

The Fage, a national student federation, called the ruling “a new obstacle to the right to protest”. The intersyndicale, the alliance of unions behind the call to march, said it would meet to decide what to do next.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes, France’s military-status police force, are deployed across the country for the day.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction exchange, runs a market on whether France declares a state of emergency, a legal regime that widens police powers. At 12:17 p.m. ET on 31 October (5:17 p.m. Paris) it priced a declaration by 31 December at 7.5% and by 31 October at 0.4%, with about US$2.69 million traded.

These prices are bets, not polls. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Americans in Paris on Saturday should expect heavy policing and crowds on the eastern outer boulevards.

For investors, the key risk is a march that spills past the approved route and deepens the political strain; our France 2027 poll tracker follows it.

What Is Not Known

The full text of the ruling has not been published beyond the passages quoted. Turnout, arrests and damage are not yet known. A calm day on the approved route would ease pressure on the government, while scenes like those of 17 October would raise it; the police figures on Saturday evening, 31 October, will show which.

It is also unclear whether organisers will keep to the approved route or call separate gatherings after their meeting. Our explainer on why France is protesting sets out the causes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Paris protest route did the court ban?

The Council of State banned the march from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation on Saturday, 31 October. It approved the outer-boulevard route instead.

Who asked the court to ban the route?

The government appealed after a Paris administrative court had allowed the central route on Friday, 30 October. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez cited public-order risks.

World.title: US Judge Bars Threats to Election Staff
World.content:
Photo: aismallard / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Three days before Election Day, federal judges are drawing a line around who may pressure the people who count America’s votes. On Friday a US judge ordered the Justice Department, the nation’s top federal law-enforcement agency, to stop threatening election officials over disputed ballots. It is the latest turn in our 2026 US midterm elections coverage.

This story is part of our coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Key Facts

Order: a US judge in California barred federal officials from threatening local vote counters, through November 16.

a US judge in California barred federal officials from threatening local vote counters, through November 16. Alaska: the Justice Department wants ballots naming a second “Sullivan” set aside, and certification halted if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

the Justice Department wants ballots naming a second “Sullivan” set aside, and certification halted if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. Early voting: nearly 49.6 million ballots were cast by Friday evening.

nearly 49.6 million ballots were cast by Friday evening. Prediction markets: Polymarket prices a Democratic Senate win at 71.5% and a Democratic House win at 94.5% (as of 11:22 a.m. ET, October 31).

What The California Judge Ordered

On Friday, October 30, US District Judge Trina Thompson of the Northern District of California issued a temporary restraining order, a short-term court order that freezes a dispute until a fuller hearing. It bars the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from threatening criminal prosecution to coerce state and local election officials, where the pressure rests only on claims that voters are ineligible.

The order also stops both agencies from demanding that officials in any state set ballots aside, purge voter lists or halt ballot processing. It runs through November 16, and labor unions and civil-rights groups brought the case.

File photo. A federal courthouse in Manhattan; the order discussed here came from a court in California. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Why The Appeals Court Matters Too

The same day, the Ninth US Circuit Court of Appeals, the federal appeals court for California and other Western states, again refused the Justice Department’s request to pause a ruling on more than 20,000 California ballots. The 2–1 decision found the department had not met its burden of proof.

It was the second rejection in a week. The administration argues that a data-matching programme flags voters who may not be eligible, while election officials say such matches can be wrong.

The Alaska Fight Over Two Sullivans

In Alaska, the Justice Department asked a federal court to set aside all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a second candidate who shares a name with the Republican senator. It also asked the court to block certification of the result if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

US District Judge Sharon Gleason set a fast schedule, with replies due at noon Alaska time on Saturday (4 p.m. ET). A ruling could follow once that briefing closes. Mary Peltola, the Democratic Senate nominee, denies any role in recruiting the second Sullivan and called the claims “offensive”.

How Many Americans Have Already Voted

The University of Florida Election Lab, which tracks early voting, counted 49,564,545 ballots cast early by Friday evening.

The final Emerson College Polling national survey, taken October 24–26 among 1,000 likely voters, put Democratic House candidates ahead 52% to 42%. Its credibility interval, a margin-of-error measure, is plus or minus 3 percentage points.

What Prediction Markets Say

Senate control: Democratic Party 71.5%, Republican Party 28.5% on Polymarket, with about US$13.3 million traded.

Democratic Party 71.5%, Republican Party 28.5% on Polymarket, with about US$13.3 million traded. House control: Democratic Party 94.5%, Republican Party 5.5% on Polymarket, with about US$33.8 million traded.

These prices are bets, not polls, and they were read at 11:22 a.m. ET on October 31. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means For US Readers

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. Expect results to arrive in stages, because states set their own polling hours and count mail, provisional and challenged ballots on their own timetables. A close Senate race may stay open for days if courts are still ruling.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the Alaska judge will set ballots aside or limit certification. Nor is it clear whether the Justice Department will appeal the California order.

No one can yet say whether the early-vote surge favours either party. Official results are final only when each state finishes counting.

Sources

Federal court orders (N.D. Cal., Ninth Circuit, D. Alaska); Emerson College Polling national survey, October 24–26, 2026; University of Florida Election Lab; Polymarket.

World.title: Florida Jails Six in Cuban Smuggling Ring
World.content:
File photo: Tampa International Airport, Florida. The ring bought flights for its clients; the Justice Department does not name an airport. Photo: Andrew Heneen / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

Published Saturday, 31 October, 11:01 a.m. ET (11:01 a.m. Havana) · Source: US Department of Justice, US Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida

A smuggling ring that sold Cubans a route into America for up to US$40,000 a head has reached a Florida courtroom. Five Cuban nationals and one US citizen were sentenced on Thursday, 29 October, as the latest chapter in the story we follow on our Cuba news hub, where we track Havana and Washington.

The US Department of Justice, which prosecutes federal crimes, says the group also filed more than 1,700 false asylum claims. It touches the wider Cuba and US tensions: how Cubans reach the United States, and who profits.

Key Facts What happened: A federal court in Florida sentenced six people on 29 October to two to four years in prison.

The scheme: They charged Cubans US$1,500 to US$40,000 each and filed over 1,700 false asylum claims.

The money: Prosecutors say the group laundered more than US$22 million between 2021 and 2025.

What is next: Three co-defendants await sentencing, and two more are at large, meaning not in custody.

This story is part of our coverage of the cuba news. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: US Immigration Agency Reportedly Arrests Cuban, 70

In plain English Prosecutors say a group of Cubans and one American sold illegal trips to the United States, then sold fake asylum paperwork to the same customers. Asylum is protection for people who say they would be persecuted at home, and a false story in an application is a federal crime.

Six Sentences, Two to Four Years

All six had pleaded guilty to charges that include smuggling for money, asylum fraud and money laundering, meaning the hiding of illegal profits.

The longest term, four years, went to Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez, who managed the group’s immigration-services business. Prosecutors say she personally filed hundreds of fraudulent asylum applications.

Who got what Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez, 27: four years, for running the fake immigration-services business.

four years, for running the fake immigration-services business. Layra Libertad Treto Santos, 30: 30 months, plus US$95,000 forfeited.

30 months, plus US$95,000 forfeited. Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero, 32: two years, plus US$2.9 million forfeited.

two years, plus US$2.9 million forfeited. Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos, 31: two years, plus US$150,000 forfeited.

two years, plus US$150,000 forfeited. Walbis Pozo-Dutel, 32: two years.

two years. Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez, 29: two years.

Twelve people were charged in all. A seventh defendant, Erik Ventura-Castro, was sentenced to 30 months on 29 July.

Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

How the Ring Worked

The group advertised on social media aimed at Cubans living on the island. It smuggled clients across the southern border and also used fake travel permits to bring them through airports.

File photo, September 2012: a US Border Patrol vehicle and surveillance tower near Nogales, Arizona. Photo: Josh Denmark, US Customs and Border Protection, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

The permit is called ESTA, the Electronic System for Travel Authorization, an online visa waiver for visitors from approved countries. Cuban residents are not eligible, so the ring claimed in its applications that clients had not been in Cuba since 2011.

Once clients were inside the United States, the group sold them asylum paperwork in exchange for a fee. It spent more than US$600,000 with one airline between July 2022 and November 2024.

What Washington Says About It

Joseph B. Edlow, director of US Citizenship and Immigration Services, the agency that handles visas and asylum claims, called the sentences “a clear warning to anyone seeking to profit by exploiting, abusing, or undermining America’s legal immigration system.” He added that his agency “will bring to bear all law enforcement resources at its disposal.”

The Justice Department filed the case under Operation Take Back America, a department initiative that, in its own words, aims to put more criminals behind bars and enforce the rule of law.

What It Means for US Readers

Prosecutors charged the paperwork side of the scheme alongside the border crossing, and the longest term went to Vega-Perez, who ran the asylum-filing business.

For Cuban-American families sending money to relatives, the case shows what prosecutors call a fraudulent immigration business that sold paperwork to Cubans. Our guide on whether Americans can travel to Cuba explains the travel rules.

What Is Not Known

The Justice Department speaks of “thousands” of smuggled Cubans but gives no exact figure. It does not say how many of the 1,700 asylum claims were approved.

The release also does not give the time of the hearings or a sentencing date for the three defendants still waiting. We have not seen a response from Havana or from the defendants’ lawyers.

More: Cuba news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did the ring charge Cuban migrants?

Prosecutors say it charged between US$1,500 and US$40,000 per person. Some groups travelled on private planes the conspirators chartered.

Who is still waiting for sentencing?

Yuniel Lima-Santos, Gisleivy Peralta Consuegra and Lazaro Alain Cabrera-Rodriguez await sentencing. Two other defendants, Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres and Frandy Aragon-Diaz, are at large.

Sources: US Department of Justice press release of 29 October 2026 (justice.gov); US Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Florida (justice.gov/usao-mdfl); US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

World.title: Europe’s Gen Z Protest Wave Explained
World.content:
GERMANY · ANALYSIS

Key Facts Why it matters The protests test whether European governments can fund defence increases while cutting domestic services, a trade-off that directly affects US investors in European assets.

The numbers The Federal Employment Agency counted 2.994 million registered unemployed in September 2026.

What to watch Whether Germany’s turnout matches online registrations, and whether Italy’s CGIL general strike turns youth protests into sustained industrial action.

What it means for you US travellers should expect route restrictions and possible curfews in Paris and other large European cities, while investors should watch whether protest pressure forces costly fiscal concessions.

Gen Z protests Europe are spreading as Germany’s youth movement mobilises on 31 October 2026, demanding affordable housing, better education and an end to conscription plans. For US investors and travellers, the wave signals a new political risk: governments may be forced to choose between defence spending and domestic services, with consequences for European assets and urban security.

Germany, Europe’s largest economy, is now the latest stage for a generational revolt that has already shaken France and Italy. This analysis explains what is driving the movement, how far it could spread and what it means for American money and mobility, drawing on the Europe Intelligence Brief published today.

What Is Driving Europe’s Youth Revolt

The immediate grievances differ by country, but the underlying complaint is the same: young Europeans believe the post-2008 social contract no longer works for them. Housing, education, wages and public services are becoming less affordable just as governments ask younger citizens to accept higher taxes, weaker welfare provision and greater military obligations.

In Germany, the movement Gen Z regelt, roughly “Gen Z has got this”, has called demonstrations in 23 German cities on 31 October 2026, and more than 134,000 people had signalled on its website that they intended to take part. The campaign focuses on education funding, healthcare, climate protection, affordable living and opposition to renewed military conscription.

Social media has supplied the connective tissue. Organisers can circulate calls, slogans and turnout estimates rapidly across borders, while student groups and unions borrow tactics from one another.

The result resembles a common European mood more than a centrally coordinated organisation.The economic backdrop sharpens the message.Energy prices rose approximately 15 percent in September 2026.

Friedrich Merz at a CDU event, from the February 2025 election campaign. Archive photo.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Numbers That Matter

Germany’s protest wave is large by national standards, though organisers’ estimates should be treated as aspirations rather than verified attendance. The key figures as of October 2026 are:

These numbers reveal a movement that is broad but not yet unified. Germany’s protests are dispersed and publicly nonviolent, while France has seen stricter policing.

Spain’s movement is distinct, centred on housing insecurity rather than a single anti-government campaign.

Friedrich Merz, Germany's chancellor and CDU leader. Archive photo.

The Actors And What Each Wants

The movement has stated that protests should remain peaceful and rejected extremist symbols, racism and hate speech. The Bundesschülerkonferenz, Germany’s national school-student umbrella body, has distanced itself from Gen Z regelt while supporting students’ concerns.

The Economic And Business Stakes

For US investors in European assets, the protests matter less for headline crowd sizes than for whether they alter fiscal and policy assumptions. The central trade-off is between defence spending and domestic services, a tension that runs through every national variant of the movement.

Higher European defence budgets may benefit aerospace, cyber-security and military suppliers, but they can also intensify youth anger if financed through cuts to education, healthcare or housing programmes. Germany’s protesters explicitly oppose diverting public money toward defence while domestic services deteriorate.

The fiscal response carries sovereign risk. Governments may offer subsidies and public investment to calm protests, but markets could penalise countries where new spending appears unfunded or politically unstable.

Italy already faces high debt and limited fiscal space, making concessions financed through additional borrowing a potential pressure on sovereign spreads.Housing intervention poses a different risk.Spain’s movement has pushed rent and home ownership to the centre of politics, and a government under pressure may pursue rent controls, tax changes or restrictions affecting short-term rentals.

Those policies could benefit tenants in the near term but reduce supply or increase uncertainty for property investors if implemented abruptly.

What It Means For The United States And Latin America

US investors should focus on whether protests alter fiscal and policy assumptions in Europe’s largest economies. Three trade-offs are especially important: defence versus domestic services, fiscal response versus sovereign risk, and housing intervention versus property returns.

European defence spending could still rise even if protests continue. The relevant question is not simply whether budgets increase, but whether governments can explain who pays, which programmes are cut and how quickly new capabilities deliver security.

For Latin America, the protests offer a cautionary parallel. Countries across the region face similar generational pressures over housing, education and public services, and the European experience shows how quickly youth frustration can become a political force.

Latin American governments watching Europe may see both a warning and a template.Organisers registered 10,000 participants for the rally at the Brandenburg Gate, and Berlin police planned about 1,000 officers for Saturday.Travellers should avoid protest routes, check local prefecture and police notices, and avoid assuming that a daytime peaceful rally will remain peaceful after dark.

The Scenarios: What Would Stabilise Or Tip The Crisis

The stabilising scenario is one in which governments offer credible material concessions on education, housing or healthcare funding, while protesters remain peaceful and distinct from rioters. Germany’s movement has so far stressed nonviolence, and if that holds, it could become a model for issue-focused pressure rather than confrontation.

The tipping scenario is escalation through heavy-handed policing or isolated violence. Broad restrictions or mass arrests can increase turnout and radicalise previously moderate participants, while looting or attacks can shift public opinion toward tougher policing.

Either path would deepen the generational divide.A third scenario is strike contagion.Labour support could convert weekend rallies into disruptions of transport, schools, logistics and manufacturing, particularly in Italy where CGIL has already called a general strike.

That would raise the economic cost and force governments to choose between negotiation and confrontation.The most consequential scenario for investors is policy volatility.

Governments could respond with abrupt controls on rents, energy, migration or defence procurement, creating uncertainty that postpones hiring, construction, retail expansion and infrastructure decisions.

What It Means for You

If you hold European equities or real estate, the protests are a signal to review your exposure to sectors most affected by policy shifts: defence contractors, property developers, retailers and transport operators. The risk is not the demonstrations themselves but the fiscal and regulatory responses they provoke.

If you are travelling to Europe in the coming weeks, plan around protest dates and locations. Paris remains the highest-risk city, with route restrictions and curfews, but demonstrations are spreading to German and Italian cities as well.

The broader lesson is that generational politics is becoming an investment variable. Governments that ignore youth demands risk prolonged instability, while those that concede too much risk fiscal stress.

The balance each country strikes will shape European markets for years.

What Is Not Known

More than 134,000 people had signalled on the movement’s website by Monday 26 October that they planned to take part.The status of any German conscription law is unclear from available reporting.Protesters oppose a possible or newly introduced military-service framework, but the official text, commencement date, eligibility rules and service duration have not been confirmed.Spain’s political situation is also uncertain.

Reporting suggested that housing protests forced the government to call snap elections, but this claim requires confirmation from Spain’s official electoral and government institutions. The identity of Spain’s current prime minister and the status of any election must be verified before drawing conclusions.

What to Watch

The immediate test is whether Germany’s 31 October turnout matches online registrations, and whether protests remain peaceful. A peaceful, well-attended demonstration would strengthen the movement’s legitimacy; violence or low turnout would weaken it.

France has seen looting and 1,314 arrests in one weekend, and local authorities, including in Nice, imposed night curfews for minors.If these events coordinate, the movement could shift from weekend rallies to sustained industrial action.Spain’s housing demands are another marker, particularly if they enter an election campaign.

The response of Spain’s government will indicate whether housing becomes a defining political issue across Europe.Finally, watch whether governments announce concrete education, housing or healthcare funding rather than policing measures alone.

The difference between a protest wave and a political realignment may come down to whether young Europeans see material change, not just rhetorical acknowledgement.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Gen Z regelt in Germany?

Gen Z regelt is a German youth-led protest initiative that called demonstrations in 23 German cities on 31 October 2026. The movement demands greater education funding, lower living costs, stronger climate protection and opposition to a possible return of compulsory military service.

Why are young Europeans protesting in 2026?

Young Europeans are protesting because housing, education, wages and public services are becoming less affordable while governments ask them to accept higher taxes and greater military obligations. The movement reflects a belief that the post-2008 social contract no longer works for younger generations.

Is the protest movement the same across Europe?

No. Germany’s movement is dispersed and publicly nonviolent, France’s is confrontational with strict policing, Italy’s merges student demands with union-led strikes, and Spain’s centres on housing insecurity. The movements share a common mood but lack a unified platform or leadership.

What does this mean for US investors in Europe?

US investors should watch whether protests alter fiscal and policy assumptions, particularly the trade-off between defence spending and domestic services. Governments may offer costly concessions to calm protests, creating sovereign risk, or impose abrupt controls on rents and short-term rentals, affecting property returns.

Should US travellers avoid Europe during the protests?

US travellers should expect the most immediate effects in Paris and other large cities, including altered march routes, restricted central areas, night-time curfews and transport delays. Travellers should avoid protest routes and check local police notices, especially at night and during major weekends.

What are the next key dates to watch?

Spain has a reported general strike on 11 November 2026, and France’s third weekend of protests is underway as of 31 October 2026.

World.title: Why North Korea Rejects Denuclearisation
World.content:
NORTH KOREA · ANALYSIS

Key Facts What is happening North Korea rejected a joint US, South Korean and Japanese call for complete denuclearisation and UN sanctions enforcement in October 2026.

Why it matters Pyongyang now treats nuclear weapons as a permanent constitutional guarantee, not a negotiable programme, which changes what diplomacy can achieve.

The numbers North Korea amended its constitution in 2023 to enshrine nuclear-weapons policy.

Who is who Kim Jong Un leads North Korea and frames nuclear expansion as a permanent strategic mission; the United States, South Korea and Japan maintain the goal of complete denuclearisation.

What to watch Monitor whether Pyongyang shifts from constitutional permanence toward a test moratorium or fissile-material freeze, and whether Russia continues to shield it from sanctions monitoring.

What it means for you US investors and policy readers should expect continued sanctions risk, cyber threats and regional military tension rather than a near-term diplomatic opening.

North Korea rejects denuclearisation because it treats nuclear weapons as the central guarantee of regime survival and diplomatic leverage, not as a negotiable programme. For US readers, this means the goal of complete, verifiable and irreversible disarmament is now effectively blocked by Pyongyang’s constitutional and strategic posture.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

North Korea sits at the centre of one of the world’s most militarised regions, facing US troops in South Korea and a trilateral alliance with Japan. This analysis explains why Pyongyang refuses to give up its arsenal and what changed after the failed 2018-19 summit process, drawing on the Asia Intelligence Brief.

The Core Logic of Regime Survival

North Korea’s leadership draws a direct lesson from governments that surrendered strategic weapons or accepted intrusive disarmament arrangements. Nuclear weapons reduce the risk that the United States and its allies could attempt regime change, while ballistic missiles raise the potential cost of military intervention.

For Pyongyang, the relevant comparison is not simply the Korean Peninsula but Iraq, Libya and other cases in which governments lacked a credible nuclear deterrent. North Korea therefore views denuclearisation as potentially existential: once its weapons are dismantled, its bargaining power and ability to deter a superior coalition would disappear.

The practical implication is that sanctions relief, economic aid or diplomatic recognition are unlikely to persuade North Korea to surrender its entire arsenal unless they are accompanied by a much broader restructuring of the regional security system. That restructuring would have to address the US military presence and alliance structure that Pyongyang cites as the original threat.

North Korean troops and artillery at a military drill, in an image released by state media. Archive photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on North Korea Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Constitutional Status Changes the Calculus

North Korea has moved beyond describing nuclear weapons as temporary bargaining assets. Its 2022 law on nuclear forces established rules governing nuclear use and authorised pre-emptive use in specified circumstances, and in 2023 the country amended its constitution to enshrine its nuclear-weapons policy.

That constitutionalisation matters because it raises the political cost of reversal. Giving up nuclear weapons would no longer mean abandoning a policy choice by the leadership; it would require dismantling a declared constitutional pillar of national defence.

Soldiers marching in formation at night, from archive coverage of North Korean troops.

The Sanctions State and Its Limits

UN sanctions remain in force under the Security Council’s Resolution 1718 framework, which includes an arms embargo and restrictions on goods, finance, shipping and items that could contribute to North Korea’s nuclear, ballistic-missile or other weapons-of-mass-destruction programmes. The sanctions regime has constrained North Korea’s access to foreign currency, energy, industrial equipment and international trade.

But it has not stopped weapons development. The UN’s political affairs leadership said sanctions had slowed progress by constraining finance and access to resources, while stressing that their effectiveness depends on universal implementation.

Three developments have weakened enforcement. Russia vetoed renewal of the UN sanctions-monitoring panel’s mandate in 2024, and a Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team was subsequently established to document violations and evasion.

UN discussions have cited ship-to-ship transfers, prohibited cargo movements and techniques including maritime spoofing. North Korea increasingly relies on cyber operations, overseas workers, illicit shipping and foreign military cooperation to generate funds or obtain technology.

A 2026 US, EU and Australian statement specifically cited overseas workers, malicious cyber activity and unlawful DPRK-Russia cooperation as sources supporting weapons programmes. Sanctions therefore remain a major economic constraint but a weaker diplomatic lever than during the earlier talks.

Russia Has Changed the Strategic Calculation

Russia-North Korea ties have become the most important change since the 2018-19 diplomacy. The United States says North Korea has transferred arms and military materiel to Russia.

This relationship benefits both sides. For Russia, North Korean artillery, missiles, ammunition and personnel can support Russia’s war effort while reducing dependence on other suppliers.

For North Korea, Russia offers diplomatic cover and economic channels.For both governments, cooperation weakens the US-led sanctions coalition and challenges the assumption that international isolation will eventually force Pyongyang back to negotiations.Russia’s opposition to renewing the UN expert panel also reduced transparency around sanctions violations.The partnership does not make North Korea economically secure.

Russia cannot fully replace North Korea’s broader trade and supply networks. But it gives Pyongyang enough strategic breathing room to reject talks that demand immediate disarmament.

A South Korean official speaks beside the national flag. Archive photo.

Why the Trilateral Alliance Reinforces Defiance

The United States, South Korea and Japan have deepened their trilateral coordination. From the allies’ perspective, this is a rational response to North Korea’s missile tests, nuclear expansion and growing Russia relationship.

From Pyongyang’s perspective, however, trilateral cooperation confirms its argument that it faces an integrated hostile bloc. The more closely Washington, Seoul and Tokyo coordinate, the more North Korea can present nuclear weapons as the only reliable counterweight.

This creates a security dilemma. North Korean missile development prompts stronger allied cooperation, which prompts Pyongyang to expand and diversify its arsenal, which produces more sanctions and exercises, which makes a return to the pre-2018 negotiating environment increasingly unlikely.

The immediate risk is not necessarily deliberate war. It is miscalculation involving missile launches, military exercises, maritime incidents, cyberattacks or an assumption that the other side will back down.

What North Korea Might Negotiate

A complete surrender of its nuclear arsenal is improbable under present conditions. More realistic negotiating outcomes would be limited or phased arrangements: a test moratorium, limits on intercontinental ballistic missiles, a freeze on fissile-material production, international monitoring at selected facilities, restrictions on exports of missile technology, hotlines and military risk-reduction measures, or partial sanctions relief for verifiable steps.

North Korea could also seek recognition as a de facto nuclear state without receiving formal acceptance as a legitimate nuclear-weapon state under the Non-Proliferation Treaty. That would resemble a managed-arms-control approach rather than denuclearisation.

The major obstacle is sequencing. Washington and its allies want irreversible concessions; Pyongyang wants benefits before surrendering capabilities.

The longer North Korea modernises, the less attractive complete disarmament becomes and the more likely future diplomacy will focus on arms control.

What It Means for You

For US investors and executives, the practical consequences are sanctions compliance risk, exposure to North Korean cyber operations and continued regional military tension. Companies with supply chains, data or personnel in East Asia should treat North Korea-linked cyber threats as a persistent operational risk rather than a geopolitical abstraction.

Policy readers should understand that the goal of complete denuclearisation is now largely rhetorical. The realistic near-term question is whether any arms-control arrangement can be reached, not whether Pyongyang will surrender its arsenal.

For Latin American governments and businesses, the relevance is indirect but real. North Korean sanctions evasion has historically involved shipping and financial networks that touch multiple jurisdictions, and any tightening of enforcement could affect port and trade compliance far from the Korean Peninsula.

What Is Not Known

No verified official North Korean estimate of warhead numbers, nuclear spending or GDP is available as of October 2026. The Congressional Research Service notes that North Korea publishes no official figure for its nuclear inventory or related expenditure.

The precise scale and nature of Russia-North Korea military technology transfers remain contested. The United States asserts that transfers have occurred, but independent verification is limited because Russia blocked the UN expert panel that previously documented such activity.

It is also unclear whether any internal North Korean debate exists about the costs of constitutional nuclear status. The available evidence points only to public reaffirmation of permanence, not to signals of flexibility.

What to Watch

Watch whether Pyongyang continues to describe nuclear weapons as a permanent national-defence policy or instead reopens language about a conditional moratorium. Any move away from constitutional permanence would be significant, but the available evidence points in the opposite direction.

Monitor the IAEA’s reporting on Yongbyon and fissile-material production. Track the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team’s findings on maritime evasion and cyber-enabled revenue.

Any documented increase in ship-to-ship transfers or overseas worker remittances would indicate that sanctions are weakening further as a lever.Finally, watch Russia’s diplomatic behaviour at the UN.If Moscow continues to shield Pyongyang from new sanctions or monitoring mechanisms, North Korea’s incentives to negotiate will remain low through 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does North Korea refuse to give up nuclear weapons?

North Korea treats nuclear weapons as the central guarantee of regime survival, military deterrence and diplomatic leverage, not as a negotiable programme that can be exchanged for sanctions relief.

What changed after the 2018-19 summit process?

After the Hanoi summit failed over sanctions relief and dismantlement scope, Pyongyang concluded it had more to gain from expanding its deterrent than from trading pieces of it away, and it resumed weapons development.

Is North Korea’s nuclear status written into its constitution?

Yes, North Korea amended its constitution in 2023 to enshrine its nuclear-weapons policy, following a 2022 law that established rules governing nuclear use and authorised pre-emptive use in specified circumstances.

How has Russia changed North Korea’s calculation?

Russia provides diplomatic cover and economic channels, while North Korea supplies arms and personnel to Russia, weakening the US-led sanctions coalition and reducing Pyongyang’s isolation.

What would North Korea be willing to negotiate?

More realistic outcomes than complete denuclearisation include a test moratorium, limits on intercontinental ballistic missiles, a fissile-material freeze, or partial sanctions relief for verifiable steps.

What should US investors watch for in 2027?

Watch IAEA reporting on fissile-material production, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team’s findings on evasion, and any shift in Pyongyang’s constitutional language toward a conditional moratorium.
