World.title: Boko Haram and Nigeria’s Jihadist War Explained
World.content:
NIGERIA · ANALYSIS

Key Facts What is happening Nigeria’s Operation Hadin Kai claimed 48 insurgents killed (the army did not say which faction) in Borno and Yobe on 29–30 October 2026, while repelling coordinated attacks on military positions.

Why it matters The attacks show both insurgent factions retain offensive capacity, meaning Nigeria’s northeast remains a long-term security and investment risk despite tactical military gains.

The numbers The military reported 48 insurgents killed, one Nigerian soldier killed, two lightly wounded, and 42 AK-47 rifles recovered in the two engagements, according to Captain Mohammed Goni on 30 October 2026.

What to watch Whether Operation Hadin Kai sustains air-ground coordination, whether the taxation network of ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province) survives, and how insecurity shapes Nigeria’s 2027 election environment.

What it means for you US investors and policy readers should treat northeast Nigeria as a persistent operational risk zone where military claims do not yet translate into stable civilian administration or predictable business conditions.

ISWAP and Boko Haram are rival jihadist factions fighting for control of northeastern Nigeria, and their October 2026 attacks on military bases show neither has been strategically defeated. For US readers, the conflict matters because it shapes counter-terrorism cooperation, regional stability around Lake Chad, and the risk premium attached to one of Africa’s largest economies.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Nigeria’s northeast is the epicentre of a sixteen-year insurgency that has displaced millions and strained state authority across Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states. This analysis, drawing on the Africa Intelligence Brief, explains who the two main factions are, how strong they remain, and what the military campaign actually achieves beyond headline casualty counts.

The October 2026 Trigger

Nigeria’s Joint Task Force, North East, under Operation Hadin Kai, said troops repelled attacks in Bitta, Gwoza Local Government Area, Borno State, and at the North East Theatre Training School in Buni Yadi, Gujba Local Government Area, Yobe State. The fighting ran from the night of 29 October into the early hours of 30 October 2026.

According to Acting Media Information Officer Captain Mohammed Goni, the military claimed 48 insurgents were killed, without saying how many belonged to Boko Haram or to ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province). One Nigerian soldier died and two were lightly wounded, while recovered materiel included 42 AK-47 rifles, five PKT machine guns, four general-purpose machine guns, one 60mm mortar, 105 AK-47 magazines, two video cameras and thousands of rounds of ammunition.

These are military claims, not independently verified casualty figures. The term “neutralised” may include killed or otherwise put out of action, although the October statement described 48 terrorists as killed and provided no location-by-location breakdown.

The episode matters because the targets were military positions rather than isolated civilian sites. It suggests insurgents retained the confidence and intelligence to mount coordinated assaults.

The city gate of Abuja, Nigeria's capital. File photo, not linked to the story. Photo: Rio Times library

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Boko Haram (Nigeria) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Origins and the 2016 Split

The rivalry subsequently became violent, with both movements competing for recruits, taxation, territory, weapons and influence around the Lake Chad basin.

Office towers in central Lagos, Nigeria's commercial capital. File photo, not linked to the story. Photo: Rio Times library

Boko Haram Versus ISWAP

The distinction between the two factions is operationally important. Negotiations with Boko Haram do not automatically reach ISWAP, and recent reporting on a possible government–Boko Haram dialogue explicitly described ISWAP as a separate rival that was not included.

Boko Haram, whose leader Bakura Doro took over in 2022 (Niger claimed in August 2025 to have killed him, which the group denied), is more locally focused and associated with the legacy of Shekau’s movement. It relies heavily on coercion, looting and extortion, described in reporting as ghanima, and is fragmented into regional factions operating in southeastern Borno, north-central Nigeria and the Mandara Mountains.

ISWAP, whose deputy leader Abu Bilal al-Minuki was killed in a joint Nigerian-US operation in May 2026, is formally tied to Islamic State central leadership and its wider caliphate project. It is more centralised and bureaucratic, with commanders, judges, tax officials and morality enforcers, and it attempts to regulate predation and present itself as a governing authority.

A June 2026 policy brief, “Replacing the State” by Idayat Hassan for the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI), described ISWAP as a proto-state that governs, taxes, adjudicates disputes and provides services such as healthcare, Islamic education, sanitation and credit. This does not make ISWAP benign: it is a coercive jihadist authority, but its ability to provide predictable rules can create reluctant accommodation among civilians who face little effective protection from the formal state.

Territory, Tactics and Strength

The Lake Chad basin, where borders with Niger, Chad and Cameroon make surveillance and pursuit difficult, provides cross-border movement that complicates military containment.Boko Haram’s tactics include raids on villages and military positions, kidnapping, looting, improvised explosive devices, and attacks designed to punish communities cooperating with the state.Its organisational fragmentation makes it harder to defeat through a single decapitation strike, because local commanders can survive even when senior leaders are killed.ISWAP has generally displayed greater military and administrative sophistication, with coordinated assaults on military bases, intelligence collection before operations, taxation of agriculture, fishing, trade and livestock, and limited services in areas where state institutions are weak.

The October 2026 attacks on Bitta and Buni Yadi demonstrate that both factions retain offensive capacity.There is no reliable public, independently verified fighter count as of October 2026.Strength is better assessed through capabilities: ISWAP remains the more institutionally capable faction, Boko Haram remains resilient despite fragmentation, and neither appears to control a conventional state-like territory.

Tinubu Square, a public plaza in central Lagos. File photo, 2014. Photo: Rio Times library

What Operation Hadin Kai Achieves

Operation Hadin Kai can deliver four concrete benefits. First, it protects military installations, preventing the capture of weapons, vehicles, intelligence and personnel that insurgents could use to sustain future attacks.

Second, it raises the cost of attacking. The reported combination of intelligence, surveillance, target-acquisition and reconnaissance capabilities, air support and ground forces can make large assaults riskier, and the recovery of heavy and crew-served weapons suggests the counterattack disrupted an operation with substantial firepower.

Third, it creates local security windows. Successful operations can temporarily reopen roads, allow humanitarian access and enable civil authorities to return, gains that matter for farmers, traders, schools and investors in transport and logistics.

Fourth, it generates intelligence. Captured weapons, cameras, documents, detainees and battlefield communications can reveal routes, commanders and supply networks, making the military’s use of surveillance potentially more important than the headline casualty count.

But the campaign has clear limits. A tactical victory does not remove the tax system that finances ISWAP, air strikes and raids may kill fighters without restoring civilian administration, and insurgents can retreat across borders or disperse into rural communities.

Holding territory requires police, courts, local administration, roads, markets and services after the military arrives.

Humanitarian Cost and Business Risk

The insurgency has produced a long-running humanitarian crisis in northeastern Nigeria. The principal burdens are displacement from villages and agricultural areas, disrupted farming, fishing and trade, food insecurity, kidnapping and forced recruitment, school closures, and civilian deaths from attacks, IEDs and counterinsurgency operations.

The conflict also creates a difficult civilian choice. ISWAP may impose taxes and harsh religious rules, while Boko Haram factions may extort or attack communities, and government forces may offer protection but remain unable to maintain a constant presence outside bases and major towns.

For investors and expatriates, the humanitarian issue is also a business-risk issue. It affects labour mobility, insurance costs, supply-chain reliability, agricultural output, road security and the viability of infrastructure projects in the northeast.

The northeastern insurgency is not located in Nigeria’s main oil-producing core in the Niger Delta, but insecurity still affects the investment environment indirectly. Investors should watch whether insecurity forces larger defence spending and crowds out infrastructure, and whether instability weakens the naira, raises logistics costs or worsens perceptions of Nigerian sovereign risk.

The US Counter-Terrorism Angle

US–Nigeria security cooperation is relevant in three areas: intelligence sharing and analysis, training and equipment for Nigerian security forces, and regional efforts against Islamic State and al-Qaeda-linked networks. The practical value of cooperation depends less on public declarations than on whether intelligence reaches field commanders quickly and whether civilian protection improves.

For Washington, Nigeria matters because instability in the Lake Chad basin can spread across Niger, Chad and Cameroon. It also affects migration, organised crime, arms trafficking and the security of a major African state with substantial energy resources.

For Abuja, US cooperation can improve targeting and logistics, but it carries political sensitivities. Nigerian authorities are likely to resist arrangements perceived as foreign control, while US support may face scrutiny if operations produce civilian casualties or alleged abuses.

What It Means for You

For US investors and executives, the October 2026 battles are a reminder that Nigeria’s northeast remains a persistent operational risk zone. Military claims of tactical success do not yet translate into stable civilian administration, predictable logistics or safe conditions for agricultural and infrastructure investment.

For policy readers, the conflict tests whether US security assistance can help Nigeria move from attrition warfare to a model that restores state authority. The answer will shape regional stability around Lake Chad and the credibility of counter-terrorism partnerships in West Africa.

For expatriates and businesses with Nigerian exposure, the practical implication is to treat security conditions as highly localised. Risk assessments should distinguish between the Niger Delta oil-producing areas and the northeastern insurgency theatre, and between Boko Haram’s fragmented rural networks and ISWAP’s more institutionalised proto-state model.

What Is Not Known

Casualty announcements, captured weapons and attack frequency provide indicators, but they cannot establish total force size.The October 2026 military claims have not been independently verified, and the announcement did not provide a location-by-location casualty breakdown.It is also unclear whether the Bitta and Buni Yadi attacks were coordinated or coincidental, and whether the insurgents’ objective was to capture weapons, test defences or signal continued relevance.Boko Haram, whose leader Bakura Doro took over in 2022 (Niger claimed in August 2025 to have killed him, which the group denied), and ISWAP, whose deputy leader Abu Bilal al-Minuki was killed in a joint Nigerian-US operation in May 2026, are rival jihadist factions that split in 2016.

Finally, it is not known whether the reported government–Boko Haram dialogue will produce any durable agreement, or whether ISWAP would exploit any such deal to expand its own influence among communities seeking protection.

What to Watch

Watch whether Operation Hadin Kai sustains its air-ground coordination beyond October 2026. The test is whether this produces lasting security gains rather than cyclical attack-and-response patterns.

Watch ISWAP’s taxation network. The group’s financial strength depends on its ability to tax agriculture, fishing, trade and livestock in areas where state institutions are weak, and any disruption to that revenue base would be more strategically significant than a single casualty count.

Watch the humanitarian situation through the end of 2026 and into early 2027. Displacement, food insecurity and restricted access to health services and markets will shape civilian attitudes toward both the insurgents and the state, and could influence the 2027 election environment.

Watch for any formal announcement on the reported government–Boko Haram dialogue. If negotiations proceed, the key question is whether ISWAP remains excluded and whether that exclusion drives more aggressive ISWAP attacks to undermine any agreement.

Finally, watch US–Nigeria security cooperation signals through the first quarter of 2027. Any shift in intelligence sharing, training or equipment support would affect Nigeria’s operational tempo and the broader regional counter-terrorism posture around Lake Chad.

Related reading: Igbo People, Language and Culture in Nigeria Explained; Nigeria’s Presidential Challenger Atiku Abubakar; Nigeria Neighbours Explained, West Africa in 2026; more from Nigeria.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between Boko Haram and ISWAP?

Boko Haram is more locally focused and fragmented, relying on coercion and looting. ISWAP is tied to Islamic State central leadership and operates as a more centralised proto-state with taxation, courts and limited services.

How strong are ISWAP and Boko Haram in 2026?

Both factions retain offensive capacity, as shown by the coordinated attacks on military positions in Borno and Yobe on 29–30 October 2026, but neither appears to control conventional state-like territory.

What did Operation Hadin Kai claim in October 2026?

The military claimed 48 Boko Haram and ISWAP fighters were killed in Bitta, Borno State, and Buni Yadi, Yobe State, on 29–30 October 2026. One Nigerian soldier died, two were wounded, and 42 AK-47 rifles were among the recovered weapons.

Where do ISWAP and Boko Haram operate?

The Lake Chad basin allows cross-border movement through Niger, Chad and Cameroon.

How does the insurgency affect US investors?

The northeast is not Nigeria’s main oil-producing zone, but insecurity raises logistics costs, insurance premiums and sovereign risk perceptions. Investors should treat security conditions as highly localised and distinguish between the Niger Delta and the northeastern insurgency theatre.

What is the humanitarian cost of the conflict?

Civilians face a difficult choice between ISWAP taxation, Boko Haram extortion and limited government protection outside major towns.

Will the conflict end before Nigeria’s 2027 election?

There is no evidence of a strategic endgame as of October 2026. The conflict is one of attrition, and the key variables are whether ISWAP’s taxation network is disrupted and whether any government–Boko Haram dialogue produces a durable agreement that does not empower ISWAP.

World.title: Canada’s Metals Face the EU Carbon Border Levy
World.content:
CANADA · ANALYSIS

Key Facts What is happening The EU carbon border levy entered its definitive phase on 1 January 2026, requiring EU importers to account for emissions embedded in covered goods including Canadian iron, steel and aluminium.

The numbers The European Commission set the Q3 2026 CBAM certificate price at €82.32 (about US$92) per tonne of CO₂, published on 5 October 2026.

What to watch CBAM certificate sales begin on 1 February 2027.

What it means for you US-listed miners and steelmakers with European customers should treat the EU carbon border levy as a reporting and margin issue, even when their production sites are outside Europe.

The EU carbon border levy, formally the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, began its definitive phase on 1 January 2026 and now imposes a carbon cost on covered imports into the European Union. For US readers, the mechanism matters because it affects Canadian metals that compete with American steel and aluminium, and because US-listed miners with European sales face new compliance and margin pressures.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Canada is one of the world’s largest exporters of iron ore, steel and aluminium, and the European Union is a major destination for those products. This analysis explains how the levy works, who actually pays it, what it means for Canadian and Latin American metal exporters, and why the issue is now entangled with Canada’s deepening strategic alliance with Brussels, as covered in the USA & Canada Intelligence Brief.

How the EU Carbon Border Levy Works

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, known as CBAM, is not a conventional customs tariff imposed on foreign governments. It is a carbon-pricing system attached to the EU Emissions Trading System, the bloc’s internal carbon market.

The legal obligation falls on the EU importer or its authorised CBAM declarant, not on the Canadian, Brazilian or Chilean producer. That importer must obtain authorised status, declare the volume and embedded emissions of covered goods, and eventually surrender certificates priced against EU carbon-market auctions.

The economic burden, however, travels through the supply chain. European buyers may demand lower prices, insist on emissions data, or shift costs onto foreign suppliers through contract terms.

The definitive regime began on 1 January 2026 after a transitional reporting period that ran from 1 October 2023 through 31 December 2025. During the transition, importers reported emissions but made no financial payments.

Certificate sales are scheduled to begin on 1 February 2027.

Which Goods Are Covered

The initial CBAM sectors are cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity. Iron, steel, aluminium and hydrogen generally use direct emissions, while cement and fertilisers require reporting of both direct and indirect emissions.

The European Commission has also proposed extending coverage to selected steel- and aluminium-intensive downstream products, alongside anti-circumvention rules. Exporters should not assume the initial list will remain permanently limited to primary metal and basic industrial products.

The carbon-cost phase-in is scheduled to reach its full effect by 2034.

The Arpoador waterfront in Rio de Janeiro, with the Dois Irmaos mountain in the distance. File photo, 2016. (Photo: MB-one, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on CBAM Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Canada’s Exposure in Numbers

The European Commission set the Q3 2026 CBAM certificate price at €82.32 (about US$92) per tonne of CO₂, published on 5 October 2026. The Q2 2026 price was €75.28 (about US$84) per tonne, and the Q1 2026 price was €75.36 (about US$84) per tonne.

The Actors and What Each Wants

The Canada–EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement removes many conventional trade barriers, but it does not automatically remove CBAM obligations. Canada’s national carbon-pricing system does not by itself secure an exemption because it is not formally linked to the EU system.

The strategic contradiction is clear. Canada and the EU want closer integration in critical minerals and industrial supply chains, yet Canadian producers of carbon-intensive goods still face CBAM compliance and potential charges.

What It Means for Canadian Exporters

For Canadian metals and cement companies, CBAM is likely to reshape competition in four ways. First, emissions data becomes a market-access requirement, because exporters need plant-level information on energy use, process emissions, production volumes and product composition.

Second, low-carbon production can become a price advantage. Canada’s hydroelectric power base can support comparatively low-emissions aluminium and metals production, but the advantage is not automatic.

Third, smaller exporters face proportionally higher compliance costs. Large producers can spread verification, legal and reporting costs across substantial volumes, while smaller mills and fabricators may find the administrative burden significant.

Fourth, trade diversion may intensify. If the United States imposes or maintains restrictions on Canadian steel and aluminium, more Canadian material could seek European buyers, increasing Canada’s exposure precisely when CBAM is being phased in.

Latin America: Brazil Steel and Chile Copper

Brazilian steel exporters face the same basic rule as Canadian producers: the EU importer bears the formal obligation, but Brazilian mills must supply reliable embedded-emissions data and will feel the cost through price negotiations.Brazil’s position is mixed.It is a major steel producer with established European trade links, but production routes vary considerably, including blast furnaces and electric arc furnaces.Brazil’s use of charcoal in parts of its steel industry can create a potential emissions advantage, but only if the biomass source, land-use impacts and accounting methodology satisfy EU requirements.

Copper is not included in the initial CBAM sectors listed by the European Commission. Chilean copper cathodes, concentrates and many copper products therefore do not face the same direct CBAM liability as steel, aluminium or cement under the current regime.

That does not mean CBAM is irrelevant to Chile. European buyers may increasingly request emissions data from copper mines, smelters and refiners even where the material is outside the formal CBAM list.

The US Angle

The United States is not exempt merely because it is a major trading partner or because American producers face domestic environmental regulation. US steel and aluminium shipments covered by CBAM can generate obligations for the EU importer under the same product rules.

US-listed mining companies with European customers should treat CBAM as a reporting and margin issue even when their mines are located outside Europe. Relevant disclosures to monitor include Scope 1 and relevant Scope 2 emissions, product-level carbon intensity, European sales exposure, customer contracts allocating CBAM costs, verification arrangements, and capital spending on low-carbon production.

The issue is especially relevant to diversified miners whose portfolios include iron ore, metallurgical coal, aluminium-related inputs, nickel or other materials used in covered supply chains. Copper-focused US-listed miners may not face direct CBAM on copper today, but they may still encounter customer data requests and future-scope risk.

What It Means for You

For US investors and executives, the EU carbon border levy is a margin and disclosure issue, not a distant European policy debate. Companies that sell steel, aluminium, cement or fertiliser into the EU, or that supply inputs to those sectors, should review their emissions data and contract terms now.

The mechanism also creates a competitive benchmark. Canadian aluminium made with hydroelectric power may gain a pricing advantage over higher-emissions competitors, including some US producers, if it can document its lower carbon intensity using EU-accepted methodology.

For US-listed miners with diversified portfolios, the key question is whether their European customers will demand emissions data and shift carbon costs onto suppliers. That can affect realised prices even when the miner itself has no direct CBAM obligation.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Canada obtained recognition of its carbon-pricing payments, a bilateral emissions-accounting arrangement, sectoral treatment for low-carbon production, or only a political commitment to continue negotiations.The official search results do not provide a current Statistics Canada value, in Canadian dollars, for Canada’s 2026 exports of CBAM-covered metals to the EU.Any precise export total would need to be compiled from merchandise-trade data using the relevant customs codes.

What to Watch

The Q4 2026 CBAM certificate price is scheduled for publication on 4 January 2027. That figure will set the carbon cost for imports during the final quarter of 2026.

Sales of CBAM certificates begin on 1 February 2027. From that date, authorised declarants can purchase certificates to cover their embedded-emissions liabilities.

Watch for formal Canada–EU implementation details. Any equivalence arrangement, carbon-price recognition or sectoral treatment would materially change the exposure for Canadian metals exporters.

Finally, monitor whether the European Commission proceeds with its proposal to extend CBAM to downstream steel- and aluminium-intensive products. That would broaden the mechanism’s reach beyond primary metals and basic industrial goods.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the EU carbon border levy?

The EU carbon border levy, formally the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, is a carbon-pricing system for selected imports into the European Union. It requires EU importers to account for greenhouse-gas emissions embedded in covered goods and eventually surrender certificates priced against the EU Emissions Trading System.

Who pays the EU carbon border levy?

The EU importer or authorised CBAM declarant pays and reports under the mechanism. The foreign producer does not directly purchase the certificate, although the cost is normally transmitted through the supply chain via lower prices, higher invoices or reduced margins.

Which goods are covered by the EU carbon border levy?

The initial CBAM sectors are cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity. The European Commission has also proposed extending coverage to selected steel- and aluminium-intensive downstream products.

Is copper covered by the EU carbon border levy?

Copper is not included in the initial CBAM sectors listed by the European Commission. Chilean copper cathodes, concentrates and many copper products therefore do not face the same direct CBAM liability as steel, aluminium or cement under the current regime.

When do CBAM certificate sales begin?

Sales of CBAM certificates are scheduled to begin on 1 February 2027.

World.title: American Pilot Overturns Mother’s Costa Rica Will Over Missing Interpreters
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Supreme Court has upheld the annulment of an American woman’s will because she signed a Spanish-language document without the two interpreters the law requires. The decision reopens an estate that includes a 55% stake in a dairy farm that sells its milk to Dos Pinos.

The ruling by the court’s Second Chamber, issued in March 2026, sides with the woman’s son, a pilot who lives in Ohio. The will had left him nothing and named his brother sole and universal heir. Besides the dairy stake, the estate includes several agricultural properties, personal property and investments, according to the facts set out in the ruling.

The woman, a U.S. citizen living in Guanacaste, signed an open will before a notary public in October 2014. She died in February 2019. Three months later, her other son, who also lived in Costa Rica, was appointed executor as the only person apparently named in the will. After learning of his mother’s death, the pilot traveled to Costa Rica in June 2019 with his legal representatives. He sought to establish his standing as a legal heir and to object to the will.

His legal team argued the document lacked the translation required by Article 584 of the Civil Code. Because no record showed that at least two interpreters had taken part, they said, the will was absolutely null. Despite the objection, the notary handling the probate declared the brother sole and universal heir in September 2019. That notary considered it enough that the notary who drew up the will had recorded that she translated it into English herself.

The pilot then sued the estate and his brother directly. Besides the language issue, he alleged that no meeting of interested parties had been called. He also said other assets had been left out of the probate, including household goods, bank accounts, cooperative shares, vehicles and investments of significant value.

He asked the court to declare the will absolutely null and end his brother’s administration of the estate. He also sought an accounting, the return of assets his brother had disposed of, and recognition of both brothers as equal heirs. The brother rejected the claims and raised several defenses, including lack of standing.

In June 2022, the Guanacaste Collegiate Civil Trial Court partially upheld the lawsuit and annulled the will. The court also voided every act that flowed from it, including the executor’s appointment and the sole-heir declaration. It ordered the brother to pay legal costs, with attorney fees set at ¢54.9 million (about $122,000).

The brother appealed to the Second Chamber. He argued that his mother understood Spanish after years in Costa Rica and had signed other documents in the language. In his view, the notary’s English translation was a professional courtesy, not a legal requirement, and the trial court had imposed conditions the law does not contain.

The magistrates disagreed. They concluded it had not been proven that the woman understood Spanish well enough to grasp the legal scope of her own will. A key piece of evidence was the will itself, in which the notary recorded that she had translated it into English because the woman did not understand Spanish well.

The court also weighed testimony from that notary and from a second notary who took part in the signing and later handled the probate. The court treated both statements with caution because both notaries had taken part in the acts under challenge. Their testimony also contradicted what the will itself recorded about the woman’s difficulty with Spanish.

According to the ruling, getting by in Spanish, living in Costa Rica for years or signing documents in the language does not show that a person understands the legal implications of a last will. The justices found that the notary’s own translation could not take the place of the two interpreters required by Article 584. They called that omission an essential defect, rejected the appeal and left the annulment in place.

Article 584 states that anyone making a will in a foreign language before a notary must do so in the presence of two interpreters of their choosing. Those interpreters translate the testator’s instructions into Spanish.

The formality carries particular weight because Costa Rican law gives testators broad control over their estates. Under Article 595 of the Civil Code, a person may leave property to whomever they choose, provided they secure financial support for certain dependents. A will that excludes an adult child can therefore stand if it meets every legal requirement.

André Cappella, an associate attorney at the firm Quatro Legal, said everyday conversation in Spanish or a history of signing documents in the language does not prove that someone understands a will’s implications. He added that it is not enough for a notary who speaks the testator’s language to translate the document. When there is doubt, he said, the prudent course is to use the two interpreters the law requires. A version of the will in the testator’s own language can also be prepared, but it does not replace the legal formalities.

Cappella said many defects in a will cannot be corrected after the testator dies. Other common grounds for annulment include a missing date, time or signature. Others are failing to read the document, using witnesses who have an interest in the estate, and failing to complete every formality in a single sitting.

Unless another valid will exists, the estate now falls under the rules for succession without a will. Under Article 572 of the Civil Code, the first order of heirs is a person’s children, parents and surviving spouse or partner. The case shows that the validity of a will in Costa Rica can depend as much on how it was signed as on what it says.

World.title: Scarlet Macaws Start Nesting in Costa Rica, and You Can Watch Live
World.content:
Scarlet macaws (Ara macao) on Costa Rica’s Central Pacific coast have begun pairing off for a new breeding season, and anyone with a phone or computer can watch part of it unfold from inside the nest. Punta Leona Beach Club & Nature Resort, in Garabito near Tárcoles, has added three camera-equipped artificial nests to its scarlet macaw conservation program, bringing the total to 11 for the 2026 season. The new nests were installed with support from Grupo INS, the state-owned insurance group.

The cameras stream live on the program’s website, lapasrojaspuntaleona.com, which also has an English-language version. The birds are wild, not captive or handled, and the cameras let researchers follow them without disturbing the nests. According to the program, courtship runs from October through December, when pairs form, search for cavities and prepare nest sites. Egg-laying and incubation follow, with the first eggs and chicks expected between December and January 2027. The nesting period runs through June.

The cameras will record how many eggs are laid in each nest, how many hatch and how many chicks survive to leave it, along with the toll taken by natural predators. Figures the program released in February show that eggs take 23 to 28 days to hatch and chicks spend 78 to 90 days in the nest before their first flight.

Across the 2017 to 2025 seasons, the program recorded 98 scarlet macaw eggs in its monitored nests. Of those, 69 hatched and 46 chicks fledged, according to the same February figures. The 11 artificial nests are named Guanacaste, Guayabón, Wisconsin, Ceibo Bajo, Ceibo Alto, Pochote, Panamá, Camíbar, Espavel, Guayacán and Alfa. In February, the program reported monitoring 17 nests, 10 natural and seven artificial. The new announcement does not say how many natural nests are being followed this season.

Each fiberglass nest stands about 1 meter (3.3 feet) tall and 50 centimeters (20 inches) across, with a cavity designed to mimic a tree hollow. The nests are mounted in trees 15 to 20 meters (49 to 66 feet) tall and lined with a layer of wood chips. Biologist Christopher Vaughan, who coordinates the project, said the program began 36 years ago and that early studies of natural nesting cavities shaped the design of the artificial ones. The first nests were built from wood, plastic and other materials in a workshop at Punta Leona, he said.

Vaughan said some of the residents who joined the nest-building effort had been poachers known as laperos, who took macaw chicks from the wild. Today they are the ones who build the artificial nests, he said, calling it an excellent example of habitat management. That history still matters. In other parts of the country, poachers continue to target macaw chicks in the Osa region during breeding season.

The program says about 215 scarlet macaws were counted in the area in the early 1990s and that current monitoring puts the number near 800, a nearly fourfold increase. Earlier program materials put the 1992 baseline at 226 birds. In April, Vaughan estimated that about 70 of the roughly 800 wild scarlet macaws in the Central Pacific live at Punta Leona itself.

Alongside the nests, the program has protected habitat and set up nurseries of native trees to reforest the region, providing future nesting trees and food sources. According to the program, the macaws nest in trees such as ceiba, gallinazo and javillo, and feed on seeds from species including royal palm, ojoche, espavel, teak and beach almond.

Scarlet macaws are now also recorded in communities including Esparza, Orotina, San Mateo, Acosta and Parrita, and around La Cangreja National Park, the program says. Nearby Carara National Park remains one of the most reliable places in the country to see them in flight. Gerald Jiménez, Punta Leona’s corporate relations manager, said the resort aims to go beyond sustainability and leave its surroundings better than it found them. The resort also called on other companies to join conservation efforts, as Grupo INS has done.

Punta Leona has also spoken out on the keeping of wild birds. In April, it opposed a draft revision of Costa Rica’s wildlife regulations that critics said could open the door to keeping macaws and parrots in captivity. The program’s long-running work with scarlet macaws rests on the opposite idea, that the birds breed and fly free.

The nest streams run around the clock, and activity inside the nests is expected to pick up from December, when the first eggs are due.

World.title: Expect Gusts Up to 85 km/h and Rain in Costa Rica This Weekend
World.content:
If you’re heading into the mountains or to northern Guanacaste today, expect strong, gusty winds. Gusts could reach 85 km/h (53 mph) in those areas on Saturday, Oct. 31, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). In the Central Valley and the North Pacific, gusts should run between 30 and 60 km/h (19 to 37 mph). That’s enough to rattle loose roofing, bring down branches and push high-sided vehicles around on exposed stretches of road.

The cause is rising atmospheric pressure over the northern Caribbean, which is driving the trade winds across Costa Rica harder than usual. The IMN expects moderate to strong winds to continue through the rest of the weekend, not just today. Rain is also in the forecast. Extra moisture is bringing showers to the Caribbean and the Northern Zone from early in the day, and that rain is expected to spread into the mountains of the Central Valley and areas to the east.

In the afternoon, the IMN expects isolated downpours in the mountains of the Central Pacific and scattered downpours with thunderstorms in the South Pacific. Along the South Pacific coast, the rain could last into the early evening, while the Central Valley may see occasional showers.

If you have a volcano hike, a canopy tour or a high-elevation park on your schedule, wind is the main thing to watch. Ridgelines and open travetake the strongest gusts, so check with your tour operator before you drive out, since wind can affect zip lines and hanging bridges.

On the road, give yourself extra time on mountain routes and across Guanacaste’s open lowlands, where crosswinds hit hardest. Watch for fallen branches and debris after strong gusts, and keep both hands on the wheel. At home, bring in or tie down anything loose on patios and balconies, from chairs to potted plants. Gusts this strong can damage roofs, snap tree limbs and bring down power lines, so outages are possible in the windiest areas.

In the South Pacific, get off the beach and out of the water at the first sound of thunder, because lightning often strikes ahead of the rain. The wind and showers also arrive as the Pacific coast wraps up its highest tides of the season, which run through today. Going out tonight for Halloween? A light jacket is a good idea in the Central Valley, where occasional showers and gusty winds could linger into the evening.

Conditions can change quickly when the trade winds pick up. Check the IMN’s latest update before heading out, and plan for a breezy, unsettled weekend across much of Costa Rica.

World.title: Grynspan Holds Lead as New Emirati Candidate Disappoints in Race to Lead UN
World.content:
Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan again finished first on Friday in the UN Security Council’s seventh informal vote in the race for secretary-general, while the new Emirati candidate delivered a disappointing showing. In a closed-door vote, the Security Council’s 15 members anonymously marked each candidate as “encourage,” “discourage” or “no opinion.”

Grynspan, who took leave from her position at UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) to campaign, received 11 “encourage” votes and four “discourage” votes, according to a diplomatic source. Diplomat Lana Nusseibeh, who recently entered the race and was appearing on the ballot for the first time, received seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes.

Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, the current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, received nine “encourage” votes, four “discourage” votes and two “no opinion” votes. Former Guyanese Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett received eight, six and one, respectively. Both finished ahead of the Emirati candidate.

Unlike the previous round, this vote did not use different-colored ballots to distinguish the votes of the Security Council’s five permanent members. In that previous round, none of the seven candidates avoided a negative vote from at least one of the countries with veto power: the United Kingdom, France, the United States, China and Russia.

Former Senegalese President Macky Sall subsequently withdrew, and Nusseibeh, 48, entered the race. Candidates may join at any point until a selection is made. Until then, she had served as minister of state at the UAE’s Foreign Ministry and as special envoy to the United Nations and the European Union. She previously served as the UAE’s ambassador to the UN from 2013 to 2024. Several human rights organizations have opposed her candidacy, accusing her country of financing paramilitary forces in Sudan.

To succeed Portugal’s António Guterres, whose second term ends at the close of this year, a candidate must secure nine votes and avoid a veto. Once a consensus is reached, the candidate’s name will be submitted to the General Assembly, which in practice follows the Security Council’s recommendation.

Under a tradition of geographic rotation that is not always observed, Latin America is laying claim to the position. Meanwhile, numerous countries are pushing for a woman to lead the UN for the first time.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Creepiest Ghost Stories and Mysterious Legends
World.content:
Every society has tales of terror that challenge our imaginations and our courage. Costa Rica has folk tales that include a priest who lost his head over a woman and now walks the land without a head, a wrastle son who was changed into a devil dog named Cadejos that roams at night, snarling and rattling his chain, and a cart that rolls through the rural areas without oxen to pull it, all because its owner built it with lumber meant for the church. These are stories that go way back in time. Some say they are superstitions. Others swear they are true.

There are also some more recent creepy stories that have gained believers because they have been repeated so many times, and they just could, maybe, possibly be true. Back in the 1900’s, cries and screams coming from a newly filled cemetery plot were reported in Heredia but by the time the bureaucracy got around to investigating and opened the casket, it was all scratched and ripped inside.

In Atenas a blond, naked ghost called Macho Chingo was reported walking along the hills. Macho is a common word for someone blond and chingo is used for someone in the buff. Some reports said he was wearing a necktie and that he’s German. In Alajuela everyone knows about the nun that haunts the old hospital building.

But there is one story from more modern times that occurred in Rio Segundo, an eastern suburb of Alajuela that just, possibly, could be true because some people swear to it. Not too long ago Rio Segundo was a decidedly rural area with big coffee haciendas and whole families lived on the land to help with the coffee work.

Among them a young man and his sweetheart. As they planned their wedding the owner of the hacienda offered the couple a vacant house on the property for them to spend their wedding night. According to custom , the groom wore white pants and a white shirt and a red cummerbund embroidered by the bride.

After the ceremony the pair took off for the vacant house located in a far corner of the farm where nobody would dare to bother them. The house was large, with multiple nooks, crannies, closets and cubbords and to the young couple, from humble backgrounds, it was a palace. Never again would they find themselves in such a spacious home. It prompted them to challenge each other in a game of hide and seek. There were so many great places to hide!

When it was the groom’s turn he hid so well that his new wife wandered from room to room in the dim light trying to find him. At first it was a game, a thrilling game, in anticipation of the night to come. But as minutes passed and then hours, she became weary and worried. Where could he be?

She wandered all through the house several times but she never found him? Did he repent getting married and fled? Or did he fall and lose consciousness? After much time searching she gave up, tired and depressed and heart broken. The love of her life was gone. As time went by she accepted the fact and returned to her parent’s home to get on with her life.

Years went by and the property was sold along with the house. The new owners took their time clearing out all the old furniture left inside including several trunks and barrels, opening them up to see if there was anything left of value inside. And there, in one of the trunks, they found a skeleton dressed in white with a red embroidered cummerbund.

There is no conclusion for this story. Did the bride weep over her lost sweetheart Or was she angry at the skeleton for messing up her life? Did she want the cummebund back? And more curious, how come the guy didn’t figure out how to escape, or was he still waiting all that time for her to find him? Will we ever know the truth behind this story?

World.title: Suspect in Playas del Coco Killing of American Will Be Held for One Year
World.content:
A 22-year-old woman suspected of killing American businessman Marc Walter Fleming in Playas del Coco will remain behind bars for at least the next year while prosecutors build their case, after a criminal court in Liberia ordered her held in pretrial detention yesterday. The Public Prosecutor’s Office said the Liberia Criminal Court granted the measure at the request of the Liberia Deputy Prosecutor’s Office.

The suspect, identified only by her last name, Ortiz, is under investigation for aggravated homicide, an offense that carries a possible sentence of up to 35 years in prison in Costa Rica. Pretrial detention is a precautionary measure and not a finding of guilt. It allows investigators to keep a suspect in custody while evidence is gathered, typically when a court considers there is a risk of flight or of interference with the investigation.

The ruling came three days after agents from the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) arrested Ortiz on Tuesday at a residential complex in San Felipe de Alajuelita, south of San José. She had been sought since October 16, when officers raided a home in La Capri de Desamparados but did not find her.

Fleming was found dead on September 27 inside his apartment in a condominium tower in Sardinal de Carrillo, in the Playas del Coco area of Guanacaste. According to the OIJ, security cameras recorded him arriving at the complex with a young woman and, about two hours later, the woman leaving alone on foot through the main gate.

Investigators allege that Fleming was struck repeatedly in the head with the glass jar of a blender. According to prosecutors, investigators consider Ortiz the last person known to have been with him before his death. Authorities have not announced a motive. The OIJ has said three Rolex watches, each estimated by investigators to be worth more than $25,000, are missing from the apartment, along with several of Fleming’s bank cards. Investigators have been tracing purchases allegedly made with those cards at businesses in Playas del Coco, Playa Flamingo and Abangares after his death.

A second suspect, a woman with the last name Zeledón, was detained on October 16 in San Miguel de Desamparados. Authorities suspect she helped Ortiz leave Guanacaste for the San José area after the killing. The same Liberia court previously ordered her held for three months, and investigators are examining whether both women allegedly used the victim’s cards.

Fleming, who had worked as a senior executive in the metals industry in California, had bought the condominium in Playas del Coco earlier this year. Security footage connected to the case circulated widely on social media in the weeks after his death, and the OIJ released photographs of Ortiz and asked the public for help locating her.

OIJ officials have credited tips from the public, along with intelligence work by the agency’s Homicide Section and its Liberia regional office, with leading agents to the suspect. The one-year detention gives prosecutors time to analyze security recordings, financial transactions and forensic evidence before deciding whether to formally accuse either woman. Neither suspect has been convicted of any crime in connection with Fleming’s death, and both are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

World.title: Costa Rica Hotel Wins Two World Travel Awards, Putting Tárcoles in the Spotlight
World.content:
A hotel on Costa Rica’s Central Pacific coast has won two international tourism awards, bringing attention to Tárcoles, a area known for its crocodile-filled river, fishing traditions and surrounding tropical forests. Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, part of Marriott International’s Autograph Collection, was named Costa Rica’s Leading Boutique Hotel 2026 and Mexico & Central America’s Leading New Hotel 2026 at the World Travel Awards.

The recognition comes less than a year after the hotel opened in January 2026 and marks an early achievement for a property competing in Costa Rica’s established tourism industry. The awards were announced at the World Travel Awards Caribbean and Americas ceremony, held in Jamaica on October 11.

Established in 1993, the World Travel Awards recognize hotels, airlines, destinations and other tourism businesses through online voting by travel industry professionals and the public. Verified industry professionals receive double voting weight, and awards are presented in national, regional and worldwide categories.

Santa Lucía’s two victories were in the national boutique hotel category and the regional new hotel category, placing it ahead of other nominated properties in Costa Rica, Mexico and Central America. José Eduardo Arteaga, general manager of Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, welcomed the recognition, saying it provides an opportunity to introduce more international travelers to Tárcoles and Costa Rica’s Central Pacific region.

Arteaga said the awards also help showcase the variety of tourism experiences available in Costa Rica, particularly in communities outside the best-known tourist destinations. Near Carara National Park and the Tárcoles River in Puntarenas province, the hotel has 84 guest rooms on a 150-hectare (371-acre) property surrounded by tropical forest.

The property combines traditional Costa Rican hacienda-style architecture with modern rooms and activities focused on nature and local culture. Guests can participate in birdwatching, guided nature experiences, traditional Costa Rican cooking and cultural activities. The hotel also offers restaurants, a spa and other amenities.

Its location provides access to Carara National Park, known for its scarlet macaws and diverse birdlife, as well as the Tárcoles River, where visitors frequently see large American crocodiles along the riverbanks. The surrounding region offers beaches, wildlife tours and outdoor activities, making Tárcoles an accessible destination for travelers exploring the Central Pacific coast.

Beyond attracting visitors, the hotel says its operations support the surrounding economy through employment in hospitality, food service, maintenance and other services. The company also reports purchasing goods and services from businesses in the area. Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda promotes what it calls regenerative tourism, an approach intended to support forest conservation and strengthen connections with nearby communities. The extent of those environmental and economic benefits has not been independently quantified.

The awards come as Costa Rica’s tourism industry continues to report growth in international arrivals and visitor spending. According to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT), Costa Rica welcomed 1,733,596 international visitors during the first six months of 2026, an increase of 7% compared with the same period in 2025.

Of those visitors, 1,605,360 arrived by air, representing year-over-year growth of 7.8%. Meanwhile, figures from the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) show that foreign visitors spent approximately $3.356 billion during the first half of 2026, an increase of 8.5% compared with the previous year.

Tourism also remains an important source of employment, accounting for 167,661 direct jobs during the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). For Santa Lucía Jungle Hacienda, the two awards offer international recognition during its first year of operation. For Tárcoles, they provide another opportunity to draw attention to a part of Costa Rica where wildlife, local traditions and tourism remain closely connected.

World.title: For First Time, Costa Rica Votes Against UN Call to End US Embargo on Cuba
World.content:
Costa Rica voted against the annual United Nations resolution calling on the United States to lift its economic embargo on Cuba, the first time the country has opposed the measure since the General Assembly began voting on it in 1992.The resolution passed on Wednesday with 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions. General Assembly resolutions are not binding, and the embargo remains in place.

Costa Rica was the only Central American country to vote no. Nicaragua and Panama voted in favor, Honduras abstained, and Guatemala and El Salvador did not take part.The vote completes a gradual shift. Costa Rica abstained in 1992 and then backed the resolution for more than three decades. In October 2025 it abstained for the first time in that span, and in July 2026 it was one of nine countries to vote against a procedural motion to reopen debate on the embargo.

The change follows a sharp break with Havana. In March, under then-President Rodrigo Chaves, Costa Rica closed its embassy in Cuba and asked Cuban diplomats to leave, citing growing restrictions on freedoms and worsening living conditions on the island. The government later reaffirmed the split.

In September, then-Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar said a review of Costa Rica’s position would mean changing how the country votes on the resolution. He said the government views the hardship facing Cubans as imposed by their own government, argued that Latin American governments had been too lukewarm toward Havana, and ruled out restoring diplomatic ties until Cuba is free. Tovar made the remarks shortly after meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Washington.

Wednesday’s vote was the first on the resolution under President Laura Fernández, who took office in May. It came two weeks after Ana Elena Pinto became foreign minister on Oct. 15, during a month of turnover in the country’s diplomatic and trade leadership that included the dismissal of the trade minister. The Foreign Ministry has not published an explanation of the vote.

Costa Rica joined a bloc of opponents that grew from seven countries in 2025 to 17 this year. Alongside the United States and Israel, it included Argentina, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Hungary and Ukraine. Support for the resolution fell from 165 votes in 2025 and 187 in 2024. Germany and Italy, which had previously voted in favor, abstained.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz rejected the idea that the embargo is the only cause of Cuba’s economic problems, arguing that there is no blockade and pointing to Cuba’s trade with other countries and some US exports to the island. He said the number of countries changing their position had tripled and that he expected it to keep growing.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla said the sanctions directly harm the Cuban people, mainly by restricting access to food, medicine and fuel, and said US pressure would not prevail over the facts. Cuban officials accused Washington of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other penalties if they supported the resolution.

The General Assembly has passed versions of the resolution regularly since 1992. The votes carry political weight but have no power to lift the embargo.

World.title: Police seek stolen $3,500 motorcycle in Punta Gorda
World.content:
Police seek stolen $3,500 motorcycle in Punta Gorda

By Zoila Palma: Police are seeking the public’s assistance in locating a stolen motorcycle belonging to Joseph Lopez of Jacinto Village, Toledo District.

The motorcycle, a red and black 2026 Lifan 250 Xtrail valued at $3,500, was reportedly stolen from Middle Street in Punta Gorda Town sometime around 2:00 a.m. on Wednesday, October 28, 2026.

The stolen motorcycle bears license plate TOL-M-7068 and VIN LF3YCN4D4PA0007.

Anyone with information that could assist police in recovering the motorcycle or identifying those responsible is urged to contact Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 Tip App, or report to the nearest police station.

World.title: Minister of National Security and COMPOL call Emergency mediation session following deadly shootings
World.content:
Minister of National Security and COMPOL call Emergency mediation session following deadly shootings

By Zoila Palma: This morning, the Minister of National Security and Commissioner of Police Richard Rosado called an emergency mediation session.

Footage from 7news Belize showed Minister Michel Chebat, COMPOL Rosado and gang-affiliated figures and mediators at the meeting.

The meeting was called after 4 people were shot dead on the Coastal Plain Highway of including a minor.
