World.title: Mopan Technical High School celebrates successful 2nd annual RAÍCES Cultural evening
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School celebrates successful 2nd annual RAÍCES Cultural evening

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School is celebrating the success of its second annual RAÍCES: A Cultural Evening, which brought together students, teachers, parents and the wider community for a night of culture, entertainment and celebration.

The event attracted an overwhelming turnout, with La Cancha Marshalleck filled to capacity as supporters gathered to celebrate the rich cultural heritage of Belize and Central America.

The classes delivered presentations showcasing the traditions, diversity and cultural identity of Belize and other Central American countries.

Students demonstrated their creativity, talent and teamwork through performances and cultural displays, highlighting the importance of preserving and celebrating the region’s heritage.

Following the event, Mopan Technical High School expressed gratitude to its students, teachers, staff, parents, performers, participants and community supporters for contributing to its success.

World.title: Belize City Mayor meets King Charles III at Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting
World.content:
Belize City Mayor meets King Charles III at Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting

By Zoila Palma: Belize City Mayor Bernard Wagner has met King Charles, Head of the Commonwealth, during engagements surrounding the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

Wagner, who serves as Chair of the Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF), had the opportunity to meet the British monarch as part of activities surrounding the high-level Commonwealth gathering.

The meeting highlights Belize City’s participation in discussions and engagements involving leaders and representatives from across the Commonwealth.

As CLGF Chair, Wagner continues to advocate for stronger local governance, sustainable urban development and greater collaboration among the Commonwealth’s 56 member nations.

World.title: International News: Nearly 6 million Haitians face severe hunger as crisis deepens
World.content:
International News: Nearly 6 million Haitians face severe hunger as crisis deepens

By Zoila Palma: Nearly six million people in Haiti are experiencing severe food insecurity, including almost two million facing emergency levels of hunger, according to a new report released Wednesday by the United Nations-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).

The report estimates that 5.94 million Haitians are struggling to access sufficient food, representing more than half of the country’s population.

The worsening crisis is being driven by escalating gang violence, widespread displacement, high food and fuel prices, and extreme weather conditions associated with El Niño.

Armed gangs have forced farmers from their lands and blocked major roads, disrupting food supplies to Port-au-Prince and other communities.

Humanitarian organizations are also struggling to reach affected families, with some forced to travel as far as 15 kilometres to access food distribution sites. The IPC warns that the number of people facing severe hunger could rise to 6.35 million by mid-2027.

Humanitarian agencies are calling for urgent assistance as violence continues to displace families and deepen food shortages.

World.title: International News: U.S. Secretary of State and Brazilian Foreign Minister agree to meet following diplomatic tensions
World.content:
International News: U.S. Secretary of State and Brazilian Foreign Minister agree to meet following diplomatic tensions

By Zoila Palma: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira have agreed to meet in the coming weeks following a brief conversation at a Group of 20 (G20) foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta.

The meeting, hosted by Rubio, is expected to take place ahead of the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for December in Miami, Reuters report.

The planned meeting comes amid diplomatic tensions between the two countries over Brazil’s failure to approve President Donald Trump’s nominee for U.S. ambassador and Washington’s decision to grant a visa to Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro following his election defeat.

World.title: Belize advances Biodiversity conservation efforts at COP17 in Armenia
World.content:
Belize advances Biodiversity conservation efforts at COP17 in Armenia

By Zoila Palma: Belize joined international representatives at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17), held from October 19 to 30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, to participate in global discussions on protecting biodiversity and strengthening conservation efforts.

Belize’s participation provided an opportunity to promote its natural heritage, build international partnerships and exchange knowledge on strategies to address biodiversity loss.

Minister of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, Orlando Habet, led Belize’s delegation during the High-Level Segment on October 27 and 28, accompanied by the technical team from the Belize National Biodiversity Office (NBIO). Belize’s participation comes as countries work to implement the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and strengthen national commitments to protecting nature.

The Corozal Sustainable Future Initiative (CSFI) also participated in COP17, with team members engaging in discussions at the Meridian Exhibition Center’s Blue and Green Zones. In the Blue Zone, discussions focused on implementing global biodiversity targets, including addressing human-wildlife conflict, improving ecological connectivity and exploring the use of technology and artificial intelligence in conservation. In the Green Zone, the team explored innovative initiatives presented by academic institutions and local businesses while exchanging experiences with organizations pursuing similar conservation goals.

Belize’s participation comes as more countries submit updated National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs), which outline national commitments to addressing nature loss.

These international engagements offer Belize opportunities to strengthen its biodiversity protection efforts and safeguard its natural resources for future generations.

World.title: Dia de los Muertos Street Fest comes alive in Benque Viejo this Sunday
World.content:
Dia de los Muertos Street Fest comes alive in Benque Viejo this Sunday

By Zoila Palma: Benque Viejo del Carmen is preparing to celebrate culture, tradition and community at the third annual Día de los Muertos Street Fest on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

The event, organized by Blazeful Vibes in collaboration with the Benque Viejo Town Council, will take place in front of Cancha Marshalleck from 4:00 p.m. until midnight.

The street fest is expected to feature more than 35 vendors offering food, drinks and local products, along with music, performances and competitions with prizes.

Entertainment will include music by DJ IconicSound Chavez, while community members can participate in competitions for Best Dressed Catrín and Catrina, Best Made Ixpasha and Best Decorated Booth for vendors.

Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a vibrant cultural tradition that honors the memory of loved ones who have passed away through remembrance, offerings, flowers and candles.

See you there!

World.title: Caricom: UK apology for slavery would be welcomed, but reparations must remain on the table
World.content:
Prime Minister of St Lucia Phillip J Pierre

GEORGETOWN, Guyana (CMC) – The Caribbean Community (Caricom) has welcomed British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s openness to a formal apology for slavery and structured dialogue with affected countries, but insists that reparatory justice must remain central to any discussions.

In a statement issued on Saturday, Caricom Chair and Saint Lucia’s Prime Minister, Philip J Pierre, said the Community was ready to engage with the United Kingdom but rejected Burnham’s position that reparations were not “the right answer”.

Burnham, who is due to attend the November 1-4 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, has said he is “open” to listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of Britain for its role in the slave trade, but ruled out considering financial reparations.

READ: UK PM ‘open’ to slavery apology but not reparations

“I do not believe that is the right answer,” he wrote in the Guardian. “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Burnham instead offered a “structured dialogue” with those affected by the slave trade: “Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do. Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he added.

Pierre said Burnham’s expression of personal sorrow and regret for the suffering caused by slavery and its continuing effects, together with his willingness to consider a formal apology on behalf of the British state, represented a significant development.

“No British Prime Minister has gone this far before. It would be wrong of us not to say so, and we welcome it in the spirit in which it appears to be offered,” Pierre said. “For more than a decade, this Community has asked for exactly such a dialogue. We are ready to engage.”

However, the Caricom Chair said the Community did not accept the argument that reparations were inappropriate or that Britain’s responsibility had ended because present-day citizens had not personally participated in slavery.

“Reparatory justice has never been about individual guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions – and that responsibility does not expire with the passing of generations,” he said.

Pierre pointed to Britain’s role in legislating for, protecting and profiting from slavery, as well as its decision to compensate enslavers at Emancipation while formerly enslaved people received no land, wealth or compensation.

He noted that the loan raised to compensate enslavers was still being repaid by British taxpayers until February 2015.

The consequences of slavery, he said, continue to be felt across the Caribbean through chronic disease, inequalities in education and opportunity, economies shaped by extraction, national debt and vulnerability to economic and climate shocks.

Pierre said a formal apology would be an important first step, but argued that it must be accompanied by practical measures to address the lasting effects of slavery.

He pointed to Caricom’s Ten-Point Plan for Reparatory Justice, which includes a formal apology, public health, education and training, cultural heritage restitution and reconnection, psychological rehabilitation, technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, debt cancellation, monetary compensation and decolonisation.

He said the proposed dialogue must allow for discussion of every element of the plan, as well as reparations for the genocide of Indigenous Peoples and the harm caused to people brought from India and China to sustain colonial systems.

“A dialogue that begins by placing reparations outside the room cannot be a complete dialogue,” Pierre said.

The Caricom Chair also acknowledged the United Kingdom’s initiative, to be led by former British prime minister Gordon Brown, to restructure the debt of the poorest Commonwealth countries.

He said the Community would examine the proposal seriously but cautioned that most Caricom member states were classified as middle- or high-income economies and were routinely excluded from concessional relief despite their vulnerability to climate and economic shocks.

“Any initiative that is to be meaningful for our region must measure vulnerability, not income alone,” he said, adding that debt relief could not be used as a substitute for reparatory justice.

Pierre said the Prime Ministerial Sub-Committee on Reparations, led by Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, and the Caricom Reparations Commission, chaired by Sir Hilary Beckles, were prepared to work with the British Government on the terms, agenda and timetable for structured dialogue.

He said he looked forward to meeting Burnham in Antigua and Barbuda in the coming days, as the country prepares to host the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

“Our ancestors did not receive justice in their lifetime. We owe it to them, and to the generations who will come after us, to see this work through – with dignity, with patience, and with resolve,” Pierre said.

World.title: UK PM ‘open’ to slavery apology but not reparations
World.content:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham chairs a meeting of the National Economic Council in Glasgow on October 30, 2026, that focuses on driving growth in every region of the United Kingdom. (Photo: AFP)

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday he was “open” to the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations.

Writing in The Guardian days before attending a Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean, and as King Charles III tours the region, the British premier argued that “we need to face up to the past”.

With London under pressure to formally apologise for its pivotal part in the trade and compensate Caribbean nations, he pledged to have “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future”.

Burnham said he wanted to “express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today”, but insisted reparations were not “the right answer”.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” he wrote in the op-ed.

The transatlantic slave trade was a “brutal and barbaric violation” of enslaved people’s rights, the UK leader added, offering a “structured dialogue with those affected”.

“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.”

Burnham also revealed he planned to launch a new debt restructuring drive for the poorest Commonwealth countries, led by former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown.

He vowed to work with “global partners” to help those countries repay “over a longer time period and with better rates”.

– ‘Suffering’ –

The issues around slavery have loomed large over King Charles’s ongoing nine-day visit to three Caribbean countries, which will include an address to the Commonwealth summit.

Burnham is also set to attend the gathering that runs from Sunday to Wednesday in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda.

The 56-member Commonwealth — which Charles, 77, helms — is mainly composed of British ex-colonies, with the UK’s central role in slavery and the treatment of its former subjects long a contentious issue within the organisation.

In the Bahamas on Tuesday, the monarch acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” during the first leg of his visit.

Meanwhile in Guyana on Friday he visited an execution site of local people during British colonial rule, pausing to reflect in a gesture seen as indicating his awareness of that past injustice.

Britain has never formally apologised for slavery or agreed to pay reparations.

The country profited for centuries from colonialism and the slave trade, but argues it also led the way in the latter’s abolition.

In 1833, the UK parliament passed a law to abolish slavery in most of the British Empire.

Denis O’Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, which advocates for reparations for slavery for Caribbean nations, said London “must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now”.

“This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice,” he added.

However UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Saturday there was “no need” to revisit the issue of formally saying sorry, while reiterating her firm opposition to reparations.

She urged the Commonwealth to “look forward” and “not endlessly backwards”.

“Slavery was an evil in which people from every continent and region participated,” she wrote on X.

“We should be honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today.”

World.title: Udinese striker Davis eyeing Reggae Boyz spot
World.content:
Udinese's British forward #09 Keinan Davis celebrates after scoring a penalty kick during the Italian Serie A football match between Inter Milan and Udinese at San Siro stadium in Milan on August 31, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

Udinese striker Keinan Davis says discussions have taken place about representing Jamaica, but the England-born forward is still awaiting the completion of his Jamaican passport application before making the next step towards international football.

Davis, who has been enjoying an encouraging spell with Italian Serie A club Udinese, provided an update on his international future during an interview with CBS Sports Golazo, revealing that conversations have already taken place about the possibility of wearing the Reggae Boyz colours.

“I’ve had some conversations,” Davis said, while explaining that sorting out his Jamaican passport remains a major priority.

The 28-year-old 6ft 3 inches striker, born in England of Jamaican descent, said the administrative process was taking some time but expressed hope that the matter would be resolved.

“The procedure takes a little time, but we’ll see what happens in the future. I’m sorting out the passport,” he explained.

He also admitted that his injury history had previously influenced discussions about committing to international football, particularly given the demands of travelling between Europe and the Caribbean.

Davis, who represented England at the Under 20 level, said that when he spoke with Udinese last year, consideration was given to whether the additional travelling associated with international duty would be the best option for him as he sought to establish himself and remain available for club football.

However, the striker indicated that his current physical condition has improved and that he is determined to maintain his fitness.

“But now I’m well and I want to continue to be well,” he said.

The latest comments will provide encouragement for Jamaica, which has been keen to strengthen its attacking options.

His potential involvement would be a significant addition to the Reggae Boyz’ attacking department, given his physical presence, pace and experience in European football.

– Howard Walker

World.title: FAO equips Jamaican farmers with adapted greenhouse technologies
World.content:
Digital tools are now being used as part of adapted greenhouse technologies to advance precise vegetable production in Jamaica.

SEVERAL vegetable farmers across Jamaica are now combining adapted greenhouse covering materials and digital sensors to improve growing conditions and support more efficient crop production.

These efforts are supported by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) project “Digital Solutions to Improve Horticultural Crop Management in the Caribbean”, which is nearing completion.

In a media release on Friday the FAO said, the project was implemented in collaboration with Jamaica’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, the project has provided beneficiary farmers with adapted greenhouse covering materials and environmental, soil and water sensors, together with technical guidance on their installation, use and application in crop management under protected cultivation systems.

The adapted covering materials were introduced to help farmers manage high temperatures that can affect crop production under protected structures, a common challenge for vegetable production across the Caribbean.

Farmers using the materials have reported noticeably cooler growing conditions and improvements in crop performance.

“The anti-thermic plastic has made a huge difference.

It keeps the greenhouse cooler and takes some of the harsh heat off the plants.

The sweet peppers are doing much better, and you can really see the difference in the plants,” said Conroy Cole, farmer in St Ann.

In Manchester, farmer Diandra Rowe reported a reduction in greenhouse temperatures of at least 2 degrees Celsius (°C) following the installation of the adapted covering materials.

“Even though this has been one of the hottest and driest summers I’ve experienced in 12 years of farming, my yields have been significantly better than in previous years.

It has also made working in the greenhouse much more comfortable,” said Rowe.

The introduction of adapted greenhouse covering materials has also opened up new business opportunities in Jamaica, with some farmers independently importing and distributing these materials to other growers, helping to expand access to the technology beyond the project beneficiaries.

Digital sensors are also 0providing farmers with site-specific information on environmental, soil and water conditions to guide irrigation, nutrient management and other crop management decisions.

Across beneficiary sites, these technologies have been applied in diverse horticultural systems, alongside practical guidance on ventilation, shading, irrigation and fertigation management.

Rowe added, “The digital sensors have given us much-needed insight into exactly what is happening inside our growing spaces in real time.

Being able to access the data remotely means we can make better-informed decisions and adjust our practices where needed.” The project also provided technical guidance and refresher training to help farmers and extension personnel interpret data generated by the environmental, soil and water sensors.

This included practical guidance on monitoring growing conditions and using sensor readings to support adjustments to irrigation, nutrient management and other day-to-day crop management practices.

“The real value of these technologies comes from using them together.

The adapted greenhouse covering helps create better growing conditions, while digital sensors provide farmers with the information to adjust irrigation, nutrient management and other practices based on actual growing conditions.

Together, they can support more efficient and productive protected agriculture,” said Anne Desrochers, FAO plant production and protection specialist and lead technical officer for the project.

Several beneficiary farmers were also affected by Hurricane Melissa, with damage to protected structures and temporary disruptions to production.

Many are now rebuilding and working to resume production, with project- supported technologies being reinstalled or incorporated into rehabilitated greenhouse systems.

The FAO team says it is now consolidating lessons from beneficiary sites and documenting farmer experiences and production results.

These findings will help inform future efforts to scale up digital and climate-responsive technologies for horticultural production in Jamaica.

World.title: Relief in sight
World.content:
Garfield Granston, who broke his spine in May, is seen at Black River Hospital.

KINGSTON Public Hospital (KPH) has pledged an urgent consultation with doctors at Black River Hospital (BRH) to determine Garfield Granston’s next steps to recovery, months after the 57-year-old was referred for specialist care and surgery following serious spinal injury.

In a press release on Friday, KPH’s management said that it had seriously reviewed Granston’s medical history and acknowledged that his surgery was delayed after its C-arm machine, required to carry out the procedure, went out of service.

Granston was referred to the Orthopaedics Outpatient Clinic at KPH in May 2026, after he had fallen from a tree and sustained fractures in two places along his spine. He was initially rushed to BRH, in St Elizabeth, where he was subsequently told that the hospital lacked the facilities to perform the procedure.

In Friday’s press release KPH outlined that after clinical assessment and diagnostic imaging, an orthopaedic consultant recommended that Granston receive supportive care and secure the necessary spinal implants for possible surgery.

The required medical equipment included 10 pedicle screws, 10 set screws, and two rods, at a total cost of $854,000.

The release said that the spinal implants were not made readily available by Granston during follow-up visits, and after the payment was made, the hospital’s equipment became unavailable. While it did not clarify whether the C-arm machine is once more operational, KPH said it remains committed to delivering medical solutions for its patients and maintains that it would move to promptly execute referral and transfer procedures.

“Urgent coordination between the orthopaedics teams at Black River Public Hospital and Kingston Public Hospital will be undertaken to review the patient’s current clinical condition and determine the appropriate next steps. Established referral and transfer procedures will be followed.

“KPH remains committed to collaborating with public health facilities to support continuity of care, facilitate appropriate clinical decision-making, and promote positive patient outcomes while safeguarding patient confidentiality and dignity,” the hospital said.

The update comes in response to a Jamaica Observer story on October 27 in which Elexso Smith disclosed her stepfather’s plight as he endured five months awaiting a surgery date from KPH.

She explained that after receiving the nearly-million-dollar bill for surgical devices, her family sought assistance from the Ministry of Health and Wellness, which provided $554,000, while the family covered the remaining $300,000.

Smith said she was shocked that her stepfather’s surgery was still delayed, even after payment was made.

“Before we pay the money at KPH, and before we got help from the health ministry, the doctor was very harsh because he was arguing, saying that we have to pay the money before we can do surgery. When we get the receipt and gave it to the doctor he said: ‘One more problem. The machine broke down,’ ” Smith told the Observer on Tuesday this week.

“Every time he is to go up there [KPH], they’re always putting him off; or if he’s sent up there, they send him back down [to BRH]. From the last time he went up there [KPH] on the 30th [of June] he has not been back there. And then when they [BRH] call up there they say he mustn’t come, or there is no bed space,” she claimed.

She added that KPH did not state a clear timeline for Granston’s surgery, leaving him to endure severe discomfort while only receiving treatment for his pain at Black River Hospital where he was initially admitted.

Smith, who acknowledged that her stepfather’s care regimen was no easy feat, had called on KPH to provide a clear timeline for the alleviation of his pain.

“I just want to find out what’s really happening with this surgery situation. It’s been months and nothing. We’re not hearing nothing at all. So we just want KPH to state what their position is with this surgery as soon as possible,” Smith said on Tuesday.

World.title: NOON Brunch goes Pink at Devon House
World.content:
Looking delightful in blush pink in support of Jamaica’s breast cancer awareness movement, Tamelia Jones (left) and Yvonne Finlayson spend their Sunday afternoon brunching on the lawns of Devon House at NOON Pink, the brunch party series.

After making its debut in April of this year, the NOON Brunch series returned on Sunday, October 25 with a pink theme and an even bigger turnout.

Held at the iconic Devon House, the event’s patrons enjoyed not only the available delicacies, but also the pulsating musical delights that kept flowing.

Tasked with getting attendees in a dancing mood were DJ Junior Pang, who got things rolling with a number of sing-a-long tunes, Shukkle Bus, and DJ Fastcar, who kept the momentum going.

Fyahman, Steelie Bashment, and Quality International also represented themselves well.

“The first staging of NOON was really an introduction to the atmosphere and overall experience we envisioned for our patrons. It gave people a taste of what we wanted the brand to represent. So, for the second staging, we built on that foundation… We expanded the variety of food options, secured the iconic Devon House as our venue, and adjusted the event time to better accommodate our patrons.

“We also maintained our commitment to delivering a diverse and experienced entertainment line-up. Ultimately, our objective was to elevate the overall experience while preserving the energy and atmosphere that made the first staging memorable,” Dane Wilson, director of brand & marketing for NOON Brunch, told the Jamaica Observer post-event.

He added that the series’ growth speaks to the brand’s potential.

“In just six months we’ve seen the brand gain significant recognition, and that’s incredibly encouraging. When I speak with people I’m often surprised by how many have already heard about NOON or have some familiarity with the experience we’re creating… Our focus now is on converting that recognition into sustained patron loyalty,” he shared.

Wilson shared that one of the most memorable moments was when the rain started to pour and Shukkle Bus kept the energy going. Instead of allowing the weather to dampen the atmosphere, patrons embraced the moment.

“At one point, there was even a conga line making its way through the crowd in the rain! It was spontaneous, energetic and genuinely unforgettable. Those are the kinds of experiences that make an event special,” he said.

Commenting on the food on offer, Wilson noted that the objective was to provide variety and quality while ensuring the food complemented the overall brunch experience.

“Food is a major part of the NOON experience, and for this staging, we wanted to ensure that patrons had a wide selection of breakfast and lunch favourites. The menu featured traditional Jamaican breakfast staples such as ackee and saltfish, callaloo, brown stew chicken, fried dumplings and festival. For lunch we had fried chicken, jerk chicken, soup, rice and peas, and, of course, curry goat. We also introduced a made-to-order omelette station, allowing guests to customise their omelettes with their preferred vegetables and proteins. Waffles, pancakes, pastries and fresh fruits completed the selection,” Wilson explained.

The event, which primarily targets young professionals between the ages of 25 and 45 who appreciate good music and great food.

The next staging will be in March 2027.

“We don’t want NOON to be defined strictly by age. Our vision is to create an inclusive, sophisticated yet relaxed environment where different generations can come together and feel equally comfortable. We want grandmothers, mothers, and daughters to be able to attend the same event, enjoy the atmosphere and create memories together. At its core, NOON is about bringing people together through food, music and a shared appreciation for a great experience,” Wilson reasoned.

World.title: Prosecution rests
World.content:
Kevin Smith, the late pastor of Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James, who is alleged to have instructed murder accused Andre Ruddock to cut the throat of a fellow worshiper on October 17, 2021.

AFTER calling 10 individuals to give evidence since September 17, the prosecution in the Andre Ruddock murder trial closed its case on Friday, opening the way for the defence to call witnesses of its own, if it so desires, next Monday.

A pathologist was the last witness to be called by the prosecution on Friday in the Home Circuit Court in downtown Kingston before it ended its case. The pathologist confirmed that 39-year-old Taneka Gardner was in fact dead and died from having her throat slashed.

If the defence, led by attorney Anthony Williams, decides to call witnesses of its own, it would be to try and prove that Ruddock is not guilty of murder in relation to the October 17, 2021 human sacrifice-type killing of Gardner at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James.

It is alleged that Ruddock was acting on instructions from his now-deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Gardner died after her throat was cut, allegedly by Ruddock.

It is a possibility that on Monday, Ruddock could decide to take the witness stand himself. In the meantime, Williams and Venice Brown, who comprise his legal team, await further instructions from him on whether or not he will testify.

The seven members of the jury appeared happy on Friday to learn that the prosecution had ended its case and that the matter, which has taken them away from their private avocations, will be behind them soon.

Williams and Brown defended Ruddock vigorously throughout the trial, although their client confessed to killing Gardner one day after the woman’s throat was cut. He had confessed to detectives in the presence of two justices of the peace that he was responsible for cutting Gardner’s throat. The confession, which Ruddock gave in a caution statement, was recorded in writing by detectives and was also video-recorded.

Following the taking of the caution statement, detectives went on to ask 42-year-old Ruddock questions to get clarity on how the gruesome events, which led to Gardner’s demise, unfolded. That question-and-answer session was also video-recorded.

The videos of both the caution statement and a question-and-answer session with detectives were played in court for the jurors to review. Ruddock did not appear to be under any threat to confess to killing Gardner, although Williams sought to convince the jurors that his client was threatened and intimidated prior to him being taken to Freeport Police Station in Montego Bay.

The main witness in the case — who said he was an adjutant to the pastor of the church, often shaving his head, carrying his Bible and helping him to get dressed — told the court that Ruddock took a knife from another member of the church and cut Gardner’s throat, after that member hesitated to carry out the pastor’s order.

The witness said Gardner did not resist, after she allegedly told the pastor that she believed he could bring her back to life if she was to have her throat cut.

World.title: ‘WE’RE PROUD!’
World.content:
Portmore United players and staff celebrate qualifying for the Concacaf Champions Cup after defeating Violette 4-3 on aggregate in the two-legged semi-final of the Caribbean Cup. Portmore won the first leg 3-1 but lost the second match 1-2 at Sabina Park in Kingston, Jamaica, on October 28, 2026. (Photo: Concacaf)

PORTMORE United Chairman Garwin Tulloch believes the club have made significant strides and are preparing to test themselves against the region’s best in next year’s Concacaf Champions Cup.

The reigning Jamaica Premier League champions will vie for the Concacaf Caribbean Cup title in December, after beating Haiti’s Violette 4-3 on aggregate, despite a 1-2 loss in their second- leg semi-final at Sabina Park on Wednesday.

Portmore’s 3-1 first-leg win was enough to secure a spot in the first-ever all-Jamaican Caribbean Cup final, joining defending champions Mount Pleasant Football Academy who beat Trinidad and Tobago’s Club Sando in their semi-final matchup.

It’s another achievement for the club since the arrival of its new leadership group in 2024, led by Tulloch’s United Sports Group.

“The technical team has learnt a lot along the way and administratively, we have improved and we’re just seeing the results on the pitch from the work of the technical team and the management of the club,” Tulloch told the Jamaica Observer.

“So it may seem like a short space of time in terms of the results on the pitch but the work went in before that.

It’s a great achievement and we’re proud.” Despite winning the now-defunct CFU Club Championship in 2005 and 2019, Portmore had not competed in regional competition for more than five years before this year’s tournament.

However, Tulloch says the team understood the importance of the Caribbean Cup — and their performances reflected that.

“To be honest, I’m very impressed, because it’s easy to motivate the youngsters and the lads at this level because the opportunity to be on the international platforms is what every aspiring young footballer tries to get,” he said.

“In fact, it’s actually harder to motivate them to play in the local competition right now because they’re focused primarily on playing Concacaf, so motivating the technical team and the players is really very difficult.

But, I have to give credit also to our coaching staff who have levelled and made responsible decisions; rotation of the squad is also very important at this time — ‘man management’ is really the word and they’ve done a very good job in doing that.” Regardless of the two-legged final against Mount Pleasant on December 1 and 5 in Kingston, Portmore will compete in the Champions Cup where they could face top clubs from the likes of USA, Mexico, Canada and Central America.

Tulloch says the club will need to take another step if they are to be competitive in the competition.

“The more you advance in the competition, logically, it’s a wider platform and it’s a harder challenge.

And at this point it takes more mettle because, traditionally, we in our region — as in the Caribbean— don’t normally fare well at that level so we’re preparing ourselves to compete at that level,” he said.

“First, we have to win the championship against Mount Pleasant — which is important for us because it gives us a bye into the round of one.

So, it’s important; it’s a wider platform and we’re looking forward to the challenge.” Portmore join Mount Pleasant and Cavalier FC as the only Jamaican clubs to qualify for the revamped Champions Cup.

Portmore return to local competition on Sunday when they visit Montego Bay United in the Legend Jamaica Premier League.

World.title: Hundreds of thousands of protesters march across France for third week in a row
World.content:
Arrests were significantly lower than during previous demonstrations, although tensions and clashes emerged in Marseille, Paris and Lyon as marches dispersed.

French authorities described the situation nationwide as “generally calm” in the early afternoon. France deployed 70,000 police officers to contain what it feared would be another day of unrest.

Many protesters wore Halloween costumes despite French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warning that face coverings could result in fines of €150.

Other European cities including Rome, Milan, Berlin and Frankfurt also experienced a day of youth-led protests against the cost of living and, in Germany, military spending.

The protests in over 30 German cities were ignited by a youth-led initiative called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z gets things done) and remained largely peaceful despite the police cancelling a planned march in Cologne after some participants wore face coverings and set off smoke bombs.

In Italy, the police carried out 60 searches across 23 cities targeting people suspected of inciting violence a mass demonstrations on Friday, according to news agency ANSA.

World.title: Putin’s potential G20 comeback risks normalizing Russian war crimes, says Kallas
World.content:
Putin hasn’t yet confirmed whether he would attend the December summit hosted in the U.S. His last in-person attendance at a G20 meeting was in 2019 — three years before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kallas’ remarks come amid growing frustration among EU countries over Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov’s attendance at a G20 ministerial gathering in Atlanta.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was hosting the meeting, called off the traditional family photo after European officials refused to stand beside Lavrov.

Kallas said in the interview that “we don’t want to stand next to him [Lavrov] in this fora,” because he’s been placed under international sanctions.

However, she added that Lavrov’s presence meant “we can also immediately fight back on these lies” from Russia.

Kallas hailed the U.S. decision on Friday to sell 500 Patriot missile interceptors to Ukraine as a “very positive development” and called on allies to toughen sanctions against Russia.

World.title: Merz ‘surprised’ by Asian pushback to ‘Made in Europe’ plan for car industry
World.content:
“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning from his five-day tour of East Asian countries on Friday evening.

Merz admitted the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”

The chancellor vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and to raise them at the next EU leaders' summit. The bloc's leaders are set to meet in Dublin on Nov. 13 for an informal gathering.

Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade” between so-called middle powers in speeches in Seoul and Tokyo. The EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged the international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted" — a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals or the tariff threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.

But the pushback from South Korea and Japan are a sharp reminder of how industry-specific frictions can hamper the implementation of the larger alliance proposed by Merz.

World.title: Burnham ‘open’ to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade
World.content:
However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay financial reparations for the slave trade, saying that they would be the wrong solution.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” the prime minister argued.

Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced in June a manifesto by Caribbean leaders setting out the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations from former colonial powers.

Burnham will attend the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, which runs through Wednesday. It will be his first foreign trip with King Charles.

It will be a crucial test for the prime minister, who will try to avoid a fight over slavery reparations that marred his predecessor Keir Starmer’s visit at the last summit in 2024.

World.title: Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries
World.content:
“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.

Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.

In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

“Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said.

The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months.

However, the White House said that it won't pay for the Patriot interceptors. "The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies," a statement from the State Department said.

World.title: Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle
World.content:
Inside, Nawrocki told Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges that were recently elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority: “You are not judges [of the Tribunal].”

The confrontation marked a dramatic escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the court’s president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański — both named by PiS and seen as loyalists — claiming authority to take over the court’s management. Święczkowski rejected the move.

In a statement issued around 5 a.m., Nawrocki accused the government of “forcibly seizing a constitutional institution”, demanded that police leave the court grounds and summoned emergency consultations with parliamentary parties for Saturday, citing a “threat to Poland’s internal security.”

Police remain deployed outside the tribunal, where PiS supporters had staged an anti-government protest camp for weeks.

The broader dispute stems from Tusk’s efforts to reverse controversial moves by former PiS governments to fill the court with judges aligned with the nationalist party. These efforts have met stiff resistance from PiS and Nawrocki, who refused to swear in some judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority.

The judges subsequently took oaths in parliament, in a ceremony Nawrocki considers null and void, while Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

World.title: Funding deadlock derails global effort to save nature
World.content:
But behind that grand gesture, governments are still struggling to unlock the hundreds of billions needed to meet global biodiversity protection targets. The reason? A profound and unresolved disagreement over where that money should come from.

“If we’re mutually unhappy that’s probably the closest we can get to on these very delicate compromises,” said a member of the Swiss delegation just before the text was adopted.

After two weeks of negotiations over how to speed up efforts to protect ecosystems, nearly 200 countries secured a hard-fought agreement to "accelerate the implementation" of the global biodiversity framework "including by increased ambition in addressing the gaps, challenges and barriers related to implementation," according to a draft of the text, the final version of which was not immediately available.

Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan, who presided over the summit, said negotiators had "achieved more than we could have expected."

But in the end, governments could not agree on how to increase the number of countries currently contributing to biodiversity finance, instead only stating the obvious: that more funds would be better.

The summit exposed a growing chasm between nations over who should be held financially responsible for funding conservation measures worldwide: historically wealthy countries whose economies have caused immense damage to the environment, or newly rich states whose economies have grown exponentially in the last three decades.

World.title: Berlin student protests: youth demands meet extremist mobilisation
World.content:
A protest rally organised by the youth initiative “Gen Z regelt” was held in Berlin on Saturday, with demonstrators calling for more investment in education and an end to rearmament.

 

Pro-Palestine activists, flags and slogans were prominently visible among the crowd gathered at the Brandenburg Gate.

The rally began at 2 p.m. Its stated demands include more money for schools and climate protection, affordable living costs and no compulsory military service. Organisers promised a peaceful event.

Even so, some shops on Unter den Linden, Friedrichstraße and Kurfürstendamm put up barricades to guard against possible looting.

Pro-Palestine presence across the square

At the entrance to the Brandenburg Gate, a man in a jumper in the colours of the Palestinian flag handed out flyers. Beside him, a representative of the daily newspaper "Junge Welt” offered brochures and copies. The paper is monitored by Germany’s domestic intelligence service, which classifies it as far-left extremist.

School student protests at the Brandenburg Gate, 31.10.2026 Kevin Köhrmann

Further along, at Platz des 18. März, Palestinian flags flew alongside anarchist and Antifa banners. Some signs focused on military spending, with slogans such as “Flunked the PISA test but passed the military medical” and “Money for social causes instead of war”. Others went further, reading “German weapons kill children in Palestine”, “No money for children’s homes, schools & women’s refuges, but money for war and genocide” and “Stop the genocide in Gaza”.

Many of those present, mostly young men and women, wore the red or black Palestinian scarf known as the kufiya. Some wore it around their necks; others wrapped it around their heads or draped it over their shoulders like a cape.

“Not a single cent left for education”

Euronews spoke to a group of young women who said they were aged 19 to 20 and doing a voluntary social year (FSJ).

They said they had come partly to show solidarity with France and the protests across Europe, but above all to make the point that young people do not feel seen or taken seriously by politicians.

“There is constant militarisation and rearmament, and there is simply not a single cent left for education and social spending,” one of them said.

Young women at school student protests in Berlin on 31.10.2026. Kevin Köhrmann

Two of the women wore a kufiya around their necks. Asked what the conflict in the Middle East has to do with the school student protests, one replied: “It has to do with the fact that we as young people, or as people in Germany in general, also have to take responsibility for the fact that weapons are produced here that are used to kill civilians and children in Palestine, in Gaza and in the West Bank.”

She added: “I do not think I could ever live with myself if I never paid any attention to this.”

“I do not want FU to support a genocide”

A little further away stood a young man with a Palestinian scarf around his neck. He studies chemistry at Freie Universität (FU), where there have repeatedly been pro-Palestine occupations in recent years.

He said he came because universities face ever more cuts, while rents are rising and students have to work on the side. “At some point it simply becomes impossible,” he said. Young people, he added, are also suffering massively from the arms build-up. “I am just angry about what is happening right now.”

He said he wears the scarf because of his university. FU has eleven cooperation projects with Israel, he said, and so indirectly supports research for war. He argued this also affects Germany, because the Federal Republic buys military equipment from Israel.

“I do not want our universities to exist to build war products. I do not want FU to support a genocide,” he said.

Student of Freie Universität at school student protests in Berlin on 31.10.2026. Kevin Köhrmann

Part of a wider European movement

The Berlin rally is part of a wave of youth-led protests across Europe. In France, demonstrations that began last month as a high school student movement have since drawn in labour unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron, while rallies were also reported in the Netherlands, Italy and Spain on Saturday.

Critics in Germany, however, say some openly radical groups were represented at the demonstration

Among the demonstrators there are also representatives of radical left-wing groups. Alongside Antifa flags, the youth organisation "Linksjugend ['solid]", the youth wing of the Left Party, is present in smaller numbers. It has long faced criticism over accusations of antisemitism. The Neukölln branch in particular has made headlines recently. The Berlin Linksjugend has also repeatedly come under fire for its anti-Israeli resolutions and its stance on the Middle East conflict.

The "Revolutionäre Linke" was also represented with its own stand. In early 2023 members of the federal working group "Revolutionäre Linke" founded the separate organisation "Jugend für Sozialismus". The background was growing conflicts with the leadership of the youth organisation, which they accused of political adaptation, a lack of class struggle and undemocratic structures.

Information stand of the "Revolutionary Left" Kevin Köhrmann

The organisation criticises the trend of more money for the Bundeswehr and less for hospitals and other social spending. "We see that it is our young generation that will be hit hardest and for the longest time."

Their goal, they say, is to build a better society. That is why they are here. It should be in the interests of every left wing organisation to take part in such events, they argue, because this is where the real power to bring about change lies.

Asked what the issue of Palestine and the conflict in the Middle East have to do with the protests, he replies, "We always put out all our information materials. However, there is also a link here. One of the major problems is that, despite everything that is happening, the Bundeswehr continues to carry out drone tests together with the Israeli army, and weapons are still being sold to Israel. We strongly condemn this. And of course it is also connected with conscription and the expansion of the Bundeswehr here."

Contradictory statements from security authorities

The press office of the Berlin police told Euronews in response to a query two days before the protests that individual groups from the left wing political spectrum were picking up on the protests in France and issuing calls to mobilise. "However, there is currently no reliable evidence of targeted extremist influence or control over this group."

Euronews research paints a different picture. Shortly before the protests in Berlin, serious threats of violence appeared in a private Telegram group. As the "Berliner Zeitung" (B.Z.) reports, one user announced possible violence with the words "I am going out with a machete". Others threatened attacks on synagogues, looting and arson.

Police officers stand in front of demonstrators during a protest under the slogan "Gen Z Takes Care of It" in Berlin, Germany, Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. AP Photo

The press office of the Berlin Senate Department for the Interior and Sport told Euronews in response to a query beforehand that actors from parts of the left wing extremist and foreign related extremist spectrum were also mobilising for the demonstrations on 31 October.

Their aim in taking part is likely, among other things, to co-opt and radicalise the protests. "Legitimate civil society protest is thereby supposed to be reinterpreted as a struggle against the rule of law and liberal democracy." In the case of individual left-wing extremist actors who are calling for participation, it must also be assumed that they have a basic interest in escalation.

Unclear structures and withdrawal of organisers

Shortly beforehand, several organisers and supporters had distanced themselves from the initiative "Gen Z regelt".

The previous spokesperson Gianni Matheja justified his withdrawal by pointing to differing views within the movement and doubts that the protests would remain peaceful. Berlin supporters Max Schneller and Battal Yali also pulled out of the initiative.

The supporters who stepped down criticised unclear responsibilities and a lack of transparency in the organisation and funding of the protests. According to research by the Tagesspiegel, the Berlin organising team had largely fallen apart for a time. Shortly afterwards, however, new members joined.

Flyer with information about the event at Rosenthaler Platz in Berlin at 17.30 p.m., distributed at the Brandenburg Gate. Kevin Köhrmann

The initiative "Gen Z regelt" emphasised the peaceful nature of the nationwide school student protests planned for Saturday 31 October. As the "Münchner Merkur" reported, citing "Die Zeit", 16-year-old co-organiser Konrad Schmitz from Wuppertal said, "We want to fight peacefully for our cause." He said he rejected extremism from both the left and the right.

The 18-year-old co-founder Akram Selo also reported numerous threats in recent days. "They think we want to copy the French; they think we want to destroy the country."

Up to 5 p.m. the protests at the Brandenburg Gate remained peaceful.

Second demonstration at Rosenthaler Platz in the police spotlight

Alongside the rally at the Brandenburg Gate, the Berlin police are also focusing on another demonstration in the capital.

Under the slogan "Gen Z has had enough!", a gathering is due to assemble at Rosenthaler Platz from 5.30 p.m. The police initially expect around 400 to 500 participants, though it cannot be ruled out that significantly more people will join the protest.

The initiative "Gen Z regelt" has clearly distanced itself from this demonstration. Nevertheless, in the afternoon dozens of men and women at the Brandenburg Gate are handing out flyers pointing to the evening event. Neither the press team nor the stewards on site are stopping them.

According to the assessment of the security authorities, the demonstration is being mobilised, among others, from the left wing political spectrum. Participants from the pro Palestine scene are also expected. The event is furthermore being promoted in the far left extremist milieu.

The planned demonstration route leads from Rosenthaler Platz along Kastanienallee, Schönhauser Allee and Danziger Straße to Prenzlauer Allee suburban railway station. Euronews is on site and will report on the demonstration.

World.title: France's third weekend of social protests sees lower turnout and early clashes in major cities
World.content:
The third consecutive weekend of the social mobilisation and demonstrations in France brought together some 320,000 participants, including 70,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry.

 

This is a lower figure than on previous days of mobilisation: the government counted 410,000 participants on Saturday 24 October, compared with 550,000 on 17 October. The organisers, for their part, said they had counted 800,000 demonstrators on each of those two days.

The lower participation could in particular be explained by disruption to public transport. In Lyon, our reporter Jean-Philippe Liabot noted that "the trams and metro trains are only running at half". In Paris, more than 40 metro stations are closed, and tram traffic is also affected.

Earlier in the day, the Interior Ministry reported a situation that was "generally calm", "without any notable incident". By 2 p.m., 27 arrests had been recorded, compared with 217 at the same time during the 24 October mobilisation.

Authorities put in place measures to limit disorder

But the authorities fear that Halloween evening could be used as a "pretext" for clashes in the streets, as marches start to disperse in some major cities.

In Lyon, our reporter observed the use of tear gas as the demonstration arrived at Place Jean-Macé, in the 7th district.

"The security forces will show the greatest firmness towards those responsible for violence and damage," the Interior Ministry warned.

The rallies began last month as a high school student movement protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labour unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron have since joined with varied demands.

Demonstration dispersing in Lyon, Euronews images

Most protesters have been peaceful, but troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have turned into rioting and looting, including the 17 October unrest that appeared to take the government by surprise.

Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have caused severe injuries.

Macron said Saturday’s marches would stay out of city centres to protect shops. Police barred entry to Place de la République and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m.

This Saturday and Sunday, unaccompanied minors face a 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Élysées, although a Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

Demonstrations held in Germany, Italy and Spain

The protests against social issues, housing and education have spread across many cities in Europe

In Germany, a youthinitiative called “Gen Z regelt", roughly “Gen Z’s got this", has rallied in many cities for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life, and against any return of military conscription.

Organisers said more than 180,000 people had signed up online, but only several thousand had marched by Saturday afternoon.

Demonstrators gather at the banks of the river. Main for a protest under the slogan "Gen Z Takes Care of It" in Frankfurt, Germany, Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. AP Photo

On Saturday, young protesters also gathered at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, demanding more investment in education and housing.

In The Hague, Netherlands, Dutch police were out in force around the downtown shopping area after online calls to protest and fears of rioting and looting.

By mid-afternoon there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances. Local media reported that police frisked some groups of black-clad youths and checked their identities.

Many stores were boarded up while in Italy, police were on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

In Barcelona, Catalan police planned to activate their highest-level alert after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings. Rioting there last Saturday led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.

Calls to protest also circulated on TikTok in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.
