The MLAsâ meeting followed Omarâs cabinet expansion last week, triggering open dissent, protests and allegations of internal bias in NC after four ministers were inducted, taking the cabinetâs strength to nine, including the CM.

He dropped Satish Sharma, leaving only two ministers from Jammu region â deputy CM Surinder Choudhary and Javed Ahmed Rana.

BJP has predicted a split in NC and collapse of Omarâs govt. âI am telling you there is unrest against the party brass. They are looking for an alternative. Govt will not remain and the party will not remain,â leader of opposition Sunil Sharma said. He described Omar as a âprince, who doesnât want to listen to any legislatorâ.

World.title: Darbar Move: J&K govt offices shift to Jammu
World.content:
Jammu prepares to host government offices for the winter session as 91 departments shift from Srinagar under the 150-year-old Darbar Move tradition

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

JAMMU: The bi-annual Darbar Move of Jammu & Kashmir govt from Srinagar to Jammu began Saturday, with 91 offices scheduled to shift operations to the winter capital ahead of their reopening on Nov 2.âOffices closed in Srinagar today and will reopen in Jammu on Nov 2,â officials said.The annual tradition that dates back 150 years was stopped by L-G Manoj Sinhaâs administration in June 2021, citing high financial costs and shift towards e-offices and paperless administration. CM Omar Abdullah restored it after taking office in 2024, as had been promised in National Conferenceâs election manifesto, and the practice resumed in Nov 2025.Ahead of offices reopening, Jammu is undergoing its customary makeover, with traffic department installing new road dividers and regulating vehicular movement.In view of convoy movement, authorities restricted heavy and medium motor vehicles carrying goods on NH-44 on Saturday-Sunday. The advisory asked transporters carrying fresh and perishable goods and livestock to plan their movement accordingly.

World.title: Can high blood sugar help immune cells fight cancer? Study offers new clues
World.content:
The Journal of Immunology

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Could the same high blood sugar that damages the body also make some immune cells better at fighting cancer? New research offers a surprising clue, finding that high blood sugar enhances the tumour-fighting ability of immune cells in mice, potentially opening a new avenue for cancer treatment.Published in, the study examined why people with type 1 diabetes have been found to have a lower risk of certain cancers, including melanoma, breast and colon cancer. Researchers found that the answer may lie in how high blood sugar changes T cells, immune cells that help the body recognise and attack cancer cells.In experiments, tumours grew more slowly in mice with high blood sugar than in mice with normal blood sugar and diabetic mice whose blood sugar was controlled with insulin. The hyperglycaemic mice also had more T cells, which were more effective at controlling tumour growth.The researchers found that high blood sugar altered a cellular signalling pathway in these immune cells, helping enhance their cancer-fighting activity. When diabetic mice received insulin, their T cells lost this heightened ability, pointing to a possible link between blood sugar levels and immune-cell function.The team then looked for similar changes in humans and found increased activity in the same signalling pathway in immune cells from blood samples of people with high blood sugar. This suggests the mechanism observed in mice may also be relevant to humans, although it does not establish that high blood sugar reduces cancer risk in people.Dr Anamika Bose, assistant professor at the National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research in India and senior author of the study, said the findings could help researchers develop T-cell-based immunotherapies by replicating the immune-cell changes seen in the experiments.The potential lies not in using high blood sugar as a treatment, but in understanding how it changes immune cells and whether those effects can be reproduced safely through targeted therapies.The findings remain preliminary. The tumour experiments were conducted in mice, and further research is needed to determine whether manipulating the same signalling pathway can improve cancer treatment in humans. The study does not suggest that patients should leave diabetes uncontrolled or alter insulin treatment.

World.title: Poonch woman suspected to have crossed LoC
World.content:
JAMMU: A married woman who went missing from Jammu & Kashmirâs Poonch district Friday is suspected to have crossed the LoC into PoK, officials said.

Rubina Kousar, a resident of Karni village near the LoC, took eight goats out for grazing but did not return.

Officials said preliminary investigation suggested she might have crossed the LoC with the livestock.

It was not immediately clear if she crossed inadvertently while grazing the goats or did so deliberately, they added. âSeveral persons living along the LoC sometimes inadvertently cross over.â

Recently, a girl from PoK was sent back to Pakistan after crossing over into Poonch.

World.title: Jamiat Governing Council passes resolutions on hate crimes, questions ‘demographic jihad’ narrative
World.content:
NEW DELHI: At its two-day national meet, the Jamiat Ulama-i- Hind (JUH)âs governing council passed resolutions calling for the establishment of special fast track courts to deal with hate crimes and cited Census data and its own research to reject the narrative that Muslims are seeking to alter the countryâs demographic balance through âdemographic jihadâ and illegal infiltration.

According to a statement issued by the JUH faction led by Maulana Mahmood Madani, the Jamiat president said, âThose conspiring to turn Muslims into outsiders and second-class citizens in their own country are, in fact, enemies of the nationâ.

He was addressing the event held in Nuh, Mewat.

Madani observed that hate speech could no longer be dismissed as a temporary instrument of electoral politics. Referring to figures that he claimed indicated more than 1,600 verified incidents of hate speeches and statements over the past year, with no FIR registered in 87% of those cases, Madani said that the situation raised serious questions about the responsibilities of law-enforcement agencies and the delivery of justice.

As part of the resolution, Jamiat sought effective implementation of the directions issued by the Supreme Court in the Tehseen S. Poonawalla case, including the appointment of district-level nodal officers of Superintendent of Police rank in every district. The landmark 2018 judgment had declared mob lynching and extrajudicial violence illegal and unconstitutional, placing a strict legal responsibility on states to prevent and punish such acts.





âI want to make it absolutely clear that we do not support the illegal presence of any foreign national in India. But who is responsible for such illegal influx? Surely, the responsibility lies with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA),â Madani added.

On demographic changes, JUH cited Census data to point out that the decadal growth rate for Muslim population had declined from 32.9% during 1981â1991 to 24.7% during 2001â2011.

The governing council also rejected the âHigh-Level Demographic Committeeâ constituted by MHA on May 26, alleging that it has an âunscientific composition and prejudiced agendaâ and sought the establishment of an impartial commission comprising experts of international standing to scientifically examine the factors influencing demographic changes.

World.title: Rahul Gandhi appeals to Delhi rally goers to do festival shopping from local traders
World.content:
Amid concerns of traders in central Delhi over the impact of the crowd expected at the INDIA bloc’s ‘Chalo Dilli’ rally on Sunday (November 1, 2026), Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday (October 31, 2026) urged people to do some festival season shopping after attending the rally.

In a video released late in the day, Mr. Gandhi appealed to people to shop for upcoming festivals like Deepavali, Chhath, and Bhai Dooj.

“The time of Diwali, Chhath, and Bhai Dooj has arrived. I want those lakhs of people coming to Delhi from outside to support the traders here,” Mr. Gandhi said.

“Protest, march, hold rallies, and along with that, do a little shopping too. It will benefit the traders,” he added.

Earlier, a traders body in central Delhi had urged the Congress leader to postpone the rally until Deepavali.

World.title: Devotees worried over conduct of Kandasashti festival at Kandakottam temple
World.content:
Devotees of the Sri Muthukumaraswamy Temple, popularly known as Kandhakottam in Rattan Bazaar in Park Town, are worried about the conduct of the Kandasashthi festival this year.

"Usually, tickets for the Laksharcharnai during the annual festival are sold just after Vijayadasami. Till date, the administration has not started selling tickets. Every year around 35,000 tickets each priced at ₹300 are sold to devotees who want to participate in the archanai that is slated to start on November 10. There is no sign of the conduct of the festival so far," said A. B. Srinivasan, a 65-year-old devotee.

Saravanan, another devotee, said that this year would be the 99th consecutive year of the Kandasashthi festival during which grand concerts would be held. "Participants of the archanai would be given prasadam including a bucket. Tenders for procuring various items such as pandals, coconuts, bags, and flowers are yet to be called for. We hear that the executive officer has gone on leave and another person has taken charge," he said.

The over 500-year-old shrine, is a scheme temple, meaning it belongs to a particular community - in this case, the Berri Chettis. A five-member team was chosen from the community as trustees last year and they have also been in charge of the daily running of the temple.

Sendilvellan, one of the trustees, said that the executive officer had taken away cheque signatory powers from the trustees and the trustees were unable to pay salaries even. "He has gone to the bank and taken signatory powers without informing us. We seem to have absolutely no powers in the day-to-day running of the temple. The court had directed the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments department to interfere only if there was any problem relating to the conduct of the temple. From last year, we have been managing the temple without any problems," he said.

Another trustee said that with just a few days left for the festival they have been running from pillar to post trying to get the powers back and conduct it. Sources in the HR&CE Department said they will look into the matter.

World.title: SRIHER hosts national conference on qualitative nursing research
World.content:
Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research organised ‘Insights 2026’, a national nursing conference on qualitative research, with over 600 participants from 25 states and online attendees from more than 12 countries.

R. Shankar Shanmugam, Registrar, Tamil Nadu Nurses and Midwives Council, inaugurated the conference. He spoke about the importance of understanding patient experiences, ethical research and critical thinking in improving healthcare.

The keynote address was delivered by K. Balaji Singh, Dean, Medical College. Nursing experts from various institutions across India participated as resource persons, sharing their insights with students, researchers and practitioners.

World.title: Police search for POCSO accused who went missing from hospital
World.content:
The police are searching for a POCSO case accused, a 61-year-old autorickshaw driver, after he went missing from a hospital in Periyar Nagar, where he was undergoing treatment for injuries sustained in an assault.

The autorickshaw driver was accused of sexually assaulting an eight-year-old girl while driving her to school in his vehicle.

He sustained injuries to his head and back in an alleged assault by the girl’s parents and relatives on Friday, the police said. Later that night, his son admitted him to the Periyar Nagar Government Hospital.

Based on a complaint lodged by the girl’s mother, the All-Women Police Station, Puzhal, registered a case under the POCSO Act.

The police subsequently learnt that the accused went missing from the hospital around 5.30 a.m. on Saturday. following which they formed special teams under the supervision of Kolathur Deputy Commissioner of Police S. Rajesh Kannan.

World.title: Ayur AI Integrative Diabetes Centre launched in Chennai
World.content:
An Ayur AI Integrative Diabetes Centre, which adopts an interdisciplinary approach to diabetes management, blending traditional Ayurvedic knowledge, modern medicine, and artificial intelligence, was inaugurated at Dr. RK Diabetic Foot and Podiatry Institute here on Saturday.

The Centre aims at combining traditional Ayurveda with modern diagnostic tools and medicines and AI-driven health assessment to develop individualised approaches to diabetes management, said the Institute’s founder and director, Rajesh Kesavan.

A clinical study involving about 100 patients has reported promising outcomes, with a 50% improvement in diabetes management and reduction in blood sugar spikes.

At the centre, dietary interventions will be customised based on individual body composition and metabolic profiles for diabetes management. An AI kiosk will facilitate AI-based health assessments.

Ayur AI founder Bala Pesala said the holistic intervention aims at achieving diabetes remission.

Samir Kumar Brahmachari, former Director General, Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, and Bandi Venkateshwarlu, assistant director, Regional Ayurveda Research Institute, Ministry of Ayush, also spoke.

World.title: DMK MLA quizzed for over two hours over remarks against CM
World.content:
DMK MLA Vasantham Karthikeyan, who represents Rishivandiyam, was quizzed by the Central Crime Branch (CCB) at Anna Nagar police station on Saturday in connection with a defamation case over his alleged remarks against Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay.

The case was registered following a complaint over Karthikeyan’s speech at a DMK protest in Kallakurichi on September 12. During the event, he criticised Mr. Vijay’s conduct in the Assembly and reportedly drew a comparison between the Chief Minister’s facial appearance and that of former Chief Minister M.K. Stalin, whose injuries were attributed to alleged custodial torture during the MISA period.

After appearing for the inquiry, Mr. Karthikeyan alleged that portions of his speech had been edited and morphed to implicate him in a false case. He said he had submitted audio evidence to the police and was prepared to contest the case legally. He also accused the TVK government of using cases to target DMK leaders.

World.title: Youth dies after car hits motorcycle in Kotturpuram
World.content:
A 25-year-old software professional died after a car rammed his motorcycle on R.G. Road near the VHS Hospital bus stop in Kotturpuram late on Friday.

The deceased, M. Madhan of Injambakkam, was employed with a private firm in Manapakkam. The police said the incident occurred around 11.45 p.m. when he was riding home on his motorcycle after work. A car moving in the same direction allegedly hit his vehicle.

Madhan suffered serious injuries to the back of his head and was rushed in an ambulance to the Government Royapettah Hospital. He succumbed to his injuries at around 1.15 a.m. on Saturday.

Following a complaint from his mother, the Traffic investigation police, Mylapore registered a case against the car driver, C. Christuraj, 39, of Perungudi. Further investigation is under way.

World.title: Rajasthan IPS officer removed after ACB probe ordered against IAS husband
World.content:
The Rajasthan government on Saturday placed an Indian Police Service (IPS) officer, Prashakha Mathur, on awaiting posting order (APO) after an investigation by the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) was approved against her husband and senior Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer Shikhar Agrawal.

Mr. Agrawal, who was also sent on APO earlier this week, is facing charges along with his family members of purchasing 40 villas in luxury resorts operated by a private firm in Udaipur and Alwar districts by allegedly abusing his position and influence and extending “undue benefits” to the firm.

While Mr. Agrawal was serving as the Additional Chief Secretary (Industries) and additionally held charge of four public sector corporations, his wife Ms. Mathur, a 1995-batch IPS officer, was posted as Additional Director General in charge of Planning, Modernisation and Welfare.

The ACB has alleged that Mr. Agrawal gave benefits such as relaxations in resort construction conditions, approvals without verification of certificates and special concessional packages to the firm. The alleged purchases of villas were made in the names of Mr. Agrawal and Ms. Mathur, their two sons, and Mr. Agrawal’s parents-in-law.

The ACB has registered a Preliminary Enquiry (PE) and launched an investigation into the allegations of abuse of official position, conflict of interest, and extending undue benefits to the firm in question.

ACB Director General Govind Gupta said the properties were allegedly purchased at prices substantially below their market value. The ACB’s probe will examine whether the alleged benefits caused substantial financial losses to the State government and whether Mr. Agrawal and his family members acquired assets disproportionate to their known sources of income.

Mr. Agrawal was appointed Additional Chief Secretary in the Chief Minister’s Office in February 2024, shortly after Bhajan Lal Sharma took oath as the CM, and served in that position till November 2025. Former CM Ashok Gehlot has demanded investigation by Central agencies into the matter, describing it as the “biggest scandal” under the Bharatiya Janata Party government.

World.title: Fakhar Zaman and Arafat Minhas lead Pakistan to tri-series glory
World.content:
Pakistan chased down 326 to beat Sri Lanka by three wickets in the final of the tri-nation series on Saturday at a packed Gaddafi Stadium, sealing the title with nine balls to spare in what was the joint-highest successful chase in an ODI final.

Shaheen Shah Afridi, the captain, finished it in style — a six slapped over midwicket off Dilshan Madushanka in the 49th over — after Hasan Nawaz had levelled the scores with a dab to backward point. Pakistan finished on 327 for seven in 48.3 overs.

For Fakhar Zaman, this was an innings that answered the questions swirling around his place in the side.

He had spent much of the first innings off the field after copping a blow while fielding, and came out to open with his team 22 for two inside four overs and the chase already wobbling.

His early stay was scratchy. He was dropped on three by Madushanka at deep third, and again on 69 by Mahesh Theekshana, who put down a return catch and later tipped a six over the rope.

But from the wreckage of Pakistan’s top order he built an innings of substance, adding 149 with Saad Baig, who made 74 off 75 in his maiden half-century.

Fakhar reached his 20th ODI fifty in the 22nd over, then his 12th ODI century in the 30th, pulling Asitha Fernando in front of square off 84 balls.

He was finally bowled by Madushanka for 127 off 99 — 11 fours and six sixes — charging and missing a slog in the 34th over, walking off to a standing ovation from a full house. It was, by common consent, a vintage Fakhar innings on the biggest occasion.

If Fakhar held the chase together, Arafat Minhas won it.

The all-rounder walked in at 230 for five in the 37th over with Pakistan needing 96 from 78 balls, and played the innings of his young career — 61 off 31 balls, with three fours and four sixes.

His check-drive six over long-on off Madushanka in the 46th over was the shot of the night, and his two sixes and a four off Asitha in the 47th brought the target within sight.

He fell in the 48th over, caught-and-bowled by Asitha, and the Gaddafi Stadium rose as one.

Sri Lanka’s innings

Pakistan had won the toss and elected to field, and the decision looked sound early as Sri Lanka’s openers Kamindu Mendis and Avishka Fernando scored briskly without risk, taking the visitors past 50 without loss inside ten overs.

Pakistan had brought in Faheem Ashraf for Shadab Khan, ruled out on medical grounds after being struck by a bouncer in the fifth ODI, while Sri Lanka replaced the pace of Eshan Malinga with the spin of Mahesh Theekshana.

The contrasting selections suggested both sides had read the conditions differently, and Pakistan’s pace attack struggled for early impact.

It was Salman Ali Agha who provided the breakthroughs, claiming both wickets to fall before the final ten overs.

Avishka missed a sweep and was leg-before in the 18th over, and four overs later Kusal Mendis stepped out and drove the ball back at Salman, who leapt to take a superb return catch.

Beyond those two dismissals the innings belonged to Kamindu, who took charge through the middle overs and brought up his century in the 34th over, cutting Faheem over the wicket-keeper’s head. Pavan Rathnayake gave him valuable support, the pair adding 146 for the third wicket, with Rathnayake making 77 off 65 balls.

Kamindu’s 131 off 128 balls, with 12 fours and two sixes, anchored the innings. At 238 for two after 40 overs, Sri Lanka looked set for a total beyond 350.

But Pakistan’s death bowling pulled it back. Shaheen trapped Kamindu leg-before in the 42nd over and dismissed Dasun Shanaka soon after for a brisk 17 off nine.

Haris Rauf had Rathnayake caught by Babar Azam at wide long-on, and he and Naseem Shah removed Dunith Wellalage and Sahan Arachchige in quick succession.

Naseem’s wayward penultimate over let Sri Lanka past 320, but they lost six for 70 in the last ten overs to finish on 325 for eight.

Pakistan’s innings

Pakistan’s reply began badly. Maaz Sadaqat charged Madushanka in the second over and edged to slip for five, and in the fourth Babar Azam, under scrutiny for his form, drove at a floated delivery and was caught by a solitary fourth slip — a trap set by Kusal Mendis and executed to perfection. Babar departed for a five-ball duck, and Lahore went quiet.

From there on , Saad joined forces with Fakhar and steadied Pakistan’s innings.

Saad brought up his maiden half-century in the 19th over, and Fakhar reached his 20th ODI fifty in the 22nd. The pair added 149, and Fakhar rode his luck — dropped on three by Madushanka, and again on 69 by Theekshana.

Saad fell for 74 off 75, chipping a full delivery back to Theekshana in the 27th over. Fakhar, growing fluent, reached his century in the 30th over. Salman Agha made 17 before Wellalage bowled him with one that skidded under his slog sweep, and Fakhar’s innings ended in the 34th over, bowled by Madushanka for 127.

That left Pakistan 220 for four, needing 106 from 96 balls, and when Salman fell at 230 for five the game was alive again. Hasan Nawaz and Arafat Minhas steadied, then accelerated. Arafat’s 61 off 31 turned the chase, and he and Hasan added 50 off 49 balls.

Asitha removed Arafat, caught-and-bowled, and Faheem Ashraf first ball in the same over to briefly raise Sri Lankan hopes, but Hasan and Shaheen held their nerve, and the captain’s six sealed it.

The win is Pakistan’s first ODI tri-series title since the Kitply Cup in Dhaka, when they beat India in the final, and it comes days after they were bowled out for 110 by this same Sri Lankan side in the league stage — a collapse that had raised fresh questions about the batting.

Those questions were answered, at least for one night, by Fakhar, whose place in the side had itself been under discussion, and by Arafat, whose striking drew comparisons with a genuine match-winner. The dew that Pakistan had hoped for arrived late, but by then the hosts had found their own momentum.

Sri Lanka, who had chased 430 against England in the league stage, will rue the missed chances — two lives for Fakhar, a dropped catch and a boundary conceded at deep cover — and a death-overs collapse with the bat that left them just short of a total that might have been enough.

World.title: Pakistan slams Afghan Taliban for 'shifting blame', 'persistent refusal' to address terrorism issues
World.content:
The information ministry on Saturday rebuked the Afghan Taliban’s stance on the ongoing conflict between the two countries, assailing its “persistent refusal to address terrorism” emanating from Afghanistan’s soil.

The statement came in response to remarks made by Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, who blamed Islamabad’s “wrong policies” for preventing a resolution to the conflict and insisted Kabul was not the cause of counterterrorism issues.

“Pakistan does not want to resolve the conflict with Afghanistan through talks,” Mujahid told Hurriyat Radio, claiming that Islamabad “lacks the necessary readiness for a peaceful resolution of differences”.

In its statement, the information ministry said the Afghan spokesman’s remarks expose the “regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan”.

“The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it added.

The ministry reiterated Pakistan’s “unequivocal” position: terrorism is a red line and the security of its citizens is non-negotiable.*

“The Afghan Taliban regime must understand that Pakistan will not tolerate terrorist sanctuaries across its borders that impact its security nor allow its people to remain targets of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan,” it stated.

Islamabad reiterated that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”.

“Shifting blame, making hollow assurances and questioning Pakistan’s policies will neither resolve the crisis nor absolve Kabul of its responsibilities. The Afghan Taliban leadership must understand that Pakistan’s security will not be held hostage to Afghan Taliban’s inaction, evasions or misplaced priorities.”

The information ministry affirmed that Pakistan reserved the right to “take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law, to eliminate threats to its national security, wherever they originate”.

It urged Kabul to recognise that the responsibility for addressing these threats “rests squarely with the Afghan Taliban regime”. “Pakistan’s resolve to protect its people must never be mistaken for weakness,” it declared.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year, facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye, failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough.

September witnessed another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

This was followed by drone incursions from across the border, which Islamabad said were shot down, and two further rounds of retaliatory airstrikes.

Those skirmishes continued in October, with Pakistani security forces responding to unprovoked fire from the Afghan side along the border in Kurram and Lower South Waziristan’s Angoor Adda, according to security sources.

On Tuesday, Afghan security forces opened unprovoked fire on border posts and residential areas in the Angoor Adda border area, which claimed the life of one local and injured a family of five.

World.title: ‘Very little, if anything, done for KP’: PM Shehbaz rails against PTI’s governance in province
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday criticised PTI’s governance in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, questioning whether the funds available to the now dysfunctional provincial government had been used transparently for the welfare and betterment of the people of the province.

His remarks came during a meeting of the PML-N’s parliamentary party from KP, held in Islamabad.

The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move had drawn criticism from the opposition, as well as Fazl, who had made efforts to reduce tensions between the federal and the KP governments.

Taking aim at the PTI, Prime Minister Shehbaz said: “They have been in power in KP for 13 years. Over these 13 years, they have raised countless slogans, delivered fiery speeches, held long marches and sit-ins, and made numerous promises.”

Recalling PTI’s promises to build hundreds of dams, generate hundreds of megawatts of solar power, and establish hospitals, universities and schools across the province, the prime minister questioned whether any of these pledges had been fulfilled during the party’s 13 years in power.

“How many universities have been established there? How many new hospitals have been built? How much has the healthcare system improved? What facilities have actually been provided to the people? And how much corruption has taken place in the process?” he asked.

The prime minister also questioned whether public funds had been utilised transparently for the welfare and betterment of the people of KP.

“From Peshawar to Kohistan and Hazara, and across the entire southern region of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the majority of people would tell you that the PTI government has done very little, if anything, to address their basic needs,” he said.

The premier maintained that by 2017-18, terrorist activities in the province had been brought to an end to “a considerable extent”.

“Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was among the provinces that made the greatest sacrifices in the fight against terrorism,” he said.

The prime minister highlighted the heavy toll terrorism had taken on the country, saying around 80,000 people had lost their lives and Pakistan’s economy had suffered losses estimated at Rs15,000 billion.

He also praised former prime minister and PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif for his policies to combat terrorism following the 2014 Army Public School tragedy, in which more than 140 students and teachers were killed.

Turning to the PTI, the prime minister said the party had spent the past two and a half years engaged in long marches and protests.

“In 2014, Chinese President Xi Jinping was scheduled to visit Pakistan. We made repeated efforts to persuade the party to call off its sit-in so that President Xi’s visit could proceed as planned, but it refused. As a result, the visit was postponed,” he said, recalling the 2014 D-Chowk protest.

He also criticised the PTI for allowing “brutal terrorists” from Afghanistan to settle in Swat.

“These were among the most painful and heartrending incidents that allowed terrorism to regain momentum,” he said.

The premier further said that thousands of civilians and security personnel had been martyred during the past two and a half years, adding that the PTI had been offered an opportunity to join hands with the federal government to combat terrorism, as it had done in the past.

He also said that hundreds of billions had been allocated to the KP government under a special National Finance Commission (NFC) arrangement to combat terrorism.

“How many Safe City projects have been initiated in KP? How much money has been spent on strengthening the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD)?” he asked.

The prime minister elaborated that even if the PTI-led KP government had spent Rs80 billion on strengthening the police and other law enforcement agencies, they would have been better equipped to tackle security challenges. “But unfortunately, that did not happen,” he added.

He said the federal government had managed to put the national economy back on its feet, but acknowledged that the recovery process would be a long journey.

The prime minister recalled that the government had formed a committee comprising members of the PPP and PML-N to hold talks with the PTI.

“Both sides held negotiations for 48 hours. I was told that the draft had been finalised and would be signed within minutes, following approval from then-chief minister Sohail Afridi. However, the approval never came, and we are still waiting,” he said.

Prime Minister Shehbaz said the federal government was compelled to impose an emergency and governor’s rule, as it had no other option.

He emphasised that the Centre’s decision had been “timely”, warning that the consequences would have been severe had it been delayed.

The prime minister urged PML-N lawmakers from KP to prioritise the basic needs of the people in their constituencies, while putting long-term projects on hold for the time being.

“Focus on short-term welfare projects so that you can help turn people’s fortunes around within the next six months to a year,” he stressed.

PTI hits back at PM’s criticism

Meanwhile, the PTI hit back at the premier’s criticism, challenging the federal government to account for its own record instead of blaming the party for KP’s security and governance problems.

PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said the prime minister had no moral authority to lecture the party on democracy and governance, alleging that the present political setup had come into power through electoral manipulation and political arrangements.

Waqas accused the federal government of shifting responsibility for the province’s worsening security situation onto the PTI provincial government. He alleged that the federal government had failed to provide the province with necessary resources and equipment for counterterrorism operations.

He also accused the Centre of focusing on political opposition rather than addressing security and governance issues, alleging that PTI leaders and workers had faced raids, arrests and intimidation.

He also challenged the premier to present a comprehensive account of his government’s four-year performance.

Less than a week after emergency and governor’s rule were imposed in the province, a joint sitting of parliament approved the federal government’s move amid a strong protest from the opposition.

The events of Oct 11 followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI — as well as negotiations to bridge their differences — after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Federal ministers alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups and asserted that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there.

The Centre and the PTI have been at odds over various issues, particularly on the counterterrorism policy, which was one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their Oct 3 talks .

The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre denied . It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticised the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban.

Additional input from Ikram Junaidi.

World.title: Germans join Europe's wave of 'Gen Z' protests; police fire water cannon on demonstrators
World.content:
German police fired a water cannon to disperse firework-hurling protesters on Saturday and were also pelted with other projectiles, as tensions rose at the end of massive youth-led protests.

In Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and dozens of other cities, demonstrators turned out for the protests organised by the group ‘GenZ regelt!’ (GenZ has got this), the latest by disillusioned youth in Europe.

Thousands of police were deployed across the country and, after mostly peaceful demonstrations, tensions rose in the evening in some places.

In the western city of Cologne, where one of the biggest demonstrations took place, police fired a water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks.

“We will not tolerate violence against emergency workers,” said a police statement.

Protesters light dlares after a demonstration organised by “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!) in Frankfurt am Mian on October 31, 2026. — AFP

Earlier, a march through the city was halted after demonstrators started setting off fireworks. A march was also temporarily halted in Frankfurt after protesters set off fireworks.

In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, Germany’s daily Bild reported.

Demonstrators had earlier taken to the streets waving signs that read “Time for resistance” and “Merz must go”, in reference to conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

They have been inspired by similar movements across Europe, including in France and Italy.

Europe-wide protests

“We’re taking to the streets for a life that everyone can afford,” said Veronika Dinter, a spokeswoman for the “GenZ regelt!” movement. “Hardly anyone still believes in a better future if everything just continues as it is.”

The movement’s complaints range from the high cost of living to poorly maintained schools, government spending cuts and, more broadly, what it sees as politicians making decisions with apparently little regard for the younger generation.

They are also unhappy with sharply increased military spending and a new voluntary service model aimed at boosting troop numbers, fearing it is a step towards bringing back conscription.

Riot Police bloct the street in front of protesters after a demonstration organised by “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!) in Frankfurt am Mian on October 31, 2026. — AFP

Several thousand demonstrators turned out in Cologne while the figure was around 5,000 in Berlin and 8,000 in Frankfurt, according to police.

There were also sizeable gatherings in other parts of the country, although the numbers were below the 170,000 nationwide that organisers had hoped for.

Authorities have been worried the protests, coinciding with Halloween, could be marred by the same kind of violence seen elsewhere in Europe.

Protests were also taking place in France for a third straight weekend.

Nationwide demonstrations there on October 17 degenerated into some of the country’s worst rioting in years.

Berlin is in contact with officials in France and Italy amid fears that radicals from overseas could seek to join the German protests.

A policeman stands next to police cars on the sidelines of a demonstration organised by “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!) in Berlin on October 31, 2026. —

But prior to the protests, authorities said that they had not seen evidence of concrete plans for violence. The “GenZ regelt!” movement explicitly rejects violence.

It stresses that “extremist groups, anti-constitutional symbols, racism and hate speech have no place with us — no matter from which side”.

Christian Volk, an expert in protest movements, said there was the potential to see a major movement emerge in Germany.

But Volk, from Berlin’s Humboldt University, told AFP there were key differences with France, which has a “completely different tradition when it comes to confrontational forms of protest”.

World.title: 1 dead, over 13 injured during stampede at TikToker's mehndi ceremony in Sialkot
World.content:
NAROWAL: A stampede at a mehndi (henna) event and prize-distribution ceremony held by a TikToker in Sialkot left one person dead and more than 13 others injured last night, police and rescue officials said on Saturday.

The mehndi ceremony and prize-distribution event for Muhammad Ansar Jatt, a popular TikToker from Sialkot district known as “Mr Pattlo”, was scheduled for Saturday night at Faraz Cricket Ground on Daska Road, according to a statement by Rescue 1122.

In a statement, the Sialkot police said that as event organisers opened the stadium gates to allow attendees in, a stampede ensued and many fell to the ground. Citing initial information, it said 14 people were injured.

Among those, 30-year-old Muhammad Aqeel passed away while being transported to the hospital due to his critical condition, the Rescue 1122 statement said.

Sialkot police said they and Rescue 1122 personnel conducted a joint rescue operation and transported the injured to Allama Iqbal Memorial Teaching Hospital. Most of the individuals were discharged after receiving first aid, while others remained under medical care, the statement added.

According to Rescue 1122, the injured persons comprised men aged between 22 and 51 years, and hailed from various districts, including Narowal, Gujranwala, Sheikhupura, Khanewal, Okara, Sialkot, Gujrat and Bahawalpur.

However, Sialkot residents Muhammad Asif and Aamir Ali stated that more than 40 people were injured in the stampede, explaining that before the rescue teams arrived, attendees had taken several injured to nearby private hospitals and clinics for first aid on their own.

Sialkot District Emergency Officer Engineer Naveed Iqbal said the rescue service had not been informed in advance about the large gathering planned at the cricket ground. He added that four ambulances and one motorcycle ambulance participated in the rescue operation.

Following the incident, Sialkot District Police Officer (DPO) Dost Muhammad had also reached the site, accompanied by a large police contingent and the Elite Force.

Acting on the DPO’s instructions, the police took charge of security arrangements, brought the crowd under control, and ensured that rescue operations could proceed without interruption, the police statement said.

Speaking to Dawn, DPO Muhammad criticised the event organisers for opening the stadium gates ahead of schedule. The retired captain noted that granting permission for such an event fell under the purview of the district administration.

The DPO emphasised that the protection of the lives and property of citizens remains the police’s top priority. All aspects of the incident will be examined and appropriate legal action will be taken, he asserted.

Dawn has reached out to Sialkot Deputy Commissioner Awais Mushtaq for comment.

World.title: Capt Safdar's remarks about women suffering from illness draw criticism, including from CM Maryam
World.content:
LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s spouse, retired Capt Muhammad Safdar, has come under fire for disparaging remarks about women advocating for bodily autonomy.

Speaking at a Khatm-i-Nabuwwat rally in Chiniot earlier this week, Safdar took aim at the slogan “mera jism, meri marzi” (my body, my choice).

He questioned why women who assert control over their bodies turn to religious scholars for prayers when diagnosed with serious illnesses such as cancer.

“They say, ‘My body, my choice.’ But when they fall ill or develop cancer, they turn to religious scholars, seeking prayers and blessed water for a cure. They should understand that if they claim ownership over their bodies, they should also be able to cure them. In reality, the human body is under God’s control,” he said.

On Friday, Maryam responded to a post on X regarding the speech, which stated: “Maryam Nawaz’s husband, Captain Safdar, also lost his mother-in-law to cancer, yet here he is mocking women who are battling cancer.”

The chief minister’s mother, Kulsoom Nawaz, passed away in 2018 after a months-long battle with cancer.

“Heartbreaking,” the chief minister said, posting an emoji of a broken heart.

“The silent battles a woman, a wife, fights behind closed doors … The strength she must find even when she feels like breaking. Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible,” she said.

Apart from CM Maryam, users on social media also took issue with Safdar’s remarks.

“My [mother] has been a cancer patient, and God knows how we managed to get through those difficult times. Her survival was nothing short of a miracle. Listening to Capt Safdar’s remarks on this matter is utterly shameful and disgraceful!” said TV anchor Ajmal Jami on X.

He also thanked CM Maryam for her “thoughtful and compassionate words for all those brave women”.

Another user, Maheen Ghani, said: “So a woman who says ‘mera jism, meri marzi’, which is essentially about autonomy and consent, loses the right to ask for prayers when she gets cancer? Is that seriously the argument?

“To take a woman’s illness, her fear and her faith and turn them into an opportunity to humiliate her. What an ugly, twisted understanding of both women’s rights and religion.”

On the other hand, some, like journalist Benazir Shah, lauded CM Maryam for speaking out.

“It takes real courage to take a public stand like this. More power to you, Maryam Nawaz Sharif,” she said.

Lawyers’ bodies condemn remarks about Asma Jahangir

Meanwhile, two premier lawyers’ bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018. During the rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer “cursed”.

Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements.

Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action.

“The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation,” the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly “deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect”.

The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance.

“The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition,” he emphasised.

Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar.

“These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community,” the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination.

“Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination.”

The SCBA also strongly condemned derogatory remarks by Safdar against women and an illness that was “being valiantly fought back by hundreds of thousands of women across the world”.

“At a time when women are breaking barriers, such remarks are disgraceful and entirely unacceptable,” the SCBA said.

“What makes this conduct even more shameful is that his own spouse holds the highest office of Punjab chief minister, and he himself is the father of a daughter; he should have been ashamed of making such insensitive and degrading remarks directed against the women,” it said.

These statements may also attract penal consequences, the SCBA reminded and called upon the concerned authorities to take immediate and strict notice and proceed in accordance with the law.

“Such divisive, offensive, and intolerant attitudes must be firmly challenged and nipped in the bud.

“Let it be clear to all and sundry, we will not remain silent when the dignity of our legal fraternity, the legacy of a human rights champion, and the respect owed to women are attacked,” the SCBA statement said.

Nasir Iqbal from Islamabad also contributed to this report.

World.title: Sindh CM Murad blames city planners for 'ruining' Karachi
World.content:
Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah on Saturday blamed urban planners for “ruining” Karachi, adding that he saw the metropolis vastly expand and deteriorate firsthand while growing up in it.

In July 2025, a steering committee tasked with developing the Greater Karachi Regional Plan 2047 was informed that the new master plan of the country’s commercial capital would be ready within two years.

Addressing an event of the Sindh Master Plan Authority (SMPA) in Karachi, CM Murad said: “Making a master plan from scratch is easy. But considering Karachi’s deteriorated condition, it is a challenge for consultants, master planners and urban developers to fix those [conditions], and also for the executive bodies to implement the plan.”

CM Murad noted that SMPA, established under the Karachi Development Authority (KDA) in 1968, was formed to develop urban master plans for Sindh’s cities with recommendations from stakeholders.

The chief minister said 14 master plans had been completed, but plans for Karachi and Hyderabad were under development. However, a post by the CM House quoted him as saying that master plans for 17 cities were complete, with work on 14 in final stages.

Recalling that he grew up in Karachi and saw the metropolis’ expansion firsthand, Murad said, “I do not think any other city in the world has expanded as quickly as Karachi has, nor has any city in the world been ruined by planners as quickly as Karachi has.”

The chief minister, whose PPP has ruled Sindh for about 15 years, stressed that Karachi needed to be improved. He contended that from the 1960s to the 1980s, it was a “very well-planned” city which attracted foreign visitors.

Recalling an incident during the severe rains of 2020, Murad lamented that while travelling along a new dual-carriageway road from Yousuf Goth, he saw that people had set up shops along the side roads, the stormwater drains on either side of the main road and even on the median.

“The planners did a very good job, but … a lot of roads have been declared commercial in the city and, to give people a livelihood, they are allowed to set up shops on stormwater drains for very cheap rent,” he said.

“I request the help of all stakeholders in [solving] this issue. Unless the entire city comes together to make it better, then we will not be successful.”

CM Murad also regretted that on several occasions, development work faced challenges due to delays from utility service providers, including the water board.

He also pointed out the lack of mapping of utility infrastructure: “There is no mapping anywhere.”

Noting Karachi’s population of 25 million and how urban development work inconveniences Karachiites, the chief minister said that funds have been arranged to rework 143 roads, but the work had not started because of procurement issues, which he said, “take a lifetime, but that’s how things are”.

However, he stressed the importance of forums under SMPA to discuss urban planning and implementation.

“These types of forums, seminars and discussions will help us bring some improvement and right now, in every city … the mayors and divisional headquarters are all trying to emulate the development which has started in Karachi.”

World.title: Syria weighing whether to join Makkah pact: foreign minister
World.content:
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Makkah defence pact that binds Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed on Aug 7, empowers the three members to consider an armed attack on one member an attack on all.

“Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Makkah alliance,” Al Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain.

According to Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), speaking about the ongoing regional conflicts, the foreign minister expressed Damascus’s support for the Gulf states against any aggression and condemned missile and drone attacks.

“Geography is destiny, and integration is a choice. We have chosen to make our territory a bridge for prosperity and the exchange of interests, and we stand as a bulwark against turning Syria into a platform for threatening neighbouring countries,” he was quoted as saying.

Al Shaibani also condemned repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory, affirmed that occupied Golan was Syrian land, and called for a path to an independent Palestinian state.

Saudi Arabia has been rallying support against escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, including a deadly strike that closed Riyadh’s international airport for two weeks this month.

Islamabad has two defence pacts with Riyadh aimed at collective deterrence — the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between the two and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement that also includes Turkiye.

Pakistan is providing “whatever support is needed” to defend Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks, the military’s spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said earlier this month.

However, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) director general also clarified that all members of the Makkah Defence Alliance were “absolutely clear […] that this alliance has no offensive intent; it is purely defensive”.

A day earlier, he said that the wording of the pact did not bar new members after being asked about whether Iran could join the agreement.

“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.

In August, two weeks after the Makkah pact was signed, the Syrian foreign minister visited Pakistan and called on Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir.

They both discussed “regional security environment and avenues for enhanced bilateral defence and security cooperation”, ISPR said.

Amid the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, French President Emmanuel Macron made a surprise visit to Riyadh earlier this month and said France had sent troops to help shield a key Saudi oil terminal from attacks.

Also in October, the United Kingdom’s government announced it would deploy British fighter planes to help Saudi Arabia against the attacks.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.
