World.title: The government knows it has a problem, does it have a clear path forward?
World.content:
Forget the form guide. The closest thing to a sure bet this Melbourne Cup Day is another rate rise.

And unlike the punters at Flemington, millions of Australians won't have a say in how much it costs them.

The average household bears no responsibility for the wars, oil crisis and AI boom that are driving up inflation, but that doesn't save them from the economic pain.

It's why Labor's emphasis on these international factors is wearing thin with voters, who want workable solutions and help rather than explanations or excuses.

As pressure builds on the Albanese government, the remarkable caucus discipline of the past four years is fraying by the day.

No easy way out of inflation Another bad inflation result causes pain for households, business and the government. They also show that a tougher approach may well be needed to curb the problem.

The difficult economic outlook has been compounded by a succession of own goals, failures of process and poor consultation, which have sparked a litany of post-budget backdowns.

The accumulation has taken a toll, with many Labor MPs feeling like they have been left to defend decisions they had little say in shaping.

Internal discontent and anonymous griping are at a notably high watermark.

There are apparently plenty of people in government able to diagnose the problems, but what's lacking is articulation of a clear path forward.

All eyes on MYEFO

Markets are pricing a more than 80 per cent chance the Reserve Bank will lift the cash rate to 4.85 per cent on Tuesday, a level not seen since the global financial crisis in 2008.

As households do what they must to absorb the cost, focus on the federal government's role in the inflation fight will only sharpen.

Gone are the days of energy rebates and slashing the fuel excise, now almost all of the political debate is about how to cut public spending to help the RBA.

All this makes next month's mid-year economic and fiscal outlook (MYEFO) an unusually important moment for the government.

The days of handing out relief to a public struggling with cost-of-living are gone. (AAP)

Having already promised savings to help ease demand in the economy, Treasurer Jim Chalmers was this week asked if the December update would result in a "net" reduction in government spending.

He pointed out that in this year's budget and the last MYEFO, net policy decisions had made a "positive contribution over the four years" of the budget.

That is true over the forwards, but when it comes to fighting inflation, it's the shorter term that really matters. And for the current and last financial year, government decisions in those two updates added about $14 billion to the overall spend.

There is no shortage of Labor MPs who believe this MYEFO must be different, with terms like "means testing" and "net savings" a constant refrain in private conversations.

Albanese heads to CHOGM

None of this is news to Chalmers, as evidenced by his own camp pointing out it is the prime minister who ultimately rules the all-powerful expenditure review committee, where such decisions are signed off.

That sparked some ministers in Albanese's corner to argue the prime minister had been prudent in reining in some of the treasurer's budget ambitions.

The apparent deterioration in the relationship between Albanese and Chalmers has started to concern some in Labor, who fear the more time spent apportioning blame for recent events, the less the government appears focused on solutions.

Chalmers caused some raised eyebrows when he this week suggested that while he "genuinely" took responsibility for some of the "hard stuff" in the budget causing political pain for Labor, it was also up to "other ministers and the prime minister how they describe their part in that".

Jim Chalmers will be on his own to face an almost definite rate rise. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Whether or not the treasurer is unfairly copping the bulk of the criticism, as one Labor MP noted, it "matters little" to voters who "will be just as happy to blame us all".

That is likely precisely what will happen on Tuesday when the Reserve Bank is expected to lift the cash rate.

Chalmers will be left to manage the immediate fallout at home, while Albanese lands in the Caribbean for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

Those optics are not lost on the Coalition, which already started using Question Time last week to needle the prime minister about his impending absence.

The decision to attend CHOGM has puzzled many of Albanese's colleagues.

As the prime minister himself revealed, the request came directly from King Charles, and while there Albanese will hold talks with UK leader Andy Burnham and Canada's Mark Carney.

The hope is voters will understand the need for Australia to engage on the world stage, particularly when so many of the forces affecting its economy originate overseas.

But with the demands of summit season dragging Albanese abroad for almost four of the next seven weeks, expect his detractors to give the "Airbus Albo" moniker a workout.

The prime minister has ridden out plenty of political turbulence before, but this time the economic headwinds are being compounded by growing frustration within his own ranks.

Whatever happens at the Melbourne Cup, at least someone will finish the day a winner. The same can't be said for either Albanese or Chalmers.

World.title: Banks sitting on billions in savers' money as interest rates rise
World.content:
Savers with billions of dollars in Australian banks could be missing out on the benefit of rising cash interest rates as a result of onerous account conditions or because they have not opted for the right type of savings product.

Data compiled for the ABC by comparison site Canstar shows following the last RBA interest hike announcement the Commonwealth Bank, NAB, ANZ and Westpac each increased their maximum saving rates by 0.20 or 0.25 per cent.

Consumer advocates fear some of that money is sitting in high-interest savings accounts that come with strict conditions, including regular contribution amounts, and customers are falling just shy.

The competition regulator found in a 2023 retail deposits inquiry more than 70 per cent of customers never met the monthly conditions.

While each of the major banks were quick to increase the interest paid on mortgages after the September rate hike, customers with high interest savings accounts have not been finding the corresponding interest rate increases as lucrative.

Canstar said it found the rate increases were applied only to a select few of the banks' savings account products, and with strict conditions attached.

Home owners feeling the pinch Home owners are looking for ways to earn extra funds as the increase to interest rates to 4.6 per cent makes it harder to make ends meet.

Unless savers meet those requirements they reverted to a base rate for interest that the banks have kept flat at 0.10 per cent.

That means one slip-up, for example, missing the target for the minimum monthly deposit, or forgetting about the minimum withdrawal requirements, and savers receive virtually zero in interest.

Then there are customers who do not make the most of rate hikes at all, with the big four banks sitting on hundreds of billions of dollars of customers' money in accounts that are earning no interest.

Billions of dollars are sitting in bank accounts earning no interest. (Pexels: Karolina Grabowska)

As of June, the Commonwealth Bank held nearly $122 billion of its customers money in accounts earning no interest, according to its annual report.

Westpac held nearly $82 billion as of March, while NAB held about $67 billion, and ANZ held about $61 billion in the same period.

How have you been affected by increasing rates? Have you had to cut back on luxuries or essentials? Tell us

Banks need to be more proactive

Canstar's Sally Tindall said when banks announced they were passing rate rises it was not as clear-cut as it appeared.

Sally Tindall says to shop around if you are not happy with your current banking situation. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"Many customers will miss out, at least from time to time, because they don't meet those terms and conditions," she said.

She argued banks could be doing more to ensure their customers did not miss out.

"Alerting people with a proactive email or text message … close to the end of the month that tells you if you're not going to meet those terms and conditions," she said.

Melbourne saver Corey Washbourne said he did not find the conditions on his account too onerous. He adds about $50 a month to get the bonus rate.

Corey Washbourne is among the savers benefiting from high interest rates. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

He is thankful for the higher interest rates on his savings accounts, because it is protecting the value of his savings against inflation and gives him breathing room.

"It's just reassuring to know that you've got that interest coming into your savings account to top it up and act as that buffer, and you're not going backwards as much.

"There's that little bit of cushion and breathing room".

In a statement to the ABC, the Australian Banking Assocation's chief executive Simon Birmingham said banks supported customers to get the most out of their savings, including through app alerts and messages.

Simon Birmingham says in the past financial year, banks paid out more than $120 billion in interest to depositors. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"Australia's savings market is highly competitive, with hundreds of term deposit and savings account options available to customers," he said.

Across the last financial year, Mr Birmingham said banks paid out more than $120 billion in interest to depositors.

"Product offerings from banks do vary and this choice gives customers the flexibility to choose products that best suit their personal circumstances," he said.

Billions of dollars not earning interest

On top of marginal interest repayments, many Australians are missing out on the opportunity to make a bit of extra cash each month from choosing a bank account that pays no interest.

The ACCC inquiry found only 16 per cent of consumers switched their savings account in the past three years, and only 11 per cent have switched their transaction account.

Michelle Cull says it is important to read the terms and conditions to ensure the option is best suited for your personal situation. (Supplied: Michelle Cull)

Western Sydney University associate professor of accounting and financial planning Michelle Cull said consumers should be conducting "regular checks" of their banking to ensure they were getting the best deal.

Dr Cull said, for example, by exploring the option of an offset account.

"Because you are actually going to be saving the interest rate that has just gone up for paying the mortgage," she said.

"Plus you're not paying tax on it [compared to interest on savings], so there's an extra saving there."

How to check your mortgage offset account Many Australians have been missing out on the benefits of their mortgage offset account. Here's how to check whether yours is working for you, or whether you might want to get one.

But she emphasised every situation was unique, and it was important for consumers to read the fine print.

"You really need to look carefully at your own circumstances."

Behind those shiny numbers that the banks promote on their savings products, Dr Cull said there could be several caveats.

"Remembering an introductory rate is only for a limited time," she said.

RBA meets again to discuss interest rates

The Reserve Bank will meet again next week, to decide whether interest rates will hike again, for a fifth time this year, with the goal of curbing inflation.

Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook is worse than expected. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Earlier this month, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook was "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, lifting the odds of a hike in November.

Markets are putting the chances of a rate rise at 98 per cent.

Ms Tindall said if customers were not happy with their savings account, they could "take your nest egg shopping".

"There's a huge amount of banks to pick from. There's a huge amount of options even within the same bank," she said.

World.title: Olivia wasn't expected to live more than a few days, now she's a movie star
World.content:
Actor Olivia Hargroder was not expected to live more than a few days after she was born. She's now 27.

She was probably not going to talk. She's a chatterbox.

She was not expected to walk very well. She dances.

In fact, Olivia dances so well that when she was cast in the lead role of feature film Boss Cat as the rhythm-lacking Sonja, it took all Olivia's acting skills to pull it off.

"Once I found out that Sonja's not the best dancer, I found that quite hard to do," Olivia tells Australian Story with a sassy giggle. "Because I'm such a good and amazing dancer myself."

Olivia Hargroder on the set of the movie Boss Cat. (Supplied)

Confidence is not something Olivia lacks and it's a quality her mother, Kerry Read, says has helped Olivia rise above the low expectations many impose on people with Down syndrome.

"Anyone who meets Olivia will know optimism is her key operating system," Kerry says. "She's so optimistic, she's so confident.

"It's very easy when you're constantly put down in life to actually be demotivated. Life as someone with an intellectual impairment is full of those … [who] aren't optimistic about you."

Olivia Hargroder's mum, Kerry Read, was told at a pregnancy scan that her daughter may only survive a few days. (Australian Story: Marc Smith)

By the time Olivia consulted her school careers counsellor, she'd almost completed her final year at a mainstream school and had become so adept at public speaking that she'd addressed the United Nations (UN) in New York on World Down Syndrome Day.

Olivia Hargroder addressed the UN in 2017, with her mum watching proudly behind her. (Supplied)

She told the counsellor her next ambition was to study at the National Institute of Dramatic Arts (NIDA), one of Australia's most prestigious acting schools.

He just laughed, told her NIDA was for "the elite" and suggested she instead work in a bakery, which, Olivia quips, "is definitely very hard when you're gluten-free".

She got into NIDA. For one year, she studied with 12 budding thespians at its Open Young Actor's Studio, before undertaking other acting courses.

Olivia Hargroder on the set of Boss Cat with cast mates Elijah Williams (left) and Chris Bunton. (Supplied)

Then, in 2021, she started acting with Bus Stop Films, a disability-led organisation that works with about 250 young adults with intellectual disability, autism or Down syndrome to create films and equip them with skills to get jobs in the industry.

"When they asked me to audition for Boss Cat, it was actually an incredible feeling to have because I've never been a lead in a feature before," says Olivia, who lives in Redcliffe, north of Brisbane.

"It was just a dream come true."

Loading...

Olivia has other dreams. The one she's held the longest is to dance on Broadway in musicals. Her absolute biggest dream, she says, is to be a dancer on tour with her idol, Taylor Swift.

Unachievable? Don't tell Olivia that, says Kerry.

"She does have huge dreams and sometimes," Kerry says, "the most unachievable dreams she actually achieves."

'Incompatible with life'

At her routine 20-week pregnancy scan, Kerry was told her baby had a heart condition that was "apparently incompatible with life".

She was advised "very, very strongly" to have a termination.

But Kerry's desire to hold her third child in her arms for as long as she was granted — "moments, days, whatever" — overruled the experts.

Doctors told Kerry Read her unborn baby had a serious heart condition. (Supplied)

When Olivia was born, Kerry, a 40-something physiotherapist at the time, knew immediately that her daughter had Down syndrome.

"She had a gap between her first and second toes which is so classic of Down syndrome," says Kerry, who had not had scans to detect the chromosomal condition.

"But it didn't matter because every moment was precious and I never really thought that her Down syndrome was a problem. It was just, 'How long was she going to live?'"

Having survived the first few days, it was hoped Olivia would make it to three months before undergoing surgery on the hole in her heart but, at nine weeks, she was deteriorating and whisked into surgery.

Olivia Hargroder underwent heart surgery at nine weeks old. (Supplied)

She had a 20 per cent chance of survival. "I always say she's a sparky kid and she is determined to hang on," Kerry says. "And hang on she did."

To Olivia, her mum is a "superwoman".

"It wasn't just the doctors and nurses who saved my life," she says. "It was my mum."

Life-changing surgery

Kerry was told Olivia would probably not be able to speak, or her speech would be delayed. So, when Olivia was four months old, Kerry started teaching her, along with her other daughters Emily and Lucy, how to sign.

Lucy (left) and Emily Read cradle their baby sister at hospital. (Supplied)

Through play, she worked on improving Olivia's low muscle tone (which is characteristic of Down syndrome), exposed her to sensory stimulation and ensured Olivia made her own choices.

Says Emily: "Mum never limited her but Mum never forced her to do anything either. I think that's really important too, that it wasn't, 'We're going to defy the odds'. It was just Olivia is who she is."

And Olivia knew she was a dancer. She loved learning routines with her sisters and dancing to music videos.

But her kneecaps were badly misaligned and as she got older, she fell over a lot, injuring herself.

"I used to get a number of fractures," Olivia says, "but I always managed to bounce back. I always do."

Olivia Hargroder loved doing dance routines with her older sisters. (Supplied)

By her mid-teens, and still at school, Olivia was desperate to have an operation to fix her knees.

She and Kerry had consulted a number of orthopaedic surgeons when Olivia was younger but the operation could not be done until her growth plates had fused. Surgeons were also concerned about her heart (which required further surgery when she was 18) and the need for intensive rehabilitation, which some doubted a young person with Down syndrome would do.

But Olivia was determined and, at 15, she sat down and wrote a letter to one of the surgeons she'd consulted, Jeremy Bartlett.

Olivia Hargroder's kneecaps were misaligned and she injured herself frequently. (Supplied)

It read, in part:

" Dear Dr Bartlett, Can you please help me with these things that I want to do? I really want to stop falling over and I also want to stop breaking bones. "

Dr Bartlett says he was moved by the letter and decided to operate on one knee. Olivia was so committed to her rehab and improved so well, her second knee was operated on soon after.

"It changed my life," Olivia says. "I could run, I could jump, I could dance, I can do anything I wanted … I'm so, so grateful because I am just so happy to be where I am right now and with my dancing. It's just an incredible place to be."

A star is born

Dressed in hot pink and purple all the way down to her glittering dancing shoes, Olivia's Boss Cat character Sonja is on board a bus, krumping up a storm.

Olivia Hargroder's character, Sonja, uses dance as an outlet for her emotions. (Supplied)

Krumping, a high-energy street dance, play a big role in the film — used as an outlet for Sonja, who has special needs, to express her anger at the death of her mother and a plan by her grandmother to move her into an assisted-care home.

Genevieve Clay-Smith, the co-founder of Bus Stop Films and writer and director of Boss Cat, beams as she remembers that day of filming and how Olivia "gobbled it up".

"Basically, the brief was 'be a pop star' and own that bus," she says. "And Olivia brought the attitude; she really channelled pop star vibes that day."

Olivia Hargroder plays Sonja, a 23-year-old fighting to remain her home after her mother's death. (Supplied)

Genevieve says the moment she met Olivia she had a "visceral sensation in my gut" that she had found Sonja. After a rigorous audition process, she knew she was right.

Apart from her talent, Genevieve saya, Olivia is curious, asks insightful questions about her character and listens well to direction.

"I love being in front of the camera so much," Olivia says. "It just makes my whole world look just incredible … I love the freedom."

Before filming, the duo held weekly teleconferences to run through the script and to find ways to channel the types and depth of emotions required for a scene.

Behind the scenes of Boss Cat, which is due for general release in December. (Supplied)

To improve her range, Olivia created a coloured mood chart as a way to indicate that a scene required rage, joy or sadness, or a combination of those. It also helped protect her from being consumed by Sonja's emotions.

"Olivia has this gift of being able to feel deeply and to really invest and find her emotional truth," Genevieve says. "The chart … helped her harness the emotions rather than letting the emotions take over her."

Olivia Hargroder with writer and director Genevieve Clay-Smith on the set of Boss Cat. (Supplied)

Genevieve's hope is that Olivia will be cast in future roles because she's a great actress, not a great actress with Down syndrome.

"I hope that she gets to do more amazing performances that draw in audiences, captivate people, and that satisfy her and fulfil her as an actress," she says.

A home of her own

Olivia reckons she and Sonja are quite different but there are similarities. They both have a strong group of friends and dream of living independently.

"My dream is to hopefully live with my boyfriend one day," Olivia says. "It's always been my dream for the longest time."

Voting open for Australian Story countdown Since 1996, ABC's Australian Story has allowed people from all walks of life to tell their stories in their own words. More than 1,100 episodes and 30 years later, we are asking you to pick the most memorable.

She met her "handsome, gorgeous" boyfriend, Jarred, at Bus Stop Films about a year ago, and he was there to see Olivia walk the red carpet in a stunning pink gown at the movie's premiere at the Sydney Film Festival. It is set for general release on December 3, the International Day of People with a Disability.

Olivia's mother Kerry sees no reason her daughter's dream of living away from home cannot be realised.

Boss Cat premiered at the Sydney Film Festival in June. (Australian Story: Rebecca Armstrong)

"She manages perfectly well when I'm not here and will perfectly well manage her own household," she says.

"I think it's important that … there's not just an assumption that all people with Down syndrome will be forever someone's child. Her thoughts and her feelings are just the same as everyone else's and she's perfectly capable of taking agency over her own life."

Olivia's sister Lucy says Kerry has plans in place for when that time arrives, with Olivia needing some support "so she can be the most fulfilled that she can be".

"Olivia goes around smashing all your boxes," Lucy says. "She's just like, 'I don't fit in that box'. Smash!

"And she just keeps doing that. And as her sister, you have no choice but to go on that journey with her. And it makes you a bigger person. And it makes you a better person. And it makes you see the world differently."

Olivia Hargroder (second left) has the backing of older sisters Emily and Lucy Read and mum Kerry Read. (Australian Story: Marc Smith)

For now, Olivia is happy to keep dancing, acting, working at a major supermarket, going to coffee with Jarred and zipping around in her fully enclosed mobile scooter, dubbed the Popemobile.

Olivia Hargroder met her boyfriend Jarred about a year ago. (Australian Story)

Throughout her life, she's met people who see disability before they see the person, but Olivia likes to see the best in people and simply asks that others do too.

"I would say, 'Give people with Down syndrome a red hot go'," Olivia says. "They always bring something special to the table that you might not know.

"I would encourage you to take that special person into your heart … because you'll never know what they'll surprise you with."

Watch Australian Story, Bring it On! on Monday at 8pm (AEDT) on ABCTV and ABC iview.

World.title: Ex-detective says triple murderer one of the worst people he has ever dealt with
World.content:
A triple murderer who gunned down a Queensland cattle grazing family had terrorised the community for decades, stealing livestock and threatening a police officer, according to his former neighbours and an ex-detective.

Darryl Young is serving three life sentences with a non-parole period of 40 years, a sentence believed to be the longest ever handed down in Queensland, for killing his neighbours Mervyn and Maree Schwarz, and her son Graham Tighe, after he demanded the family meet him at the gate of his Bogie property in 2022.

Young is appealing against his conviction and sentence.

Maree and Mervyn Schwarz (left) and Graham Tighe were found dead at the gate of the Bogie cattle station in 2022. (ABC News/Supplied)

The 63-year-old had wrongly accused the family of cattle theft before fatally shooting three of them and shooting Ross Tighe, the sole survivor.

But it was Young who was convicted of cattle theft in 2006 after he pleaded guilty to stealing 147 head of cattle with his mother, Janelle.

Fred Swift, a former detective in Queensland's stock squad, has never spoken publicly about his dealings with Young before now.

Mr Swift described meeting Young in 1994 and revealed he was the main suspect for cattle theft in the Bowen area in north Queensland.

"Darryl was one of the worst people I ever dealt with … I did call him the spawn of the devil, I said it to his face," Mr Swift told the ABC.

" People were fearful of him and that fear was justified. "

Fred Swift says Darryl Young was the main suspect for cattle theft in Bowen. (Supplied)

Mr Swift said Young threatened him on multiple occasions.

"He was always very aggressive. He just told me, 'Watch what you're doing,'" Mr Swift said.

Young was vindictive and would react when people reported him for cattle stealing, according to Mr Swift.

"It wasn't always him stealing cattle, but it often was."

Mr Swift said after one particular complaint, Young pushed a man's cattle yards into a heap with a bulldozer and sat the machine on top of the wreckage as a warning sign.

Another time, Young drained a tank of molasses down the creek at the same man's property, Mr Swift said.

Neighbour's decades-long fight

Also speaking publicly for the first time, Steve Norman, a former neighbour of the Young family's property in Bowen, said he was among the cattle owners whose stock Young and his mother stole.

Mr Norman revealed he had been trying to get a conviction since 1986.

"You wouldn't believe what the property next to me was called when his mother owned it. Sneaky Hills. It's a great name for cattle duffers, isn't it?" Mr Norman told the ABC.

Mr Norman alleges Young cut his fences and threatened his daughters after he made reports to the stock squad.

"Every time we'd get the stock squad onto them, I'd have windmills broken, I'd have pumps pinched."

Convicted murderer and cattle thief, Darryl Young, lived in prime cattle-breeding country in Bogie. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Another time, Mr Norman said a jet pump was cut out of a bore and the 6-metre hole filled with rocks, so it was unusable.

The stock squad had received multiple reports about Darryl Young over many years, but it did not have enough concrete evidence to charge him, Mr Swift said.

But one day in 2003, Mr Swift was wandering around the Gracemere cattle yards in central Queensland, about a six and a half hour drive from Bowen, when he saw dodgy-looking brands on cattle and Darryl Young's name.

"That's when it all came tumbling down," the ex-detective said.

"[He and his mother] were changing brands, registering brands very close to their neighbours' brands and putting their brand over the old brand."

Fred Swift says Darryl Young and his mother were changing brands on cattle and registering similar ones to their neighbours'. (Supplied)

Later, Mr Swift was searching for a woman's missing cattle when he pulled into a paddock in Bowen.

"I was eating my ham and salad sandwich on wholemeal bread, and it suddenly dawned on me I was looking at stolen cattle," he said.

"They had been agisted to the farm that was there by Darryl Young. I don't think anyone else knew that they were stolen.

" It was fairly major. The number of complaints and the history and time that went by. "

Young was sentenced to two years' imprisonment, to be released after serving six months, for the cattle theft conviction in 2006.

His mother Janelle Young's two-year sentence was wholly suspended.

During the 2006 case, Judge Bob Pack said the scheme was "somewhat sophisticated" because the Gracemere cattle yard was "well away from the Bowen district", meaning there were fewer chances of the cattle being identified by their real owners.

"An under-resourced stock squad, which has been the position for many years, of course to some extent facilitates offending of this nature," Judge Pack said at the time.

The entrance to Shannonvale Station where Darryl Young lived. (ABC Tropical North: Danielle Jesser)

Mr Norman said things quietened down after Young's conviction, until the morning of the Bogie shooting in 2022.

"The police rang me up wondering where I was. I said, 'I'm in Charters Towers' and they said, 'Thank Christ for that, because Darryl Young is up here shooting people,'" Mr Norman said.

"[The police officer] was worried [about me]."

Young maintained his innocence throughout the trial this year, claiming he was never at the scene of the shooting.

'The whole system is broken'

Another of Young's former neighbours, Robert Kohler, told the ABC he never would have met him unarmed, for his own safety.

"I was fully aware of what Young was capable of," he said.

Mr Kohler lived at Sutherland Station in Bogie, a rural town about 55 kilometres from Bowen in Queensland's Whitsunday Region, from 2011 to 2018.

Robert Kohler (right), pictured with son Zac, says Darryl Young's reputation was as long as Queensland's Bruce Highway. (Supplied)

The Schwarz and Tighe family later bought the property and moved in, about a year before the 2022 tragedy.

Mr Kohler said he had near-daily issues with Young, whose home at Shannonvale Station bordered the property.

"When he moved here [in 2012], I had a cup of tea with him, and I told him he had a reputation as long as the Bruce Highway, but I'd treat him like he treated me," Mr Kohler said.

Mr Kohler said a few years later he called Queensland police's stock squad after Young was seen mustering with dogs on his property, and he later found horse and dog tracks.

But he said the stock squad did not take it seriously.

"The stock squad said, 'Oh, go up and have a look and see if you put any cattle through the gate,'" he said.

"I said, 'Isn't that your job?' and they said they were a bit busy.

"The whole system's broken mate, people take it for a joke."

Mr Kohler said he also rang the stock squad after Young was seen driving with a tarp over his truck at 2am, which he suspected had stolen cattle inside.

"They could've gone down to his yard the next day and checked to see what he had in the yard, and DNA tested [the cattle]," he said.

"He was just stealing blindly, and the police didn't want nothing to do with it at all."

The Bogie murder scene was a property gate at Shannonvale Station where Darryl Young lived. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Queensland)

Mr Kohler wants stock theft to be taken more seriously.

"[When Darryl was jailed for stock theft], he was out in six months," he said.

"All that led to where we are: three people losing their lives and one getting wounded."

Katter's Australian Party leader Robbie Katter has called for better resourcing of the unit that deals with cattle theft, now known as the Rural and Stock Crime Squad.

Robbie Katter says the Bogie shooting should be a wake-up call to the government. (Supplied: Katter's Australian Party)

Mr Katter said investigations needed proper support with mustering costs, DNA testing, and specialist police who knew the bush.

"At Bogie … I think that's the wake-up call the government needed to demonstrate that this needs to be adequately resourced," Mr Katter told the ABC.

"It would certainly be good value for the government to nip these things in the bud before they blow up or signal to others that it's easy to get away with."

Mr Swift joined the stock squad in 1984 and the Young investigation was his last job in the department. He was offered a promotion out of the unit, which he declined.

"I saw people struggling and working hard. All their efforts to no avail," he said.

"I always say, if you want to make money, you go into politics, start a religion, or steal cattle."

A Queensland Police (QPS) spokesperson did not comment on allegations that Young stole cattle or on how the stock squad handled the reports.

The spokesperson said Rural and Stock Crime Squad detectives had specialist expertise in rural and stock crime investigations, including major and organised crimes, drug offences, firearms theft and trafficking.

Investigations could be complex and protracted, often spanning large geographical areas, the QPS spokesperson said.

"The Rural and Stock Crime Squad encourages rural communities to remain vigilant by reporting suspicious activity or stock theft, securing firearms appropriately, and considering crime prevention measures such as security cameras, signage and secure property access."

The ABC has contacted Young's lawyer for comment.

World.title: Cyclone forecast tips quieter season for Australia
World.content:
El Niño headlines typically focus on extreme weather and its negative impacts.

But the world's most significant driver of meteorological variability can also produce positive outcomes, including a reduction in the number of tropical cyclones in Australia.

And modelling shows our 2026/27 cyclone season, which runs from November 1 to April 30, could be one of the quietest on record.

Category 5 Tropical Cyclone Ilsa in April 2023 heads towards the Pilbara coastline. (Supplied: NASA's Earth Observatory)

Cyclone forecast for 2026/27 season

Tropical cyclones are violent, spiralling wind and rain systems fuelled by the latent energy released as water vapour from warm seas condenses.

Technically, a tropical cyclone is defined by the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) as a low-pressure system with winds of at least 63 kilometres per hour, equivalent to gusts above 90 km/h, in at least three of the four quadrants around the centre.

Once formed they are categorised based on peak wind gusts, with a category 2 declared when speeds reach 125 km/h, a category 3 — 165 km/h, category 4 — 225 km/h, then finally a category 5 for gusts of 280 km/h or above.

The Australian area of responsibility, shown in the map below, spans from 160 degrees east, encompassing most of the Coral Sea, to 90 degrees east, more than 2,000 kilometres off the WA west coast.

The BOM's area of responsibility covers a vast region surrounding the Australian landmass. (Supplied)

The BOM no longer issues an official seasonal cyclone outlook for Australia, previously stating that climate change has reduced the accuracy of statistical models and historical relationships.

However, physical models, like the ones used for day-to-day weather forecasting, can be used as a guide for long-range cyclone predictions.

And the verdict, according to modelling from the world's leading global forecasting agency, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), is a likely range of five to eight named storms this season, compared with a long-term average of 11.

The forecast is created by running the model 51 times from slightly different starting conditions, and the range shown is the average of the results plus or minus one standard deviation.

In other words, about two thirds of the model runs show between five and eight cyclones in the Australian region this season.

The highest chance of a reduction in cyclone activity this season is off WA and in the central Coral Sea. (Supplied: ECMWF)

But the projected trend in cyclones is not uniform, with the strongest signal for a reduction, at least one standard deviation from the mean, shaded over the Indian Ocean and an area of the central and southern Coral Sea.

Near normal activity is tipped for waters off the NT, Gulf of Carpentaria and near the Queensland coast.

Most Australian cyclones don't reach the coast

While a total of five to eight tropical cyclones may sound alarming, more than half in the BOM's area of responsibility never make landfall or weaken below cyclone strength by the time they do.

Since 1970, on average three to four tropical lows cross the Australian coastline at cyclone strength or above, representing about 30 to 40 per cent of total systems.

However, the proportion of systems crossing the coast varies each year. Of the 11 systems during the 2025/26 season, five reached the coast.

The 2025-26 season brought 11 tropical cyclones, seven of which reached a category 3 or above. (Supplied: BOM)

And it only takes one system hitting a community to have serious impacts, so people in cyclone-prone areas should prepare before a cyclone forms and stay up to date with the latest forecasts and warnings. On average, however, the first system to cross the coast does not do so until late December.

It is also worth noting that the five-to-eight range is just a forecast from one model, and the final number of cyclones this season could easily fall outside that range.

How El Niño and climate change affect Australian cyclones

The forecast is consistent with past El Niño events, which since 1970 have produced a lower average of seven or eight cyclones per year, while during the opposite phase La Niña, that number is boosted to 12.

El Niño's influence is due to a combination of cooler waters off Australia's northern coast, along with a decrease in moisture, monsoon strength and convection.

While globally oceans are seeing unprecedented heat thanks to El Niño and climate change, waters are relatively cool off Australia's north coast.

Climate change is another influence on Australian tropical storms, and during the past few decades there has been a clear decline in numbers, but a higher proportion of top-end category 4 or 5 systems.

Since 2000, the annual average number of named storms has fallen to nine, well below the 1970 to 1999 mean of 13.

However, there is evidence that peak cyclone strength is increasing, so while fewer systems are forming, the amount of damage could still increase in a warmer world.

This includes the impact of rising sea levels, which leads to greater storm surge inundation.

World.title: ‘They wanted our WhatsApps’: Staff claim culture of fear at Florey
World.content:
Florey Institute staff claim financial pressures are crimping their ability to do their work.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In December 2024, researchers at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health were called into a meeting with senior leadership. Recollections differ about the tone of the meeting, but the message was clear. Taxpayer-funded research grants are the lifeblood of independent research institutes – and the Florey was not winning nearly enough. “At a time when most researchers were devastated at finding they were unsuccessful after spending months preparing applications,” one said, leadership “got up in front of everyone and berated us for not doing good enough”. “After that meeting, everyone was walking around chatting to colleagues saying ‘can you believe it? I can’t believe that happened’.” Yesterday, an investigation by this masthead revealed the venerable institute – which the Rockefeller Foundation helped establish and was named after penicillin pioneer and Nobel Laureate Howard Florey – had become embroiled in chaos as it faced financial strife and an exodus of top research talent.



Today, the investigation focuses on the scientific fallout from that turmoil – numerous complaints about the culture inside the Florey and the string of court cases in which it is now embroiled. This masthead has spoken to 22 former or current Florey staff – very few willing to be identified publicly for fear of retribution – to build a picture of a once-great institution under extreme financial pressure and facing accusations of building an unhealthy atmosphere for a workforce trying to solve dementia, Alzheimer’s, epilepsy, MND and mental health conditions. “They’ve created this culture: the scientists are the ones to blame for the problem they are in. A pure toxic culture has developed,” said a current researcher, speaking under condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. “They have taken the option to go completely corporate. You can’t do that with a research institute because you’re just going to end up getting rid of most people – and the rest are going to want to leave.” A Florey spokeswoman said falls in grant income “reflect[ed] a tightening national funding environment” and “notably, funding for dementia reduced by 48% over the same time period” according to the National Health and Medical Research Council, website and annual disease funding statistics. They denied anyone had been “berated” about grant success rates, and said the meeting discussed “low national success rates”.



“This was a constructive discussion that identified other grant schemes that our researchers could apply to.” But a confidential Florey presentation from February 2025 lamented “limited grant success in 2024 funding round, below expectations, partly due to inconsistent and inefficient grant support”. “Every funding round was just a constant disappointment,” said a former staff member. The Florey Institute’s Parkville headquarters. Joe Armao In response to poor success rates, the institute proposed implementing an internal vetting system before grants could be submitted. “The result is less grants being submitted in order to artificially inflate the apparent success rate, a metric which has absolutely no impact on researchers,” said a former researcher. A spokeswoman for the Florey said it was “committed to attracting and retaining the brightest minds in medical research, while supporting professional development and opportunities across the medical research sector”. The institute does not prevent researchers from submitting grant applications, she said.



Three current and two former researchers said the turmoil, staff losses and cost-cutting at the institute made it hard to do quality science. “It’s so sad. Seeing the good these scientists want to do and can do, but at the top there’s this group that is so focused on money, nothing else really matters,” said a former staff member. “And that’s the most disappointing thing. There was this obsession with monetising anything they could – the science got lost, it really got lost.” ‘Nickel-and-diming everything’ Yesterday, this masthead’s investigation into the Florey revealed it had been running multimillion-dollar deficits since 2022, while commercial revenues – crucial to the Florey business model – have nearly halved since 2022. “We need to continue to look at all measures that can help The Florey’s ongoing financial sustainability,” a confidential presentation from February 2025 reads.



In an effort to cut costs, “they are nickel-and-diming everything”, said a current researcher. “Every penny gets fought over.” In early 2024, Florey scientists were told they would be asked to pay “bench fees”: thousands of dollars per researcher for using the Florey’s laboratory benches to do science. Staff have been limited from accessing machines and ordering chemicals essential to basic experiments, two current researchers said. ‘They took their phones and laptops. They cut their access to the building. They asked someone to export all their WhatsApp chats.’ Researcher “They have brought in lots of different costs. They are charging extra things, and making it almost impossible to do research,” said a current Florey scientist, speaking anonymously due to fear of retribution. “Can you tell me any organisation in research that’s able to work on a cost-recovery basis? That’s not how it works.” Following complaints from staff, leadership did not end up imposing the new “bench fees”; a spokeswoman said it did not operate a full cost-recovery model.

World.title: ‘At the crossroads’: Offenders are getting younger and younger – and the crimes are more violent
World.content:
One of the boys who lunged at the owner of a nail salon with a knife.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Lotus Nail Studio in Tregear in Sydney’s west was winding down just after 6pm one Saturday late last month when the three hooded figures walked in, demanding cash and brandishing a hammer. Closed-circuit television shows one of the figures lunging with the hammer at the salon’s sole worker, a terrified 55-year-old woman who asked not to be named. The most disturbing aspect of the alleged crime was that the would-be attackers were aged just 11 and 12. Loading Across the city in Narellan Vale earlier that month, a group of teens and pre-teens allegedly swarmed a bottle shop, fighting staff and stealing cases of drinks. Five boys, aged between 12 and 15, were charged. “I couldn’t believe that was happening here, and they are so young,” said Santiago Wu, whose mother owns the store. The two incidents are tiny pieces in a mosaic of youth crime that police and experts say is seeing younger and younger children sucked from the fringes of the criminal world into violent criminal acts.



Youth crime rates across the state are mostly either stable or trending down – with the exception of murder and some forms of assault. Widespread use of encrypted phone apps and social media has allowed children to transition from misdemeanours into more serious violent criminal activity very swiftly, in some cases within weeks, experts say. The Australian Federal Police warned a federal parliamentary committee last month that “Australia is at the crossroads of a tsunami of youth crime” as online platforms and tools become more secret, sophisticated and popular. “It has certainly lowered the barrier to entry into organised crime,” says Detective acting Superintendent Jason Smith, acting head of Taskforce Falcon, the NSW Police squad charged with combating gang warfare and organised crime. Of the 530 people arrested by Taskforce Falcon so far this year, almost 50 have been children, the youngest being 14. Most are being paid peanuts. “Call it market forces or whatever you like, but the saturation of the market with young people willing to take on these roles has resulted in a drop in the amount of money being paid,” Smith says.



“We’ve got young people essentially throwing their life away for $500. “The problem is that there is a never-ending supply of young people who are willing to become involved. These people are being exploited by organised crime figures living overseas because they’re cheap, and they’re expendable.” Data collected by the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) shows fewer young people are becoming entangled in the justice system than in recent decades. “Young people today are much less likely to commit crimes,” Jackie Fitzgerald, executive director of BOCSAR, says. It’s not accurate to speak in terms of a youth crime wave, despite the involvement of children in high-profile gangland hits, she says. The latest figures, which cover up to June this year, paint a nuanced picture of youth crime across the state.



Central and inner south Sydney have the state’s highest youth crime rate, while the eastern suburbs have a higher youth crime rate per person than areas such as south-west Sydney and Blacktown. This is because the city and the east are often entertainment or social destinations for young people and accessible by public transport, and the influx of young people – a tiny proportion of whom commit crimes – skews the numbers, BOCSAR says. “The trend is steady, and if there is a tsunami of youth crime it hasn’t shown up in the numbers yet,” Alex Simpson, an associate professor of criminology at Macquarie University, says. Fitzgerald says average youth crime rates in western and northern NSW are higher than almost all parts of Sydney. “Sydney gets a lot of focus, but there are communities outside Sydney that are dealing with levels of victimisation and offending [that] are much higher,” she says. “Many people in these communities have safety concerns that people in Sydney cannot relate to.”



The apparent uptick in the number of violent crimes, including murder and assault, which appeared to begin just before the COVID-19 pandemic, follows a decade of relatively few violent crimes being committed by young people. “Over the last five years we’ve seen roughly 10 young people charged with murder, and that’s higher than we were seeing a decade ago,” Fitzgerald says. “But if we expand our view, we can see that 20 years ago, there were many more kids being charged with murder.” The numbers of murders for which children are charged are small, usually fewer than a dozen a year, and therefore are barely visible in the overall crime statistics. Police arrest a teenage boy in Armidale. Youth crime rates in western and northern NSW are higher than in almost all parts of Sydney. Photo: Louise Kennerley But the recent spike is concerning criminologists who are unsure whether the spate of violent crimes by children is an anomaly before a return to lower levels of violence, or something new. “It is a post-COVID phenomena,” Associate Professor Garner Clancey, a criminologist at the University of Sydney, says. “On the back of the pandemic we’ve got a whole new landscape that’s been affected by the ‘manosphere’, kids spending more time online, kids being de-schooled, the rise of the ‘crimfluencers’. Their exposure to anti-government commentary, pornography, deep fakes is much higher. Our prevention strategies need to be recalibrated.

World.title: Hamish Blake is useless. And he’d like you to hire him for your next job
World.content:
Just a man and his truck: Hamish Blake goes all tradie in his new show, Unskilled Adult.

Having made a fortune from being a regular guy, Hamish Blake has decided it’s time to get some real skills. You have been warned.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Hamish Blake is a bit useless. To be clear, that’s not my view, it’s his own. “I’m well into my forties and after essentially just talking for a living, I’ve got to this point in my life and realised I don’t really have any other skills,” he says in the intro to his new series, Unskilled Adult. “I look around everywhere and see people who can do actual useful stuff, and I guess I’m a bit jealous. So I wondered, could that be me.” The reality series is essentially Blake’s effort to learn by doing. He sets up a business – UA (for unskilled adult) Enterprises – ropes in a couple of similarly useless mates, typically from the world of comedy, and sets about completing actual tasks for actual people for actual money. If they think he’s done a good job, they pay him in full. If not, they pay him what they think it’s worth. Related Article Australian TV Think you’ve got what it takes to be cast on reality TV? So did I At the end of it all, they get the job done, and he gets to be, well, a little less useless. Well, that’s the theory anyway. Let’s start with the basics, Hamish. Do you really think you’re an unskilled adult? “I think it is a fair description of me, and people who feel like me, usually from the entertainment industry,” he says. “If you don’t get taught those skills [building, sewing, cooking] as a kid or in your teenage years, I guess you can just grow up without them. So this was my attempt to force myself to learn things.” Masters’ apprentices: Becky Lucas and Hamish Blake attempt to learn carpentry, and manage to keep all fingers intact. Stan



Given enough time and resources, most people could probably learn to do most of the things Blake and co set about undertaking in the series – in the first four episodes, that includes basic carpentry, welding, panel beating and catering. But UA Enterprises appears to have a predisposition for the tight turnaround – jobs typically land on a Wednesday and need to be finished by close of business on Friday – though the budget for tools, gear and lunch is seemingly unlimited. Making the task that little bit harder is that Blake and his guest workers tend to spend most of the first day gasbagging, eating and shopping; day two is typically long, and day three is where the poop really hits the oscillating wind-blowing machine. “It does a strange thing to your head when you know you have to do it, you know it’s on you,” he says, attempting to explain the procrastination. “When you don’t know how to do something, it’s just human nature that your first port of call is to do a lot of things that aren’t the thing, to make you feel like you’re getting somewhere. So a lot of planning, a lot of wild ideas – you’re on with really funny people, so everyone’s having lots of ideas – but then it does slowly dawn on you that the people who have to do all these ideas are still us.” The customers know what they’re signing up for, of course – on the off-chance they don’t recognise Blake or any of his guests (including long-time collaborator and mate Andy Lee, Flight of the Conchords’ Bret McKenzie, Spelling Bee host Guy Montgomery, comedian Becky Lucas and the ubiquitous Sophie Monk), the camera crew is a dead giveaway. But Blake insists that the job at hand is real, there’s no safety blanket – stuff up that car repair and there isn’t a new car waiting for you – and the exchange of cash is genuinely based on how they assess the work. “I’ve talked to good effect, but I haven’t really done anything you would hang your hat on as a skill.” “It was important for us to keep it real because it is central to the idea of biting off more than you can chew, and genuinely having to figure your way out of it, and not being allowed to give up. And I think if you combine those elements that creates a great adventure.”



Blake describes himself as someone who talks for a living. In reality, he’s parlayed being a regular bloke – good-looking, affable, a bit of a doofus, always willing to poke fun at himself – into a very significant media career (radio, podcasts, TV, the occasional movie role) and a considerable fortune. “I’ve talked to good effect,” he concedes. “But I haven’t really done anything that you would hang your hat on as a skill.” Has doing this show changed that at all – have you actually acquired any real skills? “Shamefully not as much as I was hoping,” he says. He tells me that before they set out on this adventure, he and his co-creator and director Tim Bartley wondered if there was any risk that he might become too capable, and thus kill the gag. “I was like, ‘I guess we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it’,” Blake says. “And we have not come to that bridge.” He did, however, become passably good at “some wood stuff”, he boasts. I think they call it carpentry, I note.



“Yeah. I think if I had to go and be an apprentice in any field, I’d be a chippy. If they’d take [me].” So since doing this, have you done anything in your own actual life, like maybe put up a shelf at home? “I did something the other day, and the family was cheering,” he says. “My kids were like, ‘He’s done it! He’s done it! He’s not unskilled’.” For a moment, he struggles to recall what it was. And then it comes to him. “We live a couple of blocks from the beach in Sydney, and I’d left a jacket in the garage and the zip had rusted. I put WD40 on it, and I used pliers. ‘Look at that everyone, come gather round. Dad’s going to do something’.” Blake with long-time colleague and mate Andy Lee. Rebecca Hallas And that’s something you wouldn’t have been able to do before this show? “How would I know what to do?”



As much as he talks up his incompetence, in the episodes I’ve seen Blake and co actually manage to do a passable job of mastering the basics. I mean, you might not hire them to build your next house, but you might entrust them with a planter box. Given the enormous following he has with tradies, is there a risk that he might inadvertently be giving the impression that being a carpenter, a bricklayer, a chef, a welder is a breeze, that two days is all anyone needs to master it? To put it bluntly, might some people think their favourite multimillionaire is being just a bit disrespectful? The one person he didn’t rope in as a guest was his wife, Zoe Foster Blake. Instagram “Look, I did actually kind of wonder the same thing,” he says. “This is certainly not us going, ‘Wow, these trades are easy. Being a chef is easy. Being a carpenter is easy. Anyone can do it.’ It’s certainly not that. I know it takes years and years to acquire mastery of these skills. But what could you get done in a few days? Can you just learn anything? Related Article Review What to stream this week: Connie Britton’s weird comedy-thriller, plus five more picks “I suppose it’s just learning the bare, bare, bare basics. There’s no risk of any bricklayers looking at it and going, ‘Well, I can’t fault them. They’re the best bricklayers I’ve ever seen.’ It’s more that thrill – and I really enjoy this in life – of being a beginner. I think anyone who has any level of proficiency in any of these things would look at [our efforts] and go, ‘That’s about what I thought people with one day of experience would be able to achieve’.” Blake has shown some of the show to an electrician mate, whose response gave him confidence that no one is going to mistakenly conclude he is passing himself off as the real deal.

World.title: The wildcard NRL option that has suddenly emerged for Nathan Cleary
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion The wildcard NRL option that has suddenly emerged for Nathan Cleary Danny Weidler Sport columnist November 1, 2026 — 5:30am

November 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nathan Cleary is a free agent as of today – and no matter how remote the chance of him leaving Penrith, the Roosters have emerged as a wildcard to have a serious crack at landing the game’s No.1 target. A week ago, the Tricolours had barely given Cleary a second thought. But the shock split with their premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has opened the door. Nathan Cleary and Sam Walker are both free agents. Artwork: Stephen Kiprillis Cleary is expected to stay at Penrith, where he has played his entire career to date. But the Roosters will at least give him something to consider beyond the Panthers and the Chiefs. PNG will have to come up with an offer with far more to it than simply relying on the lure of $1.7 million a year tax-free. In another twist, there is a meeting scheduled for next week between Roosters supremo Nick Politis and Bulldogs general manager Phil Gould – with an obvious topic of discussion.



The Bulldogs are being pushed as a potential destination for Walker, who unexpectedly came onto the market after failing to reach an agreement over a contract extension at the Roosters. The Dogs are not biting as they have minimal cap room. It’s an interesting fit, as the Bulldogs’ best player this season was their own No.7, Lachlan Galvin. Loading But it’s possible to see Walker playing halfback alongside Galvin at five-eighth. They are both instinctual players and the Dogs would need to change the way they play to accommodate Walker. It would also need the Roosters to fund some of his contract. Ironically, Galvin was brought into Origin camp this year to replicate the off-the-cuff style of Maroons pair Cameron Munster and Walker in opposed sessions.



We’ve been told the most logical fit for Walker – the Cowboys, as part of a swap with Tom Dearden – is too complicated. Maybe that’s because Dearden’s partner, Millie, will be moving to Townsville soon after the pair had their first baby recently. Dearden is tipped to honour the next year of his deal and then look at joining a Sydney club in 2028, despite being contracted at the Cowboys until the end of 2029. A club swap between Queensland Origin teammates Tom Dearden and Sam Walker appears highly unlikely. Getty As for Cleary, he is open to offers. As far as we can establish, he has not instructed his manager to tell the Roosters or Chiefs he is not interested. We know PNG are still keen because their general manager, Michael Chammas, has told the Roosters he has not been making a sneaky play for Walker.



Cleary has said he is not motivated by money. Chammas will need to be creative to get his man. Conservatively, with third-party payments, Cleary stands to clear about $2.5 million a year if he signs with the Chiefs. The Panthers are operating on a budget of about $1.7 million on the cap to retain him. Why Roosters and Walker fell out of love The Roosters’ break-up with Walker finished with a message of support from Nick Politis to the halfback. Politis is ruthless, but big-hearted when it comes to his players. However, there has long been an uneasy relationship between the Walker camp and the club he loves.



In a phone call with Politis, Walker said he was grateful for everything he has had at the Roosters. Politis told Walker he would be there to help him in the future. Today, he is trying to help him out the door. How did we get here? There were problems early. At the start of the year, some of Walker’s key advisers were ringing around and asking if the Roosters were interested in Nathan Cleary. Roosters chairman Nick Politis is one of the game’s most influential figures. NRL They were jumping at shadows at the time, and it was an indication that there was a lack of trust between Walker’s team and the Roosters. The Roosters have always been wary of Sam’s dad, Ben Walker. And they have preferred dealing with Steve Gillis, the back-up agent for Walker behind Clinton Schifcofske, his No.1 man. It was Gillis who delivered the news to Politis that Walker wanted extra money.



Complicating the issue was that the Roosters were one of the clubs sounded out earlier in the year by representatives of Tom Dearden, who wanted to see if they could accommodate their client if he moved to Sydney to be with his partner. Then there was the fact that veteran halfback Daly Cherry-Evans had been brought in for 2026 to either help or actually run the side. Sam Walker is on his way out of the Roosters. Jessica Hromas All of this can impact a player’s ego. And those who love Walker took note. Walker wanted to play on the right side of the field, traditionally the domain of the halfback. There are some who thought he was actually better suited to the five-eighth role. All of this has been swirling around in the background.



Throw in the club’s uneasy relationship with Ben Walker, and maybe then you can see why the relationship started to break down and where the demand for more dollars came from. The Roosters say they respected Walker. They made their biggest offer, $4.2 million over three years. That is the ultimate show of respect. The Roosters put years of development into Walker. They stood by him through injury and felt they deserved loyalty and perhaps a bit less of the financial demands. They didn’t like it when, a few weeks back, Walker addressed key members of the recruitment team and told them he wanted to put talks on hold. He didn’t even entertain the idea of a negotiation at that time. Remember, the Roosters also backed Walker when the coaching of Cooper Cronk didn’t seem to gel with the young seven. Those spot fires can be put out, but they can reignite when big decisions need to be made.



Everything went up in flames last week. It was not entirely unexpected, but few predicted it. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Could Sam Walker end up at the Rabbitohs? Can the Raiders still keep Hudson Young? Politis had a sense it would erupt. He was reminding people what happened with Latrell Mitchell in 2019 when a contract stand-off led to him departing for South Sydney. Politis was desperately trying to avoid a repeat. Politis is the most loyal individual you can meet in football. But cross him, and you will not be forgiven easily. The club might be flashy on the outside, but it’s built on Politis’ old-school ethos. At the core of Trent Robinson’s coaching is a line he picked up from famous American basketball coach Pat Riley. It surrounds the leadership concept of the “Disease of Me”, which he raised in his book, The Winner Within: A Life Plan for Team Players.



The term describes how players become overly focused on personal glory. Riley famously summarised the danger with the maxim, “The Disease of Me always results in the Defeat of Us.” It’s what Robinson drums into his players. The coach didn’t flinch when Walker made his decision. He is excited by the challenge ahead. Robinson keeps fresh through the cycle of talent and the challenge of getting the best out of the next crop. He won’t cop any player who doesn’t subscribe to the idea of team first. We are not saying Walker is selfish. We are just offering an insight into Robinson’s philosophy. Sam’s his own man A final word on Sam Walker.



It’s hard not to have a soft spot for him. The Roosters players still care about him, and he is a decent person. In camp with Australia’s World Cup squad in Townsville, he was seen having a deep chat with James Tedesco on the balcony of the Roosters captain’s hotel room. Nine reporter Adam Jackson said he saw them chatting for 30 minutes at the peak of the dramas last week. Kangaroos management also put players and staff around Walker, but he seemed to be fine. Walker lives down the road from me and I often bump into him at local cafés. He always has time for people. As flamboyant as he is as a footballer, he is a quiet person.



He comes across as a classic introverted extrovert. He is close to his family, loves the races and appears to love his football. He is very much his own person. He would have discussed his final contract call with his long-term partner Bella, who is the sister of retired NRL star Corey Allan. Sam Walker savoured the Roosters premiership win with Angus Crichton in the dressing rooms. Getty Images Walker goes out of his way to be friendly and welcoming. I found him fascinating after the grand final. He was the least animated and emotional player in the Roosters side. He was keen to get off the ground and into the dressing room to be with his people. He gave off the impression he had just won a regular NRL round 16 game against the Titans rather than a premiership.



Maybe he knew something we didn’t. Chiefs inspector Young Hudson Young is likely to be in Port Moresby this week to decide whether to make PNG his new home – and he can thank Sam Walker for taking the media heat off him after the Raiders withdrew their four-year $4.4 million offer. Raiders backrower Hudson Young suffered a season-ending injury in Canberra’s round 20 win over South Sydney. NRL Imagery There is plenty to the Young situation. At the core of it is the Achilles injury that ended his 2026 season. That prevented him from visiting PNG at a time when Canberra had given him permission to go.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 ‘We stopped Jarryd Hayne from getting stabbed in jail’: Fainu reveals plot against former Eels star Had he toured the Chiefs’ facilities then, he could have given the Raiders an answer. He is happy with the $900,000 per year deal offered by the Chiefs and won’t haggle. But he needs to see Port Moresby first-hand. In the background, Young has gone through a relationship breakdown, and has also had itchy feet when it comes to living in Canberra. A change of scenery has been on his mind. There have been suggestions that he is not happy with the make-up of the Raiders pack.



The truth is that, as a senior player, he is always talking to coach Ricky Stuart about the roster. Young has nothing but love for the Raiders, but he may need a new environment to keep him focused and engaged in the final years of his playing career. What is certain is that he will want to have his best year in the NRL when he returns from injury next season. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Remembering the dead, in all their glory and their failings
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion Remembering the dead, in all their glory and their failings

Jane E Sullivan November 1, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the Western Christian calendar tomorrow – 2 November – is All Souls’ Day. It is the day the church remembers the souls of the faithful departed. All Souls’ Day follows All Saints’ Day, and before it the preparatory All Hallows’ Eve on 31 October. It concludes a time of commemoration and thanksgiving. Saint Augustine of Hippo lived a life of sin before his conversion, famously asking to be delivered from temptation – but just not yet. “Saints” in early Christian tradition was a general and inclusive term for all members of the faith community. Over time customary usage came to refer to a rarefied group of exceptional individuals, officially recognised by the church. In the name of Christ, for the sake of the faith these believers risked and often lost limb or life, completed miraculous feats or led exemplary lives. Even though many saints had significant character flaws and histories of questionable behaviours, such as Saint Paul and Saint Augustine, most of us won’t make it into this venerated company. We are, however, destined to become souls. And there’s something democratic about the church making space to honour all her dead.



Whether they were churched or unchurched, sincerely remembering our dead loved ones can be complicated. Not only because it prompts thoughts of our mortality but because true remembrance means recognising the whole person. After all, the dead are human. And humans are complex. People come with sparkling brilliance as well as glaring blemishes. Death doesn’t automatically transform someone into a saint. Death doesn’t erase character faults or bad actions. But critiquing our dead loved ones feels disloyal, unfair and uncomfortable. Indeed, there are strong social conventions not to speak ill of the dead. They have no right of reply. A genuine remembrance, however, involves integrating a person’s contradictions into our memory. It means putting their foibles and failures, their struggles and vulnerabilities, alongside their virtues, their triumphs, and what made them lovable. After all in life we accommodated the whole person into our hearts. It’s striking that often for mourners the most beneficial eulogies portray the real person. As we remember our dead, inevitably our relationship with them comes into focus. Our own merits and shortcomings are seen, revealed in the context and history of the relationship. That’s fair enough, honest recollection cuts both ways. Our minds may race back to the moments when our character flaws got in the way, or when we failed them in some big or little matter. Past hurts can outlive their perpetrator. Relationship tensions may remain unresolved, and words left unspoken. Regret, shame and plain old sadness may form parts of our memory. Living with such feelings is difficult. Reality is like that. Hopefully, the unsettling parts in our relationships with the dead are held together with feelings of happiness, gratitude, and contentment.



As we commemorate All Souls’ Day, let’s truly remember our loved ones. Who knows, perhaps on a future All Souls’ Day, someone will remember us, the exquisitely human us. Jane E Sullivan lives and worships in Melbourne.

World.content:
