In the early European summer, on the glittering peninsula of Cap d’Antibes, I found myself reclining on a sun lounger next to two 40-year-old women from Melbourne. One was in a long-term relationship, the other was newly single and, together, they were taking a two-week jaunt along the French Riviera before a final stop in Paris for shopping, pain au chocolat and dinner at Hotel Costes. “I’d rather travel with a girlfriend than my partner; we’re so much more aligned,” said the former, her eyes glimmering behind huge Dior sunglasses. Women holidaying with likeminded women or alone often head to destinations that are “golf course free”. Getty Images “Would I spend my day doing this with a man?” asked the other, gesturing towards her goblet of spritz, Sally Hepworth novel and the sweep of lapis-blue sea. Unknowingly, the pair were embarking on a Hot Divorcee Summer, the rising cultural trend centred on women’s radical freedom and the pleasures of putting oneself first. After a stay at Hotel Belles Rives, the legendary art deco haunt in Juan-les-Pins, they were headed for the beach clubs of St Tropez, the perfumeries of Grasse and “nowhere with a golf course”.



Figurative rather than literal, Hot Divorcee Summer is less about marital status than a mood and an energy: untethered, unbothered and unencumbered by a man’s needs or opinions (or anyone’s needs and opinions for that matter, perhaps for the first time in a woman’s life). 



She’s equally at liberty, though, to slip to the hotel spa for a skin-tightening treatment. Self-indulgence is a prerequisite for the Hot Divorcee, but the pleasures are entirely self-prescribed: the best hotel suite, a faintly ridiculous wellness ritual, a pottery class that would have been vetoed by every previous travel companion. L’Aventure hotel Paris has an on-site nightclub so you can make a night of it. “This is about women seizing the moment and not waiting for someone else to be available to experience the places they want to go,” says Jules Perowne, founder and chief executive of global luxury travel communications consultancy Perowne International. Those places span continents, cultures and price points, but all offer a taste of the good life in one form or another. Take the island of Sardinia, which has something of a split personality. Costa Smeralda in the north-east has been an exclusive summer playground since the 1960s, one where megayachts jostle for space in the marinas and old money meets Hollywood meets Silicon Valley over long lunches and DJ sets. Yet beyond that enclave it’s rugged and rural, a succession of sugar-white beaches where Italian families practise the art of dolce far niente.



For the Hot Divorcee, this makes for an appealing combination: a boat trip through secluded coves on waters so vivid they render filters redundant; languid hours under a beach umbrella; bowls of homemade pasta and scoops of dripping gelato; an evening dressed up for dinner in Porto Cervo; a stay somewhere special, like Cala di Volpe, the rustically lavish icon that once starred in a Bond film (The Spy Who Loved Me), or the less flashy Le Dune Piscinas eco resort. In 2027, Rocco Forte Costa Smeralda and Mandarin Oriental will both open on the north-east coast, too. Or she might venture inland, where Sardinia’s famously long-lived nonnas offer ageing advice to rival any wellness or longevity retreat. An important caveat: Hot Divorcee Summer is not a self-improvement exercise. Eating, praying and loving are all welcome, but they have to happen organically, and there’s no obligation to return home transformed. Nor is it a traditional girls’ trip with shared itineraries, group decisions and expectations of collective revelry. If partying is on the agenda, it leans much more sophisticated than a rhinestone-crusted hen’s do or big, boisterous birthday. No organised fun, no matching outfits, no tiaras, no bottles announced with sparklers. To that end, L’Aventure and Le Bus Palladium, two recently opened five-star boutique hotels in Paris, boast louche underground nightclubs and live music venues – so you can make a night of it or not, without having to organise a ride home.



The new Nomade Temple in Madrid was built around experiences, too, with a speakeasy and club inspired by the city’s 1980s cultural awakening, along with a daily roster of workshops and events designed to bring people together: psychedelic breathwork sessions, social saunas, run clubs, sketch classes, vermouth and flamenco afternoons. The restaurant at Hotel Belle Rives in Juan-les-Pins, south-easterm France, offers waterfront dining. For Perowne, the Hot Divorcee Summer calls for destinations where being alone feels unremarkable. “The hotels getting it right understand that a woman travelling solo does not want to be tucked into a corner table with a book,” she explains. “At Storfjord Hotel in Norway, the new Boathouse restaurant has no tables for one. Everyone sits at a single long table while the chef cooks over open flames, and dinner becomes a supper party. At Wildland’s Killiehuntly Farmhouse in Scotland there’s no room service and no menu. Guests eat together, whatever the cook has made from the estate that day. You arrive a stranger and leave having had the best conversation of your year.” Shifts in the cultural landscape make this particular brand of women’s travel especially appealing. In Australia, 49,158 divorces were granted in 2025, a 4 per cent increase from 2024, and the average female divorcee is 44, with decades of adventures still ahead of her. Throw in the Great Wealth Transfer, in which it’s expected up to $5.4 trillion will pass between Australian generations over the next two decades – much of it into the pockets and wallets of Gen X and Millennials – and Hot Divorcee Summer begins to look like more than a buzzy catchphrase.



Meanwhile, women are questioning the assumption that romantic relationships should be the organising principle of their lives; “decentring men” has become a rallying cry. In the US, Pew Research Centre found that just 35 per cent of single women were actively looking for dates or a relationship. Instead, their next great romance may be with a place. In April 2026, Google reported that search interest in “solo travel” had hit an all-time high, and “women solo travel” was at a 15-year peak. In a recent survey by the company Solo Female Travelers, 85 per cent of respondents cited freedom and flexibility as a reason for travelling alone, while 76 per cent wanted time to relax, indulge and prioritise themselves. Cala di Volpe on the island of Sardinia, Italy, once starred in a Bond film and is the perfect venue for an exclusive summer stay. “Ever since MONA opened in Hobart, I’d always wanted to go with a partner,” says Megan McTavish, a social strategist from the Gold Coast. “I never went with my ex-husband, but still hoped I’d find someone to go with while dating. Then one day I woke up and thought, ‘What am I waiting around for?’ I looked at the money I’d saved and asked myself what I’d do if I was with a man. I would have booked a fancy hotel and a bougie, romantic meal. So I decided to do it myself, after 15 years of waiting.” After a few hours browsing the gallery at her own pace, McTavish, 41, took herself to lunch at avant-garde fine-diner Faro. “It was invigorating,” she says. “I got the degustation and focused on every morsel, with no awkward conversation with whoever would have been sitting opposite me.”



Since then, McTavish has taken herself to Melbourne solo for martinis and chocolate mousse at Maison Batard, followed by a facial at Mecca and a luxurious sleep in a king bed at 1Hotel, as well as to Byron Bay. “These trips make life feel like it’s worth living,” says McTavish, noting that the idea of a holiday romance or catching the male gaze doesn’t register for her. “I’m celibate.” One day, she hopes to visit Malta and the Maldives – “I really want to go and take those romantic couples photos by myself” – but as a single mother of one, she’s content for now with an unapologetic mini-break. “There’s a follow-on effect from doing this, even if it’s just a two-day trip that you’ve saved and budgeted for,” says McTavish. “A lot of women have subconsciously learnt to accept crumbs in our lives, so this is about setting the bar high for ourselves. On the surface it might look like a lot of fancy lunches and beauty treatments, but it’s also about treating yourself so well that you’ll never accept the bare minimum or mistreatment from anyone else.” While the Hot Divorcee Summer was enjoying its debut season, another social trend was gathering momentum: the Year of the Hobby, a renewed enthusiasm for pursuits that have little to do with work or productivity.



The two cultural currents intersect in a Venn diagram, an overlap populated by retreats for learning, making and doing, set against beautiful, far-flung backdrops. Think textile-making in Guatemala, the dyeing technique of shibori in Japan and basket-weaving in Spain’s Mallorca, all led by local artisans via Thread Caravan. Or the Marnie Rays women’s surf retreat in Ericeira, Portugal, or sensory immersion meets contemporary arts with Bonfire in Iceland. The speakeasy-style Rose Bar at Delano Miami Beach. Perhaps the most resonant subcategory here is the reading retreat, because what says “I’m putting myself first” like sun-lounging in silence with a group of like-minded women, tearing through pages of Nancy Mitford, Elizabeth Strout or whichever author sets your imagination alight? Megan Christopher founded Ladies Who Lit, a travelling book club, three years ago and now hosts up to 75 retreats in villas, castles, ranches and even yachts across 15 countries every year. Each retreat revolves around a loose schedule of reading, conversation and leisurely meals, with optional activities and plenty of quiet time – although a recent retreat in Seville, Spain, culminated in a raucous night of karaoke. “Obviously, the women who come on our retreats are readers, but I think what they’re actually drawn to is the time and space we give them to just be them,” says Christopher. “They’re not somebody’s wife; they’re not somebody’s mum. They don’t need to think about what they’re having for dinner, or if the kids’ uniforms have been washed. Once we remove all those elements, they get a chance to not only relax but to be themselves, potentially for the first time ever as an adult.”



For 2027, the line-up includes the first Australian retreat in the Byron Bay hinterland – set in the Californian-cool country estate Sun Ranch – and a cowboy-themed one in Vancouver, Canada. Christopher says newly divorced or separated women comprise a significant subset of the Ladies Who Lit community. “There’s probably at least one guest on every trip who’s in that situation,” she adds. Related Article Tours Women-only travel boom continues with launch of new trips Of course, there’s an inherent contradiction in the Hot Divorcee label. Taken literally, it puts a gloss on something that, for most women, is anything but glamorous. Divorce can take an enormous emotional and financial toll, and the freedom to spend lavishly on a holiday is hardly universal. You needn’t be rich to partake, countered comedian Tatty Macleod when breaking down the trend. “Ideally, it’s champagne in the Med, but if it’s cava in a paddling pool that will also do, babe.”



What a Hot Divorcee Summer does offer, regardless of age, relationship status or circumstance, is an invitation not to take oneself too seriously, a healthy disregard for convention, a zest for growing older and a reframing of what endings can mean. And it can restore a sense of possibility. Never mind the giant hat, that’s the greatest souvenir of all. NEW STAYS THAT CAPTURE THE DIVORCEE SUMMER SPIRIT DELANO, MIAMI BEACH, US

Once the heart of South Beach’s 1990s social scene, the legendary Delano has emerged from a six-year renovation with its glamour intact but its priorities slightly rearranged. Wellness has joined the party, without quite replacing it. From $799 a night. See delanohotels.com/miami-beach

CASA BONAVITA, ATTARD, MALTA

The Mediterranean island’s most stylish new stay features unabashedly pretty interiors (the Folly suite is the stuff of slumber party dreams) and the warmth of a family home. It’s the kind of place where company might be found without being sought. From $895 a night. See casabonavita.com

CASA MARGARITA GUEST HOUSE, MEXICO CITY, MEXICO

Originally the home of Mexican writer Margarita Quijano – who hosted salons for leading thinkers, particularly women – this restored 1902 mansion feels fitting for the independently minded. Stay for the book clubs and poetry gatherings, and the lively cafes, restaurants and galleries on the doorstep. From $500 a night. See casamargaritamexico.com





THE WHALE, NAROOMA, NSW

This new coastal motel by Merivale has all the makings of a free-spirited escape when an overseas jaunt isn’t on the cards: boho design, a retro magnesium pool, bespoke vinyl selection and a Queen Chow restaurant on site. From $440 a night. See merivale.com

The Whale is a new coastal hotel by Merivale in the NSW South Coast town of Narooma. THE PACKING LIST Related Article Travel tips Lonely Planet’s 20 expert tips for solo women travellers A vintage silk scarf

Tied around the neck or knotted under the chin for boat rides.

A copy of Strangers by Belle Burden

The year’s most talked-about divorce memoir.

An exceptionally good black one-piece swimsuit

The kind that will last for the next 10 summers. See Eres or Canvs Bottega.

A wide-brimmed sunhat

Inconvenient on aeroplanes, excellent everywhere else.

Venetian slippers

For making an otherwise ordinary outfit look like something worn by an eccentric Italian aristocrat. See Piedaterre or Le Monde Beryl.

A repurposed silver cigarette case

Inside: a hotel matchbook and the telephone number of an admirer, scrawled on a receipt.

A Mary Poppins bag

To house all of the above. It could be a raffia basket picked up at a local market, a canvas tote from Hotel Il Pellicano or a battered Goyard Saint Louis GM.

World.title: I’m 64 with just $93,000 in super. Should I add to it before retiring?
World.content:
November 1, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’m 64, a self-employed freelance creative writer, own my home, and have $93,000 in super, $110,000 in my access account and $170,000 in savings. I intend to keep working, as I love my work, but I don’t expect any massive income from that – and it will also drop off as I age. It’s been pretty difficult to get to this point, and it’s taken many sacrifices, but owning my own home is fantastic. I will reach pension age in August 2029. To maximise my pension and associated benefits, should I make the maximum $32,500 super contribution, plus the $23,000 of available catch-up contribution, or would I be better keeping that money in the bank? Adding more into your super can leave you better off in retirement, but it depends on your level of income. Simon Letch Firstly, well done on what you’ve achieved. Building this level of financial security on the variable income that often comes with freelance creative work is impressive. The next point to note is that money inside or outside of super doesn’t make a great deal of difference to your age pension entitlement. Either way this wealth will be included in the asset and income test, and the calculation methodology is usually identical.



The advisability of making tax-deductible super contributions, including the catch-up contributions, depends on your level of taxable income. Money that you send to super as a concessional contribution is taxed at 15 per cent when it arrives in the fund. For you to get a benefit therefore, your personal tax rate must be greater than this. There is no tax payable on your first $18,200, and then 17 per cent is payable from their up to $45,000 (inclusive of Medicare levy). Meaningful gains through tax-deductible super contributions therefore don’t accrue until your income is above $45,000. This does not mean you shouldn’t contribute to super. It is likely that the returns in super will be better than bank interest. But it may be that making after-tax contributions (non-concessional in super jargon), produces a better result for you. And the limits on these types of contributions are much more generous. My wife and I are both retired with account-based pensions and are contemplating moving from our large, high maintenance home into a more suitable abode. This will either require purchasing land and building anew or purchasing an existing dwelling and undertaking major renovations. Regardless, our preferred approach is to purchase and build/renovate first, then sell and move in when ready. Given the only funds to which we have access are in our account-based pensions, is there a cost-effective way of funding this swap without using an expensive bridging loan or having the majority of proceeds of the sale locked out of super?



Depending on the amounts involved, potentially you could withdraw monies out of super, and then replenish using the downsizer provisions. Downsizer contributions require that the home you are selling has been yours for at least 10 years. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Does bequeathing my shares in my will incur capital gains tax? Noel Whittaker Money columnist You can contribute $300,000 per person through this mechanism. Importantly, there is no age limit on downsizer contributions, though you can only do this once in your lifetime. If you are under 75 years of age when you sell your current home, you may also be able to get money back into super via non-concessional contributions. Spreading the contributions over a couple of financial years, you could potentially get up to $520,000 each back into super and then create new account-based pensions. Alternatively, it may be that bridging loan costs are just one of the many costs that need to be factored into this transaction.



Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists. World.title: Skipping meals to pay the rent? Your spending habits aren’t to blame
World.content:
MoneySavingMoney psychology Opinion Skipping meals to pay the rent? Your spending habits aren’t to blame Victoria Devine Money columnist November 1, 2026 — 5:01am

November 1, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of the most pervasive and damaging money myths I’ve seen play out time and again over the years is people blaming themselves for financial circumstances, even when they are entirely outside their control. While we might recognise inflation or higher mortgage rates as reasons for our depleted savings or an increase in debt, for example, studies consistently show that even when people know these factors are at play, they ultimately are still likely to blame their own spending habits for the fact that they are struggling to make ends meet. If you are struggling, there’s a good chance you’re also feeling overwhelmed. Dionne Gain But two studies released this week have highlighted how common it has become recently for Australians to be struggling right now, and just how little any one individual financial decision or habit is to blame for the pain being felt. The first was the annual Foodbank Hunger Report, which showed that 3.6 million households (33 per cent) across Australia now suffer what is known as food insecurity. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation, food insecurity is when a person doesn’t have regular access to enough nutrient-rich food to meet the needs of a healthy and balanced diet.



Though the vast majority of us have all felt or experienced financial strain or stagnation lately, the sheer number of people who reported either struggling to afford the food they need, or said they were skipping meals and going without food due to unaffordability, which is recognised as severe food insecurity, is genuinely sobering. According to Foodbank, the highest rates of food insecurity were reported among Indigenous households (57 per cent), while 45 per cent of all households with children also suffered – a number that grew to 60 per cent in single-parent households. Let me be clear: if you are struggling to put food on the table or to keep the roof over your head, just know that you are not alone. Even within what are considered median income households across Australia, 37 per cent reported having experienced food insecurity over the past 12 months. At the same time, 15 per cent of households that experienced food insecurity and reported finding it difficult to secure employment increased from 11 per cent in 2025 to 15 per cent in 2026. The number of reported job losses also rose – from 10 per cent to 13 per cent. Somewhat unsurprisingly, younger people are almost two times more likely to struggle than people aged over 55 (48 per cent compared with 19 per cent).



Following similar generational lines, one of the starkest of divides can be found among people who rent and people who own property. More than half of all renters (51 per cent) reported food insecurity, while it affected just 12 per cent of people who owned their house outright. When you consider the fact that rents have risen nationally by 40.6 per cent over the past five years – compared to 12.2 per cent in the five years prior – it’s little wonder people have so much less left over when their paycheck lands (and why it’s become so much harder to find savings for a house deposit). The second report that stopped me in my tracks this week came from the University of NSW and found that 91 per cent of homelessness and emergency housing services have experienced unprecedented demand for support over the past two years. One comment I haven’t been able to get out of my mind is a frontline worker telling this masthead that demand for support is so high they are handing out tents and directing people to safe camping areas. “Women leaving family violence are being asked, ‘do you have a lock on your car?’ And if you have a lock on your car, you’re considered to be safe,” one worker said.



The idea that things have become so dire that a tent or a car now qualifies as a home, particularly for vulnerable people fleeing violence or unsafe environments, is profoundly staggering and an indication of just how serious and pervasive the cost of living crisis has become. Editor's pick Opinion

AI Young investors love AI stocks. Are they falling into a debt trap? Victoria Devine Money columnist And it’s not only fair to say that numerous things have gone seriously wrong along the way to see us having ended up here, but also to reiterate that factors well beyond any one person’s spending habits or money decisions are at play here. If you are struggling, there’s a good chance you’re also feeling overwhelmed. When that happens, one of the best things you can possibly do is speak to someone and try to feel less alone, but also seek some guidance about how to move forward. For some people, a chat to a trusted friend or family member can be enough to help ease some of that mental burden. But another great place to start can be the National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007). This is a not-for-profit organisation that offers free financial counselling advice (without selling anything or making money from you) and can help you assess where you’re at, lay out options that may be available to you and your rights, and connect you with other services and community support.



Yet as I said earlier, time and again, I see people who are struggling in these kinds of situations feel shame or guilt – as though if they’d simply been better with their money or made one or two different decisions in the past, they might not be here. So let me be clear: if you are struggling to put food on the table or to keep the roof over your head, just know that you are not alone. As the research findings spell out in neon lights, many people are having the same experiences that you are right now – and a lot of them are people you likely wouldn’t expect. And while many things are within our control and there are always new things to learn, not everything is, and it’s important to remember that when you’re just trying to do your best. National Debt Helpline: 1800 007 007 Victoria Devine is an award-winning retired financial adviser, a bestselling author and host of Australia’s No.1 finance podcast, She’s on the Money. She is also founder and director of Zella Money.

World.title: ‘They wanted our WhatsApps’: Staff claim culture of fear at Florey
World.content:
Florey Institute staff claim financial pressures are crimping their ability to do their work.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In December 2024, researchers at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health were called into a meeting with senior leadership. Recollections differ about the tone of the meeting, but the message was clear. Taxpayer-funded research grants are the lifeblood of independent research institutes – and the Florey was not winning nearly enough. “At a time when most researchers were devastated at finding they were unsuccessful after spending months preparing applications,” one said, leadership “got up in front of everyone and berated us for not doing good enough”. “After that meeting, everyone was walking around chatting to colleagues saying ‘can you believe it? I can’t believe that happened’.” Yesterday, an investigation by this masthead revealed the venerable institute – which the Rockefeller Foundation helped establish and was named after penicillin pioneer and Nobel Laureate Howard Florey – had become embroiled in chaos as it faced financial strife and an exodus of top research talent.



Today, the investigation focuses on the scientific fallout from that turmoil – numerous complaints about the culture inside the Florey and the string of court cases in which it is now embroiled. This masthead has spoken to 22 former or current Florey staff – very few willing to be identified publicly for fear of retribution – to build a picture of a once-great institution under extreme financial pressure and facing accusations of building an unhealthy atmosphere for a workforce trying to solve dementia, Alzheimer’s, epilepsy, MND and mental health conditions. “They’ve created this culture: the scientists are the ones to blame for the problem they are in. A pure toxic culture has developed,” said a current researcher, speaking under condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. “They have taken the option to go completely corporate. You can’t do that with a research institute because you’re just going to end up getting rid of most people – and the rest are going to want to leave.” A Florey spokeswoman said falls in grant income “reflect[ed] a tightening national funding environment” and “notably, funding for dementia reduced by 48% over the same time period” according to the National Health and Medical Research Council, website and annual disease funding statistics. They denied anyone had been “berated” about grant success rates, and said the meeting discussed “low national success rates”.



“This was a constructive discussion that identified other grant schemes that our researchers could apply to.” But a confidential Florey presentation from February 2025 lamented “limited grant success in 2024 funding round, below expectations, partly due to inconsistent and inefficient grant support”. “Every funding round was just a constant disappointment,” said a former staff member. The Florey Institute’s Parkville headquarters. Joe Armao In response to poor success rates, the institute proposed implementing an internal vetting system before grants could be submitted. “The result is less grants being submitted in order to artificially inflate the apparent success rate, a metric which has absolutely no impact on researchers,” said a former researcher. A spokeswoman for the Florey said it was “committed to attracting and retaining the brightest minds in medical research, while supporting professional development and opportunities across the medical research sector”. The institute does not prevent researchers from submitting grant applications, she said.



Three current and two former researchers said the turmoil, staff losses and cost-cutting at the institute made it hard to do quality science. “It’s so sad. Seeing the good these scientists want to do and can do, but at the top there’s this group that is so focused on money, nothing else really matters,” said a former staff member. “And that’s the most disappointing thing. There was this obsession with monetising anything they could – the science got lost, it really got lost.” ‘Nickel-and-diming everything’ Yesterday, this masthead’s investigation into the Florey revealed it had been running multimillion-dollar deficits since 2022, while commercial revenues – crucial to the Florey business model – have nearly halved since 2022. “We need to continue to look at all measures that can help The Florey’s ongoing financial sustainability,” a confidential presentation from February 2025 reads.



In an effort to cut costs, “they are nickel-and-diming everything”, said a current researcher. “Every penny gets fought over.” In early 2024, Florey scientists were told they would be asked to pay “bench fees”: thousands of dollars per researcher for using the Florey’s laboratory benches to do science. Staff have been limited from accessing machines and ordering chemicals essential to basic experiments, two current researchers said. ‘They took their phones and laptops. They cut their access to the building. They asked someone to export all their WhatsApp chats.’ Researcher “They have brought in lots of different costs. They are charging extra things, and making it almost impossible to do research,” said a current Florey scientist, speaking anonymously due to fear of retribution. “Can you tell me any organisation in research that’s able to work on a cost-recovery basis? That’s not how it works.” Following complaints from staff, leadership did not end up imposing the new “bench fees”; a spokeswoman said it did not operate a full cost-recovery model.

World.title: ‘At the crossroads’: Offenders are getting younger and younger – and the crimes are more violent
World.content:
One of the boys who lunged at the owner of a nail salon with a knife.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Lotus Nail Studio in Tregear in Sydney’s west was winding down just after 6pm one Saturday late last month when the three hooded figures walked in, demanding cash and brandishing a hammer. Closed-circuit television shows one of the figures lunging with the hammer at the salon’s sole worker, a terrified 55-year-old woman who asked not to be named. The most disturbing aspect of the alleged crime was that the would-be attackers were aged just 11 and 12. Loading Across the city in Narellan Vale earlier that month, a group of teens and pre-teens allegedly swarmed a bottle shop, fighting staff and stealing cases of drinks. Five boys, aged between 12 and 15, were charged. “I couldn’t believe that was happening here, and they are so young,” said Santiago Wu, whose mother owns the store. The two incidents are tiny pieces in a mosaic of youth crime that police and experts say is seeing younger and younger children sucked from the fringes of the criminal world into violent criminal acts.



Youth crime rates across the state are mostly either stable or trending down – with the exception of murder and some forms of assault. Widespread use of encrypted phone apps and social media has allowed children to transition from misdemeanours into more serious violent criminal activity very swiftly, in some cases within weeks, experts say. The Australian Federal Police warned a federal parliamentary committee last month that “Australia is at the crossroads of a tsunami of youth crime” as online platforms and tools become more secret, sophisticated and popular. “It has certainly lowered the barrier to entry into organised crime,” says Detective acting Superintendent Jason Smith, acting head of Taskforce Falcon, the NSW Police squad charged with combating gang warfare and organised crime. Of the 530 people arrested by Taskforce Falcon so far this year, almost 50 have been children, the youngest being 14. Most are being paid peanuts. “Call it market forces or whatever you like, but the saturation of the market with young people willing to take on these roles has resulted in a drop in the amount of money being paid,” Smith says.



“We’ve got young people essentially throwing their life away for $500. “The problem is that there is a never-ending supply of young people who are willing to become involved. These people are being exploited by organised crime figures living overseas because they’re cheap, and they’re expendable.” Data collected by the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR) shows fewer young people are becoming entangled in the justice system than in recent decades. “Young people today are much less likely to commit crimes,” Jackie Fitzgerald, executive director of BOCSAR, says. It’s not accurate to speak in terms of a youth crime wave, despite the involvement of children in high-profile gangland hits, she says. The latest figures, which cover up to June this year, paint a nuanced picture of youth crime across the state.



Central and inner south Sydney have the state’s highest youth crime rate, while the eastern suburbs have a higher youth crime rate per person than areas such as south-west Sydney and Blacktown. This is because the city and the east are often entertainment or social destinations for young people and accessible by public transport, and the influx of young people – a tiny proportion of whom commit crimes – skews the numbers, BOCSAR says. “The trend is steady, and if there is a tsunami of youth crime it hasn’t shown up in the numbers yet,” Alex Simpson, an associate professor of criminology at Macquarie University, says. Fitzgerald says average youth crime rates in western and northern NSW are higher than almost all parts of Sydney. “Sydney gets a lot of focus, but there are communities outside Sydney that are dealing with levels of victimisation and offending [that] are much higher,” she says. “Many people in these communities have safety concerns that people in Sydney cannot relate to.”



The apparent uptick in the number of violent crimes, including murder and assault, which appeared to begin just before the COVID-19 pandemic, follows a decade of relatively few violent crimes being committed by young people. “Over the last five years we’ve seen roughly 10 young people charged with murder, and that’s higher than we were seeing a decade ago,” Fitzgerald says. “But if we expand our view, we can see that 20 years ago, there were many more kids being charged with murder.” The numbers of murders for which children are charged are small, usually fewer than a dozen a year, and therefore are barely visible in the overall crime statistics. Police arrest a teenage boy in Armidale. Youth crime rates in western and northern NSW are higher than in almost all parts of Sydney. Photo: Louise Kennerley But the recent spike is concerning criminologists who are unsure whether the spate of violent crimes by children is an anomaly before a return to lower levels of violence, or something new. “It is a post-COVID phenomena,” Associate Professor Garner Clancey, a criminologist at the University of Sydney, says. “On the back of the pandemic we’ve got a whole new landscape that’s been affected by the ‘manosphere’, kids spending more time online, kids being de-schooled, the rise of the ‘crimfluencers’. Their exposure to anti-government commentary, pornography, deep fakes is much higher. Our prevention strategies need to be recalibrated.

World.title: Hamish Blake is useless. And he’d like you to hire him for your next job
World.content:
Just a man and his truck: Hamish Blake goes all tradie in his new show, Unskilled Adult.

Having made a fortune from being a regular guy, Hamish Blake has decided it’s time to get some real skills. You have been warned.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Hamish Blake is a bit useless. To be clear, that’s not my view, it’s his own. “I’m well into my forties and after essentially just talking for a living, I’ve got to this point in my life and realised I don’t really have any other skills,” he says in the intro to his new series, Unskilled Adult. “I look around everywhere and see people who can do actual useful stuff, and I guess I’m a bit jealous. So I wondered, could that be me.” The reality series is essentially Blake’s effort to learn by doing. He sets up a business – UA (for unskilled adult) Enterprises – ropes in a couple of similarly useless mates, typically from the world of comedy, and sets about completing actual tasks for actual people for actual money. If they think he’s done a good job, they pay him in full. If not, they pay him what they think it’s worth. Related Article Australian TV Think you’ve got what it takes to be cast on reality TV? So did I At the end of it all, they get the job done, and he gets to be, well, a little less useless. Well, that’s the theory anyway. Let’s start with the basics, Hamish. Do you really think you’re an unskilled adult? “I think it is a fair description of me, and people who feel like me, usually from the entertainment industry,” he says. “If you don’t get taught those skills [building, sewing, cooking] as a kid or in your teenage years, I guess you can just grow up without them. So this was my attempt to force myself to learn things.” Masters’ apprentices: Becky Lucas and Hamish Blake attempt to learn carpentry, and manage to keep all fingers intact. Stan



Given enough time and resources, most people could probably learn to do most of the things Blake and co set about undertaking in the series – in the first four episodes, that includes basic carpentry, welding, panel beating and catering. But UA Enterprises appears to have a predisposition for the tight turnaround – jobs typically land on a Wednesday and need to be finished by close of business on Friday – though the budget for tools, gear and lunch is seemingly unlimited. Making the task that little bit harder is that Blake and his guest workers tend to spend most of the first day gasbagging, eating and shopping; day two is typically long, and day three is where the poop really hits the oscillating wind-blowing machine. “It does a strange thing to your head when you know you have to do it, you know it’s on you,” he says, attempting to explain the procrastination. “When you don’t know how to do something, it’s just human nature that your first port of call is to do a lot of things that aren’t the thing, to make you feel like you’re getting somewhere. So a lot of planning, a lot of wild ideas – you’re on with really funny people, so everyone’s having lots of ideas – but then it does slowly dawn on you that the people who have to do all these ideas are still us.” The customers know what they’re signing up for, of course – on the off-chance they don’t recognise Blake or any of his guests (including long-time collaborator and mate Andy Lee, Flight of the Conchords’ Bret McKenzie, Spelling Bee host Guy Montgomery, comedian Becky Lucas and the ubiquitous Sophie Monk), the camera crew is a dead giveaway. But Blake insists that the job at hand is real, there’s no safety blanket – stuff up that car repair and there isn’t a new car waiting for you – and the exchange of cash is genuinely based on how they assess the work. “I’ve talked to good effect, but I haven’t really done anything you would hang your hat on as a skill.” “It was important for us to keep it real because it is central to the idea of biting off more than you can chew, and genuinely having to figure your way out of it, and not being allowed to give up. And I think if you combine those elements that creates a great adventure.”



Blake describes himself as someone who talks for a living. In reality, he’s parlayed being a regular bloke – good-looking, affable, a bit of a doofus, always willing to poke fun at himself – into a very significant media career (radio, podcasts, TV, the occasional movie role) and a considerable fortune. “I’ve talked to good effect,” he concedes. “But I haven’t really done anything that you would hang your hat on as a skill.” Has doing this show changed that at all – have you actually acquired any real skills? “Shamefully not as much as I was hoping,” he says. He tells me that before they set out on this adventure, he and his co-creator and director Tim Bartley wondered if there was any risk that he might become too capable, and thus kill the gag. “I was like, ‘I guess we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it’,” Blake says. “And we have not come to that bridge.” He did, however, become passably good at “some wood stuff”, he boasts. I think they call it carpentry, I note.



“Yeah. I think if I had to go and be an apprentice in any field, I’d be a chippy. If they’d take [me].” So since doing this, have you done anything in your own actual life, like maybe put up a shelf at home? “I did something the other day, and the family was cheering,” he says. “My kids were like, ‘He’s done it! He’s done it! He’s not unskilled’.” For a moment, he struggles to recall what it was. And then it comes to him. “We live a couple of blocks from the beach in Sydney, and I’d left a jacket in the garage and the zip had rusted. I put WD40 on it, and I used pliers. ‘Look at that everyone, come gather round. Dad’s going to do something’.” Blake with long-time colleague and mate Andy Lee. Rebecca Hallas And that’s something you wouldn’t have been able to do before this show? “How would I know what to do?”



As much as he talks up his incompetence, in the episodes I’ve seen Blake and co actually manage to do a passable job of mastering the basics. I mean, you might not hire them to build your next house, but you might entrust them with a planter box. Given the enormous following he has with tradies, is there a risk that he might inadvertently be giving the impression that being a carpenter, a bricklayer, a chef, a welder is a breeze, that two days is all anyone needs to master it? To put it bluntly, might some people think their favourite multimillionaire is being just a bit disrespectful? The one person he didn’t rope in as a guest was his wife, Zoe Foster Blake. Instagram “Look, I did actually kind of wonder the same thing,” he says. “This is certainly not us going, ‘Wow, these trades are easy. Being a chef is easy. Being a carpenter is easy. Anyone can do it.’ It’s certainly not that. I know it takes years and years to acquire mastery of these skills. But what could you get done in a few days? Can you just learn anything? Related Article Review What to stream this week: Connie Britton’s weird comedy-thriller, plus five more picks “I suppose it’s just learning the bare, bare, bare basics. There’s no risk of any bricklayers looking at it and going, ‘Well, I can’t fault them. They’re the best bricklayers I’ve ever seen.’ It’s more that thrill – and I really enjoy this in life – of being a beginner. I think anyone who has any level of proficiency in any of these things would look at [our efforts] and go, ‘That’s about what I thought people with one day of experience would be able to achieve’.” Blake has shown some of the show to an electrician mate, whose response gave him confidence that no one is going to mistakenly conclude he is passing himself off as the real deal.

World.title: The wildcard NRL option that has suddenly emerged for Nathan Cleary
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion The wildcard NRL option that has suddenly emerged for Nathan Cleary Danny Weidler Sport columnist November 1, 2026 — 5:30am

November 1, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nathan Cleary is a free agent as of today – and no matter how remote the chance of him leaving Penrith, the Roosters have emerged as a wildcard to have a serious crack at landing the game’s No.1 target. A week ago, the Tricolours had barely given Cleary a second thought. But the shock split with their premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has opened the door. Nathan Cleary and Sam Walker are both free agents. Artwork: Stephen Kiprillis Cleary is expected to stay at Penrith, where he has played his entire career to date. But the Roosters will at least give him something to consider beyond the Panthers and the Chiefs. PNG will have to come up with an offer with far more to it than simply relying on the lure of $1.7 million a year tax-free. In another twist, there is a meeting scheduled for next week between Roosters supremo Nick Politis and Bulldogs general manager Phil Gould – with an obvious topic of discussion.



The Bulldogs are being pushed as a potential destination for Walker, who unexpectedly came onto the market after failing to reach an agreement over a contract extension at the Roosters. The Dogs are not biting as they have minimal cap room. It’s an interesting fit, as the Bulldogs’ best player this season was their own No.7, Lachlan Galvin. Loading But it’s possible to see Walker playing halfback alongside Galvin at five-eighth. They are both instinctual players and the Dogs would need to change the way they play to accommodate Walker. It would also need the Roosters to fund some of his contract. Ironically, Galvin was brought into Origin camp this year to replicate the off-the-cuff style of Maroons pair Cameron Munster and Walker in opposed sessions.



We’ve been told the most logical fit for Walker – the Cowboys, as part of a swap with Tom Dearden – is too complicated. Maybe that’s because Dearden’s partner, Millie, will be moving to Townsville soon after the pair had their first baby recently. Dearden is tipped to honour the next year of his deal and then look at joining a Sydney club in 2028, despite being contracted at the Cowboys until the end of 2029. A club swap between Queensland Origin teammates Tom Dearden and Sam Walker appears highly unlikely. Getty As for Cleary, he is open to offers. As far as we can establish, he has not instructed his manager to tell the Roosters or Chiefs he is not interested. We know PNG are still keen because their general manager, Michael Chammas, has told the Roosters he has not been making a sneaky play for Walker.



Cleary has said he is not motivated by money. Chammas will need to be creative to get his man. Conservatively, with third-party payments, Cleary stands to clear about $2.5 million a year if he signs with the Chiefs. The Panthers are operating on a budget of about $1.7 million on the cap to retain him. Why Roosters and Walker fell out of love The Roosters’ break-up with Walker finished with a message of support from Nick Politis to the halfback. Politis is ruthless, but big-hearted when it comes to his players. However, there has long been an uneasy relationship between the Walker camp and the club he loves.



In a phone call with Politis, Walker said he was grateful for everything he has had at the Roosters. Politis told Walker he would be there to help him in the future. Today, he is trying to help him out the door. How did we get here? There were problems early. At the start of the year, some of Walker’s key advisers were ringing around and asking if the Roosters were interested in Nathan Cleary. Roosters chairman Nick Politis is one of the game’s most influential figures. NRL They were jumping at shadows at the time, and it was an indication that there was a lack of trust between Walker’s team and the Roosters. The Roosters have always been wary of Sam’s dad, Ben Walker. And they have preferred dealing with Steve Gillis, the back-up agent for Walker behind Clinton Schifcofske, his No.1 man. It was Gillis who delivered the news to Politis that Walker wanted extra money.



Complicating the issue was that the Roosters were one of the clubs sounded out earlier in the year by representatives of Tom Dearden, who wanted to see if they could accommodate their client if he moved to Sydney to be with his partner. Then there was the fact that veteran halfback Daly Cherry-Evans had been brought in for 2026 to either help or actually run the side. Sam Walker is on his way out of the Roosters. Jessica Hromas All of this can impact a player’s ego. And those who love Walker took note. Walker wanted to play on the right side of the field, traditionally the domain of the halfback. There are some who thought he was actually better suited to the five-eighth role. All of this has been swirling around in the background.



Throw in the club’s uneasy relationship with Ben Walker, and maybe then you can see why the relationship started to break down and where the demand for more dollars came from. The Roosters say they respected Walker. They made their biggest offer, $4.2 million over three years. That is the ultimate show of respect. The Roosters put years of development into Walker. They stood by him through injury and felt they deserved loyalty and perhaps a bit less of the financial demands. They didn’t like it when, a few weeks back, Walker addressed key members of the recruitment team and told them he wanted to put talks on hold. He didn’t even entertain the idea of a negotiation at that time. Remember, the Roosters also backed Walker when the coaching of Cooper Cronk didn’t seem to gel with the young seven. Those spot fires can be put out, but they can reignite when big decisions need to be made.



Everything went up in flames last week. It was not entirely unexpected, but few predicted it. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Could Sam Walker end up at the Rabbitohs? Can the Raiders still keep Hudson Young? Politis had a sense it would erupt. He was reminding people what happened with Latrell Mitchell in 2019 when a contract stand-off led to him departing for South Sydney. Politis was desperately trying to avoid a repeat. Politis is the most loyal individual you can meet in football. But cross him, and you will not be forgiven easily. The club might be flashy on the outside, but it’s built on Politis’ old-school ethos. At the core of Trent Robinson’s coaching is a line he picked up from famous American basketball coach Pat Riley. It surrounds the leadership concept of the “Disease of Me”, which he raised in his book, The Winner Within: A Life Plan for Team Players.



The term describes how players become overly focused on personal glory. Riley famously summarised the danger with the maxim, “The Disease of Me always results in the Defeat of Us.” It’s what Robinson drums into his players. The coach didn’t flinch when Walker made his decision. He is excited by the challenge ahead. Robinson keeps fresh through the cycle of talent and the challenge of getting the best out of the next crop. He won’t cop any player who doesn’t subscribe to the idea of team first. We are not saying Walker is selfish. We are just offering an insight into Robinson’s philosophy. Sam’s his own man A final word on Sam Walker.



It’s hard not to have a soft spot for him. The Roosters players still care about him, and he is a decent person. In camp with Australia’s World Cup squad in Townsville, he was seen having a deep chat with James Tedesco on the balcony of the Roosters captain’s hotel room. Nine reporter Adam Jackson said he saw them chatting for 30 minutes at the peak of the dramas last week. Kangaroos management also put players and staff around Walker, but he seemed to be fine. Walker lives down the road from me and I often bump into him at local cafés. He always has time for people. As flamboyant as he is as a footballer, he is a quiet person.



He comes across as a classic introverted extrovert. He is close to his family, loves the races and appears to love his football. He is very much his own person. He would have discussed his final contract call with his long-term partner Bella, who is the sister of retired NRL star Corey Allan. Sam Walker savoured the Roosters premiership win with Angus Crichton in the dressing rooms. Getty Images Walker goes out of his way to be friendly and welcoming. I found him fascinating after the grand final. He was the least animated and emotional player in the Roosters side. He was keen to get off the ground and into the dressing room to be with his people. He gave off the impression he had just won a regular NRL round 16 game against the Titans rather than a premiership.



Maybe he knew something we didn’t. Chiefs inspector Young Hudson Young is likely to be in Port Moresby this week to decide whether to make PNG his new home – and he can thank Sam Walker for taking the media heat off him after the Raiders withdrew their four-year $4.4 million offer. Raiders backrower Hudson Young suffered a season-ending injury in Canberra’s round 20 win over South Sydney. NRL Imagery There is plenty to the Young situation. At the core of it is the Achilles injury that ended his 2026 season. That prevented him from visiting PNG at a time when Canberra had given him permission to go.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 ‘We stopped Jarryd Hayne from getting stabbed in jail’: Fainu reveals plot against former Eels star Had he toured the Chiefs’ facilities then, he could have given the Raiders an answer. He is happy with the $900,000 per year deal offered by the Chiefs and won’t haggle. But he needs to see Port Moresby first-hand. In the background, Young has gone through a relationship breakdown, and has also had itchy feet when it comes to living in Canberra. A change of scenery has been on his mind. There have been suggestions that he is not happy with the make-up of the Raiders pack.



The truth is that, as a senior player, he is always talking to coach Ricky Stuart about the roster. Young has nothing but love for the Raiders, but he may need a new environment to keep him focused and engaged in the final years of his playing career. What is certain is that he will want to have his best year in the NRL when he returns from injury next season. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Remembering the dead, in all their glory and their failings
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion Remembering the dead, in all their glory and their failings

Jane E Sullivan November 1, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the Western Christian calendar tomorrow – 2 November – is All Souls’ Day. It is the day the church remembers the souls of the faithful departed. All Souls’ Day follows All Saints’ Day, and before it the preparatory All Hallows’ Eve on 31 October. It concludes a time of commemoration and thanksgiving. Saint Augustine of Hippo lived a life of sin before his conversion, famously asking to be delivered from temptation – but just not yet. “Saints” in early Christian tradition was a general and inclusive term for all members of the faith community. Over time customary usage came to refer to a rarefied group of exceptional individuals, officially recognised by the church. In the name of Christ, for the sake of the faith these believers risked and often lost limb or life, completed miraculous feats or led exemplary lives. Even though many saints had significant character flaws and histories of questionable behaviours, such as Saint Paul and Saint Augustine, most of us won’t make it into this venerated company. We are, however, destined to become souls. And there’s something democratic about the church making space to honour all her dead.



Whether they were churched or unchurched, sincerely remembering our dead loved ones can be complicated. Not only because it prompts thoughts of our mortality but because true remembrance means recognising the whole person. After all, the dead are human. And humans are complex. People come with sparkling brilliance as well as glaring blemishes. Death doesn’t automatically transform someone into a saint. Death doesn’t erase character faults or bad actions. But critiquing our dead loved ones feels disloyal, unfair and uncomfortable. Indeed, there are strong social conventions not to speak ill of the dead. They have no right of reply. A genuine remembrance, however, involves integrating a person’s contradictions into our memory. It means putting their foibles and failures, their struggles and vulnerabilities, alongside their virtues, their triumphs, and what made them lovable. After all in life we accommodated the whole person into our hearts. It’s striking that often for mourners the most beneficial eulogies portray the real person. As we remember our dead, inevitably our relationship with them comes into focus. Our own merits and shortcomings are seen, revealed in the context and history of the relationship. That’s fair enough, honest recollection cuts both ways. Our minds may race back to the moments when our character flaws got in the way, or when we failed them in some big or little matter. Past hurts can outlive their perpetrator. Relationship tensions may remain unresolved, and words left unspoken. Regret, shame and plain old sadness may form parts of our memory. Living with such feelings is difficult. Reality is like that. Hopefully, the unsettling parts in our relationships with the dead are held together with feelings of happiness, gratitude, and contentment.



As we commemorate All Souls’ Day, let’s truly remember our loved ones. Who knows, perhaps on a future All Souls’ Day, someone will remember us, the exquisitely human us. Jane E Sullivan lives and worships in Melbourne.

World.title: How the ‘hot divorcee’ trope is shaping how women travel now
World.content:
Reviews & adviceTravel tips How the ‘hot divorcee’ trope is shaping how women travel now Kathryn Madden November 1, 2026 — 5:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In the early European summer, on the glittering peninsula of Cap d’Antibes, I found myself reclining on a sun lounger next to two 40-year-old women from Melbourne. One was in a long-term relationship, the other was newly single and, together, they were taking a two-week jaunt along the French Riviera before a final stop in Paris for shopping, pain au chocolat and dinner at Hotel Costes. “I’d rather travel with a girlfriend than my partner; we’re so much more aligned,” said the former, her eyes glimmering behind huge Dior sunglasses. Women holidaying with likeminded women or alone often head to destinations that are “golf course free”. Getty Images “Would I spend my day doing this with a man?” asked the other, gesturing towards her goblet of spritz, Sally Hepworth novel and the sweep of lapis-blue sea. Unknowingly, the pair were embarking on a Hot Divorcee Summer, the rising cultural trend centred on women’s radical freedom and the pleasures of putting oneself first. After a stay at Hotel Belles Rives, the legendary art deco haunt in Juan-les-Pins, they were headed for the beach clubs of St Tropez, the perfumeries of Grasse and “nowhere with a golf course”.



Figurative rather than literal, Hot Divorcee Summer is less about marital status than a mood and an energy: untethered, unbothered and unencumbered by a man’s needs or opinions (or anyone’s needs and opinions for that matter, perhaps for the first time in a woman’s life). 



She’s equally at liberty, though, to slip to the hotel spa for a skin-tightening treatment. Self-indulgence is a prerequisite for the Hot Divorcee, but the pleasures are entirely self-prescribed: the best hotel suite, a faintly ridiculous wellness ritual, a pottery class that would have been vetoed by every previous travel companion. L’Aventure hotel Paris has an on-site nightclub so you can make a night of it. “This is about women seizing the moment and not waiting for someone else to be available to experience the places they want to go,” says Jules Perowne, founder and chief executive of global luxury travel communications consultancy Perowne International. Those places span continents, cultures and price points, but all offer a taste of the good life in one form or another. Take the island of Sardinia, which has something of a split personality. Costa Smeralda in the north-east has been an exclusive summer playground since the 1960s, one where megayachts jostle for space in the marinas and old money meets Hollywood meets Silicon Valley over long lunches and DJ sets. Yet beyond that enclave it’s rugged and rural, a succession of sugar-white beaches where Italian families practise the art of dolce far niente.



For the Hot Divorcee, this makes for an appealing combination: a boat trip through secluded coves on waters so vivid they render filters redundant; languid hours under a beach umbrella; bowls of homemade pasta and scoops of dripping gelato; an evening dressed up for dinner in Porto Cervo; a stay somewhere special, like Cala di Volpe, the rustically lavish icon that once starred in a Bond film (The Spy Who Loved Me), or the less flashy Le Dune Piscinas eco resort. In 2027, Rocco Forte Costa Smeralda and Mandarin Oriental will both open on the north-east coast, too. Or she might venture inland, where Sardinia’s famously long-lived nonnas offer ageing advice to rival any wellness or longevity retreat. An important caveat: Hot Divorcee Summer is not a self-improvement exercise. Eating, praying and loving are all welcome, but they have to happen organically, and there’s no obligation to return home transformed. Nor is it a traditional girls’ trip with shared itineraries, group decisions and expectations of collective revelry. If partying is on the agenda, it leans much more sophisticated than a rhinestone-crusted hen’s do or big, boisterous birthday. No organised fun, no matching outfits, no tiaras, no bottles announced with sparklers. To that end, L’Aventure and Le Bus Palladium, two recently opened five-star boutique hotels in Paris, boast louche underground nightclubs and live music venues – so you can make a night of it or not, without having to organise a ride home.



The new Nomade Temple in Madrid was built around experiences, too, with a speakeasy and club inspired by the city’s 1980s cultural awakening, along with a daily roster of workshops and events designed to bring people together: psychedelic breathwork sessions, social saunas, run clubs, sketch classes, vermouth and flamenco afternoons. The restaurant at Hotel Belle Rives in Juan-les-Pins, south-easterm France, offers waterfront dining. For Perowne, the Hot Divorcee Summer calls for destinations where being alone feels unremarkable. “The hotels getting it right understand that a woman travelling solo does not want to be tucked into a corner table with a book,” she explains. “At Storfjord Hotel in Norway, the new Boathouse restaurant has no tables for one. Everyone sits at a single long table while the chef cooks over open flames, and dinner becomes a supper party. At Wildland’s Killiehuntly Farmhouse in Scotland there’s no room service and no menu. Guests eat together, whatever the cook has made from the estate that day. You arrive a stranger and leave having had the best conversation of your year.” Shifts in the cultural landscape make this particular brand of women’s travel especially appealing. In Australia, 49,158 divorces were granted in 2025, a 4 per cent increase from 2024, and the average female divorcee is 44, with decades of adventures still ahead of her. Throw in the Great Wealth Transfer, in which it’s expected up to $5.4 trillion will pass between Australian generations over the next two decades – much of it into the pockets and wallets of Gen X and Millennials – and Hot Divorcee Summer begins to look like more than a buzzy catchphrase.



Meanwhile, women are questioning the assumption that romantic relationships should be the organising principle of their lives; “decentring men” has become a rallying cry. In the US, Pew Research Centre found that just 35 per cent of single women were actively looking for dates or a relationship. Instead, their next great romance may be with a place. In April 2026, Google reported that search interest in “solo travel” had hit an all-time high, and “women solo travel” was at a 15-year peak. In a recent survey by the company Solo Female Travelers, 85 per cent of respondents cited freedom and flexibility as a reason for travelling alone, while 76 per cent wanted time to relax, indulge and prioritise themselves. Cala di Volpe on the island of Sardinia, Italy, once starred in a Bond film and is the perfect venue for an exclusive summer stay. “Ever since MONA opened in Hobart, I’d always wanted to go with a partner,” says Megan McTavish, a social strategist from the Gold Coast. “I never went with my ex-husband, but still hoped I’d find someone to go with while dating. Then one day I woke up and thought, ‘What am I waiting around for?’ I looked at the money I’d saved and asked myself what I’d do if I was with a man. I would have booked a fancy hotel and a bougie, romantic meal. So I decided to do it myself, after 15 years of waiting.” After a few hours browsing the gallery at her own pace, McTavish, 41, took herself to lunch at avant-garde fine-diner Faro. “It was invigorating,” she says. “I got the degustation and focused on every morsel, with no awkward conversation with whoever would have been sitting opposite me.”



Since then, McTavish has taken herself to Melbourne solo for martinis and chocolate mousse at Maison Batard, followed by a facial at Mecca and a luxurious sleep in a king bed at 1Hotel, as well as to Byron Bay. “These trips make life feel like it’s worth living,” says McTavish, noting that the idea of a holiday romance or catching the male gaze doesn’t register for her. “I’m celibate.” One day, she hopes to visit Malta and the Maldives – “I really want to go and take those romantic couples photos by myself” – but as a single mother of one, she’s content for now with an unapologetic mini-break. “There’s a follow-on effect from doing this, even if it’s just a two-day trip that you’ve saved and budgeted for,” says McTavish. “A lot of women have subconsciously learnt to accept crumbs in our lives, so this is about setting the bar high for ourselves. On the surface it might look like a lot of fancy lunches and beauty treatments, but it’s also about treating yourself so well that you’ll never accept the bare minimum or mistreatment from anyone else.” While the Hot Divorcee Summer was enjoying its debut season, another social trend was gathering momentum: the Year of the Hobby, a renewed enthusiasm for pursuits that have little to do with work or productivity.



The two cultural currents intersect in a Venn diagram, an overlap populated by retreats for learning, making and doing, set against beautiful, far-flung backdrops. Think textile-making in Guatemala, the dyeing technique of shibori in Japan and basket-weaving in Spain’s Mallorca, all led by local artisans via Thread Caravan. Or the Marnie Rays women’s surf retreat in Ericeira, Portugal, or sensory immersion meets contemporary arts with Bonfire in Iceland. The speakeasy-style Rose Bar at Delano Miami Beach. Perhaps the most resonant subcategory here is the reading retreat, because what says “I’m putting myself first” like sun-lounging in silence with a group of like-minded women, tearing through pages of Nancy Mitford, Elizabeth Strout or whichever author sets your imagination alight? Megan Christopher founded Ladies Who Lit, a travelling book club, three years ago and now hosts up to 75 retreats in villas, castles, ranches and even yachts across 15 countries every year. Each retreat revolves around a loose schedule of reading, conversation and leisurely meals, with optional activities and plenty of quiet time – although a recent retreat in Seville, Spain, culminated in a raucous night of karaoke. “Obviously, the women who come on our retreats are readers, but I think what they’re actually drawn to is the time and space we give them to just be them,” says Christopher. “They’re not somebody’s wife; they’re not somebody’s mum. They don’t need to think about what they’re having for dinner, or if the kids’ uniforms have been washed. Once we remove all those elements, they get a chance to not only relax but to be themselves, potentially for the first time ever as an adult.”



For 2027, the line-up includes the first Australian retreat in the Byron Bay hinterland – set in the Californian-cool country estate Sun Ranch – and a cowboy-themed one in Vancouver, Canada. Christopher says newly divorced or separated women comprise a significant subset of the Ladies Who Lit community. “There’s probably at least one guest on every trip who’s in that situation,” she adds. Related Article Tours Women-only travel boom continues with launch of new trips Of course, there’s an inherent contradiction in the Hot Divorcee label. Taken literally, it puts a gloss on something that, for most women, is anything but glamorous. Divorce can take an enormous emotional and financial toll, and the freedom to spend lavishly on a holiday is hardly universal. You needn’t be rich to partake, countered comedian Tatty Macleod when breaking down the trend. “Ideally, it’s champagne in the Med, but if it’s cava in a paddling pool that will also do, babe.”



What a Hot Divorcee Summer does offer, regardless of age, relationship status or circumstance, is an invitation not to take oneself too seriously, a healthy disregard for convention, a zest for growing older and a reframing of what endings can mean. And it can restore a sense of possibility. Never mind the giant hat, that’s the greatest souvenir of all. NEW STAYS THAT CAPTURE THE DIVORCEE SUMMER SPIRIT DELANO, MIAMI BEACH, US

Once the heart of South Beach’s 1990s social scene, the legendary Delano has emerged from a six-year renovation with its glamour intact but its priorities slightly rearranged. Wellness has joined the party, without quite replacing it. From $799 a night. See delanohotels.com/miami-beach

CASA BONAVITA, ATTARD, MALTA

The Mediterranean island’s most stylish new stay features unabashedly pretty interiors (the Folly suite is the stuff of slumber party dreams) and the warmth of a family home. It’s the kind of place where company might be found without being sought. From $895 a night. See casabonavita.com

CASA MARGARITA GUEST HOUSE, MEXICO CITY, MEXICO

Originally the home of Mexican writer Margarita Quijano – who hosted salons for leading thinkers, particularly women – this restored 1902 mansion feels fitting for the independently minded. Stay for the book clubs and poetry gatherings, and the lively cafes, restaurants and galleries on the doorstep. From $500 a night. See casamargaritamexico.com





THE WHALE, NAROOMA, NSW

This new coastal motel by Merivale has all the makings of a free-spirited escape when an overseas jaunt isn’t on the cards: boho design, a retro magnesium pool, bespoke vinyl selection and a Queen Chow restaurant on site. From $440 a night. See merivale.com

The Whale is a new coastal hotel by Merivale in the NSW South Coast town of Narooma. THE PACKING LIST Related Article Travel tips Lonely Planet’s 20 expert tips for solo women travellers A vintage silk scarf

Tied around the neck or knotted under the chin for boat rides.

A copy of Strangers by Belle Burden

The year’s most talked-about divorce memoir.

An exceptionally good black one-piece swimsuit

The kind that will last for the next 10 summers. See Eres or Canvs Bottega.

A wide-brimmed sunhat

Inconvenient on aeroplanes, excellent everywhere else.

Venetian slippers

For making an otherwise ordinary outfit look like something worn by an eccentric Italian aristocrat. See Piedaterre or Le Monde Beryl.

A repurposed silver cigarette case

Inside: a hotel matchbook and the telephone number of an admirer, scrawled on a receipt.

A Mary Poppins bag

To house all of the above. It could be a raffia basket picked up at a local market, a canvas tote from Hotel Il Pellicano or a battered Goyard Saint Louis GM.

World.title: I’m 64 with just $93,000 in super. Should I add to it before retiring?
World.content:
November 1, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’m 64, a self-employed freelance creative writer, own my home, and have $93,000 in super, $110,000 in my access account and $170,000 in savings. I intend to keep working, as I love my work, but I don’t expect any massive income from that – and it will also drop off as I age. It’s been pretty difficult to get to this point, and it’s taken many sacrifices, but owning my own home is fantastic. I will reach pension age in August 2029. To maximise my pension and associated benefits, should I make the maximum $32,500 super contribution, plus the $23,000 of available catch-up contribution, or would I be better keeping that money in the bank? Adding more into your super can leave you better off in retirement, but it depends on your level of income. Simon Letch Firstly, well done on what you’ve achieved. Building this level of financial security on the variable income that often comes with freelance creative work is impressive. The next point to note is that money inside or outside of super doesn’t make a great deal of difference to your age pension entitlement. Either way this wealth will be included in the asset and income test, and the calculation methodology is usually identical.



The advisability of making tax-deductible super contributions, including the catch-up contributions, depends on your level of taxable income. Money that you send to super as a concessional contribution is taxed at 15 per cent when it arrives in the fund. For you to get a benefit therefore, your personal tax rate must be greater than this. There is no tax payable on your first $18,200, and then 17 per cent is payable from their up to $45,000 (inclusive of Medicare levy). Meaningful gains through tax-deductible super contributions therefore don’t accrue until your income is above $45,000. This does not mean you shouldn’t contribute to super. It is likely that the returns in super will be better than bank interest. But it may be that making after-tax contributions (non-concessional in super jargon), produces a better result for you. And the limits on these types of contributions are much more generous. My wife and I are both retired with account-based pensions and are contemplating moving from our large, high maintenance home into a more suitable abode. This will either require purchasing land and building anew or purchasing an existing dwelling and undertaking major renovations. Regardless, our preferred approach is to purchase and build/renovate first, then sell and move in when ready. Given the only funds to which we have access are in our account-based pensions, is there a cost-effective way of funding this swap without using an expensive bridging loan or having the majority of proceeds of the sale locked out of super?



Depending on the amounts involved, potentially you could withdraw monies out of super, and then replenish using the downsizer provisions. Downsizer contributions require that the home you are selling has been yours for at least 10 years. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Does bequeathing my shares in my will incur capital gains tax? Noel Whittaker Money columnist You can contribute $300,000 per person through this mechanism. Importantly, there is no age limit on downsizer contributions, though you can only do this once in your lifetime. If you are under 75 years of age when you sell your current home, you may also be able to get money back into super via non-concessional contributions. Spreading the contributions over a couple of financial years, you could potentially get up to $520,000 each back into super and then create new account-based pensions. Alternatively, it may be that bridging loan costs are just one of the many costs that need to be factored into this transaction.



Paul Benson is a Certified Financial Planner at Guidance Financial Services – Retirement Planning specialists.
